title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT
abstract: Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS (p = 0.04)...

title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

title: Improved Training of Strong Stochastic Flow Maps
abstract: Stochastic flow maps promise few-step sampling of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) by learning to directly jump between times along the solution path, yet training these models to learn this solution map remains difficult. The primary obstacle is the Brownian path itself: it is an infinite-dimensional object which needs to be passed to the neural network and is nowhere differentiable, which makes the implementation of derivative-based losses that power the state-of-the-art deterministic flow maps just out of reach. We identify two core design principles which address these issues: a) represent the Brownian path with a basis which carries higher-order local information, and b) train with an objective that forces the network to use the full representation of the path, not just the first order. To address this, we leverage the shifted Legendre polynomial expansion with a Wong-Zakai styled objective, unlocking derivative-based losses. Finally, we propose a recipe for fine-tuning large pre-trained flow models into strong stochastic flow maps. We ablate through this design space on several toy problems and use our findings to transform a large flow model into a strong stochastic flow map on ImageNet, achieving roughly a three-fold improvement in FD-DINOv2 over SSFM at four NFE.

title: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
abstract: Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi-agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. We study repeated retraining in multi-agent performative prediction and identify a spectral threshold that separates stable learning from worst-case learning obstruction. Prior work often collapses cross-agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix $Γ$, which records how strongly one agent's deployment can move another agent's best response, defined from per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local-information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order $1/(ρ(Γ)-1)$. Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.

Ahmed Mahrous

headings: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
4 The Reduction: From Retraining Dynamics to $\Gamma$
5 Subcritical Regime: Contraction and Bounded Excess Loss
body_start:
Abstract

Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi-agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. We study repeated retraining in multi-agent performative prediction and identify a spectral threshold that separates stable learning from worst-case learning obstruction. Prior work often collapses cross-agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix $\Gamma$ , which records how strongly one agent’s deployment can move another agent’s best response, defined from per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local-information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order $1/(\rho(\Gamma)-1)$ . Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.

## 1 Introduction

Many learning systems, once deployed, change the environment that later generates their training data. A credit scoring model can change how applicants behave; an algorithmic trading strategy can move the price data on which future strategies are trained. This feedback effect is the focus of performative prediction. Existing theory largely studies the case of one learner facing the consequences of its own deployment. Many real systems, however, contain multiple learners whose deployments jointly shape the environment.

The multi-agent setting is not simply a larger version of the single-agent problem; it introduces different difficulties. Feedback can travel across agents: one agent’s deployment changes the data distribution, which changes another agent’s retraining problem, which may itself affect the data distribution or other agents. Stability therefore depends not only on the overall strength of performativity, but also on how feedback is routed through the agent network.

We ask whether there is a general threshold separating stable multi-agent performative learning from unavoidable learning failure. When does repeated retraining converge to a stable equilibrium?

We answer this question through a reflexivity matrix $\Gamma$ with entries $\Gamma_{ij}:=a_{ij}/\mu_{i}$ , measuring how strongly agent $j$ ’s deployment can move agent $i$ ’s best response, after normalizing by the curvature of agent $i$ ’s objective. Thus $\Gamma$ records who affects whom, and how strongly, in the performative feedback network.

Our main result is a phase transition at $\rho(\Gamma)=1$ , where $\rho(\Gamma)$ is the spectral radius of $\Gamma$ . This quantity captures the largest asymptotic amplification factor of the feedback network. If $\rho(\Gamma)<1$ , cross-agent feedback dissipates: repeated retraining is a contraction in a Perron–Frobenius weighted norm, converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, and incurs bounded cumulative excess loss. Above the threshold, this positive guarantee cannot be extended. We construct supercritical systems in which every decentralized local-information learner suffers cumulative loss that grows linearly with time, regardless of the retraining rule. Under sensitivity and curvature assumptions, the spectral radius of the reflexivity matrix gives a sharp boundary for general stability guarantees: below one, all systems satisfying our assumptions contract, while above one, there exist supercritical systems for which decentralized learning incurs linear cumulative loss.

## Contributions.

First, we introduce the reflexivity matrix $\Gamma$ , a nonnegative matrix whose entry $\Gamma_{ij}$ records how strongly agent $j$ ’s deployment can move agent $i$ ’s best response, as determined by per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature constants. We prove an entrywise best-response sensitivity bound that reduces nonlinear retraining dynamics with general strongly convex losses to a spectral comparison through $\Gamma$ , making Perron–Frobenius theory available. Second, we prove the subcritical side of the threshold: if $\rho(\Gamma)<1$ , repeated retraining is a contraction in a Perron–Frobenius weighted norm, yielding a unique performatively stable equilibrium, geometric convergence from any initialization, and cumulative dynamic excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Third, we prove the supercritical side: for a rank-one family with $\rho(\Gamma)=1+\varepsilon$ , every decentralized local-information learner incurs cumulative excess loss $\Omega(\Delta^{2}T)$ over horizons $T=O(1/\varepsilon)$ . Together, these results identify $\rho(\Gamma)=1$ as a boundary for general stability guarantees under primitive gradient-sensitivity and curvature assumptions, and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work when $k=1$ .

## 2 Related Work

This paper draws on three lines of research. The first is the single-agent theory of performative prediction, which introduces the framework we extend. The second is the multi-agent theory of performative prediction and decision-dependent games, which is where our contribution is most directly positioned. The third is the combined tradition of spectral methods for network games and statistical lower bound techniques, from which we import two standard technical tools.

## Performative prediction.

Perdomo et al. (2020) introduced performative prediction in a single-agent setting, formalizing performative stability and convergence of repeated retraining under sensitivity conditions. Subsequent work largely retained this single-agent viewpoint while extending the framework to stochastic, causal, nonconvex, and sequential settings (Mendler-Dünner et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2022; Hardt et al., 2022; Mofakhami et al., 2023; Mandal et al., 2023). Closest to our threshold result, Anagnostides et al. (2026) established hardness and lower bounds at the single-agent scalar threshold. We depart from this line by studying decentralized multi-agent retraining, where performative feedback is cross-agent and the scalar threshold is replaced by the spectral condition $\rho(\Gamma)=1$ .

## Multi-agent performativity.

The multi-agent extension is the most direct predecessor of our work, and the literature divides into three strands.

The first establishes scalar contraction conditions for convergence. Narang et al. (2023) formalized $n$ -player performative prediction with a scalar aggregate threshold $\rho<1$ , and analogous scalar conditions appear in cooperative consensus learning (Li et al., 2022), decentralized games with coupled constraints (Yan and Cao, 2024), and a Wasserstein-free variant (Zhong et al., 2025). We depart from this strand on two axes. We replace the scalar aggregate with a matrix $\Gamma$ that preserves per-agent-pair feedback, and we pair the upper bound with a worst-case information-theoretic lower bound above the threshold.

The second develops spectral characterizations in special models. Wang et al. (2023) derived a necessary-and-sufficient spectral condition for a linear-quadratic mean-squared-error model on multiplex networks. Their spectral object is a weighted adjacency matrix with exogenous structure, and the condition is specific to the linear-quadratic model. Our $\Gamma$ is built from primitive per-agent quantities, applies to general strongly convex losses, and is paired with a lower bound.

The third identifies dynamical phase transitions. Piliouras and Yu (2023) proved a transition from stability to Li–Yorke chaos as update aggressiveness grows under scalar aggregate influence. Their threshold is dynamical and concerns the long-run behavior of specific update rules; ours is information-theoretic and applies to every decentralized local-information learner. Farina and Perdomo (2026) show that, for bounded losses, no-regret online learning yields approximate performative stability of a mixture over joint deployment histories, without regularity assumptions on the distribution maps. Our subcritical result guarantees geometric convergence of the last retraining iterate to a unique performatively stable equilibrium under curvature and sensitivity assumptions.

## Spectral methods and lower bounds.

Two technical traditions supply tools used in our analysis without serving as competing frameworks. Spectral conditions for equilibrium uniqueness and stability are well established in network games (Ballester et al., 2006; Bramoullé et al., 2014; Parise and Ozdaglar, 2019), where the spectral radius governs payoff coupling: agent $j$ ’s action enters agent $i$ ’s utility directly. In our setting, it governs distributional feedback through $D(w)$ , and $\Gamma$ is built from gradient sensitivities and curvature constants rather than payoff coefficients. Our lower bound uses the two-point method (Tsybakov, 2009); recent extensions to interactive (Chen et al., 2024) and decision-dependent (Cutler et al., 2024) settings do not cover our performative learning setting. Our construction is tailored to multi-agent performative feedback over a finite horizon.

## 3 Model

This section specifies the multi-agent performative prediction model used throughout the paper. We describe the agents, their objectives, the dynamics of repeated retraining, and the assumptions that underlie the reduction of Section 4.

There are $k$ agents. Each agent $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ chooses a deployment $w_{i}$ from a feasible set $\mathcal{W}_{i}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}$ . The joint deployment profile is $w:=(w_{1},\dots,w_{k})\in\mathcal{W}:=\mathcal{W}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{W}_{k}$ .
The deployed profile induces a shared endogenous distribution $D(w)$ over observations $z\in\mathcal{Z}$ . This distribution represents the data-generating process that all agents face after the profile $w$ has been deployed. The dependence of $D$ on $w$ captures the performative nature of the system: the environment that agents observe is shaped by their own collective actions.

Each agent $i$ has a loss function $\ell_{i}:\mathcal{W}_{i}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ and aims to minimize its performative risk

 $F_{i}(u_{i};w)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{z\sim D(w)}\big[\ell_{i}(u_{i};z)\big].$ 

(1)

The two arguments of $F_{i}$ play distinct roles. The first, $u_{i}$ , is the candidate action optimized by agent $i$ . The second, $w$ , is the deployed profile that determines the environment through $D(w)$ . Retraining couples these roles by replacing the deployed profile with agents’ optimized actions.

For each agent $i$ and each deployed profile $w$ , the best response is

 $B_{i}(w)\;:=\;\argmin_{u_{i}\in\mathcal{W}_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i};w).$ 

(2)

Assumption 1 below ensures that this minimizer exists and is unique. The joint best-response map is $B(w):=\big(B_{1}(w),\dots,B_{k}(w)\big)$ .
An equilibrium of the system is a profile that is consistent with every agent’s best response.

Definition 1 (Performatively stable equilibrium).

A profile $w^{\star}\in\mathcal{W}$ is a performatively stable equilibrium if $w^{\star}=B(w^{\star})$ .

At a performatively stable equilibrium, each agent’s deployed action is optimal for the distribution induced by the joint deployment. Existence of such an equilibrium is not assumed; it is derived in Section 5 as a consequence of the spectral condition on the reflexivity matrix.

We study the repeated retraining dynamics in which every agent simultaneously replaces its current deployment with its best response,

 $w_{t+1}=B(w_{t}),\qquad t=0,1,2,\dots,$ 

(3)

with initialization $w_{0}\in\mathcal{W}$ . The central question of the paper is when the sequence $\{w_{t}\}$ converges to a performatively stable equilibrium, and when convergence fails.

## Main assumptions.

Three assumptions are used throughout the paper. The first two are local to individual agents and enter the reduction of Section 4. The third is a mild regularity condition on the feasible sets that allows application of Banach’s fixed-point theorem.

Assumption 1 (Strong convexity in own action).

For each agent $i$ and every fixed deployed profile $w\in\mathcal{W}$ , the map $u_{i}\mapsto F_{i}(u_{i};w)$ is $\mu_{i}$ -strongly convex on $\mathcal{W}_{i}$ , with $\mu_{i}>0$ .

Strong convexity makes $B_{i}(w)$ unique and quantifies agent $i$ ’s resistance to gradient perturbations. Larger $\mu_{i}$ means that the best response is less sensitive to changes in the data distribution.

Assumption 2 (Gradient sensitivity to the deployed profile).

For each $i$ , $F_{i}$ is continuously differentiable in $u_{i}$ , and there exist nonnegative constants $a_{ij}\geq 0$ for all $i,j\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that for every agent $i$ , every candidate action $u_{i}\in\mathcal{W}_{i}$ , and every pair of deployed profiles $w,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}$ ,

 $\|\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i};w)-\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i};w^{\prime})\|\;\leq\;\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{ij}\,\|w_{j}-w_{j}^{\prime}\|.$ 

Gradient sensitivity quantifies how a change in the deployed profile affects each agent’s first-order condition. The coefficient $a_{ij}$ measures how much agent $j$ ’s deployment disturbs agent $i$ ’s gradient. If agent $j$ has no effect on agent $i$ ’s optimization problem, then $a_{ij}=0$ . Larger values of $a_{ij}$ indicate stronger cross-agent coupling. The diagonal coefficient $a_{ii}$ captures agent $i$ ’s own self-reflexive effect through the environment.

Assumptions 1 and 2 are the only two channels through which agents interact mathematically in this paper. Every downstream result is derived from these two assumptions and their combination in Section 4. The reflexivity matrix $\Gamma$ of Section 4 is built from exactly the parameters $\{\mu_{i}\}$ and $\{a_{ij}\}$ introduced here.

Assumption 3 (Unconstrained domains).

Each feasible set is $\mathcal{W}_{i}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}$ .

This makes $\mathcal{W}$ complete under the norms used below, enabling Banach’s fixed-point theorem, and ensures that retraining stays in $\mathcal{W}$ .

Throughout, $x_{i}$ denotes agent $i$ ’s block of a vector
 $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}$ , with Euclidean norm
 $\|\cdot\|$ . The spectral radius of $M$ is $\rho(M)$ , and for
 $q\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{k}$ we write
 $\|x\|_{q}:=\max_{i}\|x_{i}\|/q_{i}$ .

## 4 The Reduction: From Retraining Dynamics to $\Gamma$ 

The retraining dynamics $w_{t+1}=B(w_{t})$ are nonlinear and couple all $k$ agents through the shared endogenous distribution $D(w)$ . Direct analysis of these dynamics is difficult without additional structure. This section introduces the reduction used throughout the paper: under the assumptions of Section 3, changes in the nonlinear map $B$ are bounded entrywise by a nonnegative matrix $\Gamma$ . The spectral properties of $\Gamma$ can therefore be used to bound the dynamics of $B$ .

The first step bounds the shift in any agent’s best response induced by a shift in the deployed profile. The bound is linear and decomposes cleanly across agents.

Theorem 2 (Best-response sensitivity).

Under Assumptions 1–2 and 3, for every agent $i$ and every pair of deployed profiles $w,w^{\prime}$ ,

 $\|B_{i}(w)-B_{i}(w^{\prime})\|\;\leq\;\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{a_{ij}}{\mu_{i}}\,\|w_{j}-w_{j}^{\prime}\|.$ 

Proof.

Fix an agent $i$ and let $u_{i}:=B_{i}(w)$ and $u_{i}^{\prime}:=B_{i}(w^{\prime})$ . First-order optimality gives $\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i};w)=0$ and $\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i}^{\prime};w^{\prime})=0$ . Strong convexity of $F_{i}(\cdot;w)$ (Assumption 1) yields $\mu_{i}\|u_{i}-u_{i}^{\prime}\|\leq\|\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i};w)-\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i}^{\prime};w)\|$ . Substituting the first optimality condition and then the second gives $\mu_{i}\|u_{i}-u_{i}^{\prime}\|\leq\|\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i}^{\prime};w)\|=\|\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i}^{\prime};w)-\nabla_{u_{i}}F_{i}(u_{i}^{\prime};w^{\prime})\|$ . The right-hand side is a gradient difference at a fixed action $u_{i}^{\prime}$ across two deployed profiles, which Assumption 2 bounds by $\sum_{j}a_{ij}\,\|w_{j}-w_{j}^{\prime}\|$ . Dividing by $\mu_{i}>0$ yields the claim.
∎

The proof uses each structural assumption once: gradient sensitivity bounds the performative change in agent $i$ ’s gradient, and strong convexity converts it into a best-response change. Their interaction appears only through $a_{ij}/\mu_{i}$ , the ratio of agent $j$ ’s disturbance to agent $i$ ’s curvature, which measures how much $j$ can shift $i$ ’s best response.

The weights in Theorem 2 define the central object of the paper.

Definition 3 (Reflexivity matrix).

The reflexivity matrix is the $k\times k$ nonnegative matrix $\Gamma$ with entries $\Gamma_{ij}:=a_{ij}/\mu_{i}$ , for $i,j=1,\dots,k$ .

In terms of $\Gamma$ , Theorem 2 states that for every $i$ and every $w,w^{\prime}$ ,

 $\|B_{i}(w)-B_{i}(w^{\prime})\|\;\leq\;\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Gamma_{ij}\,\|w_{j}-w_{j}^{\prime}\|.$ 

(4)

The vector of best-response shifts is therefore dominated entrywise by the product of $\Gamma$ with the vector of action shifts.

The matrix $\Gamma$ is the central reduction object. It is built from primitive per-agent quantities rather than imposed as an aggregate Lipschitz constant, and its nonnegativity makes Perron–Frobenius theory available for the weighted-norm contraction argument below. The rank-one construction in Section 6 saturates (4) along the Perron direction, so the same spectral radius governs both the upper and lower sides of the threshold.

For a direct com
limitations: Several modeling choices delimit our results. The main guarantees assume strong convexity in each agent’s own action and exact best-response retraining; Appendix C controls approximate retraining under explicit error bounds. Sharper finite-sample rates, weaker curvature assumptions, and gradient updates remain directions for future work. We also treat the reflexivity matrix as fixed across rounds. If the interaction structure evolves, a natural extension is to study time-varying matrices $\Gamma_{t}$ , where tools such as joint spectral radii may be needed to characterize stability. The lower bound establishes that no universal positive guarantee can extend above the threshold, since at least one supercritical family forces linear cumulative excess loss; it does not assert that every supercritical $\Gamma$ is unlearnable. Characterizing which supercritical systems remain learnable is open for future work. Coordination among agents may shift the threshold, while damped retraining is a natural design lever for stabilizing otherwise unstable systems.

title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory
abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.

body_start:
Abstract

Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.

## 1 Introduction

Direct preference optimization (DPO) formulates alignment as a logistic comparison of policy–reference likelihood ratios, with gradient contributions from both chosen and rejected responses (Rafailov et al., 2023). In large-vocabulary language-model training, materialized logits can dominate memory consumption (Wijmans et al., 2025), and attention I/O and operator fusion also affect memory use and training throughput (Dao et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2025). These costs motivate our question of which computations a preference-training step can omit.

Figure 1: Stochastic interventions on the DPO computation graph. The two response branches share policy parameters. Rewards average policy–reference log-ratios over scored response positions. Fixed-reference computations use matching prefixes and positions and are omitted. Sampling outcomes and counts are schematic.

Prior work changes token supervision through confidence-based token selection or weighting (Yoon et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), reward-based selection (Yang et al., 2025b), and weighting from contrastive model predictions (Liu et al., 2025), while memory-efficient kernels change output-score computation (Wijmans et al., 2025; Hsu et al., 2025). This distinction motivates our question: which parts of a DPO step can be omitted, and how do their resource savings relate to changes in the optimization objective?

Preference-objective structure affects optimization (Chen et al., 2026), while shared-parameter updates can couple response likelihoods (Yuan et al., 2025) and reduce preferred-response probability (Razin et al., 2025). Our token-level analysis examines this coupling (Appendix C.1), and Proposition 1 separates reward preservation in expectation from the nonlinear loss.

We introduce a framework that samples the DPO computation graph to control training cost (Fig. 1). Each training step jointly selects the executed response prefixes, the positions used to estimate rewards, and the branches that carry gradients. These selections precede sequence execution, vocabulary projection, and backpropagation, allowing computation to be omitted throughout the step. This view unifies position, sequence, and branch pruning through their effects on the sampled objective and its gradient. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by reward sampling, while inverse-probability weighting makes the branch gradient conditionally unbiased for that objective.

Our contributions are:

• 

a unified framework for sampling DPO computation across response execution, token scoring, and backpropagation, with separately configurable sampling decisions.

• 

a characterization of the position and prefix objective changes, tolerance conditions that relate their optimal gaps to the retention rate and the truncation level, and a conditionally unbiased branch estimator with a stated convergence rate.

• 

controlled comparisons showing that full supervision retains most output-memory savings, that branch pruning reduces training time across model families, and that mean accuracy is slightly lower while open-ended score changes vary by benchmark (Secs. 4.2, 4.4 and 4.5).

## 2 Related Work

## Token-level credit in preference optimization.

A growing family of methods changes where DPO assigns credit through confidence-based token selection (Yoon et al., 2025), confidence-dependent weighting of varied tokens (Jiang et al., 2025), trained oracles for token rewards (Yang et al., 2025b), and contrastive token weights (Liu et al., 2025). Other approaches use optimal-transport reweighting (Li et al., 2025a), gradient-attribution priors (Yang et al., 2026), prefix-level ratio matching (Nguyen et al., 2026), implicit-reward credit (Zhao et al., 2026), attention-derived weights (Huang et al., 2026), minimal-edit emphasis in clinical dialogue (Lai et al., 2026a), or token-level KL control (Zeng et al., 2024). Our framework places supervision selection within the computation of a complete DPO step. Matched selection controls motivate uniform membership (Sec. E.1), and full-retention controls distinguish supervision deletion from implementation savings (Tab. 1).

## Efficient preference training.

Cut Cross-Entropy avoids materializing the token-by-vocabulary logit matrix (Wijmans et al., 2025), and Liger-Kernel uses fusion and chunked cross-entropy computation to reduce memory and improve training throughput (Hsu et al., 2025). FlashAttention relates attention efficiency to memory accesses rather than FLOP counts alone (Dao et al., 2022), while activation checkpointing trades recomputation for lower activation storage (Chen et al., 2016). Related efficiency work covers flow training (Du et al., 2022) and diffusion inference (Li et al., 2025b). SePO reports reduced GPU training hours through offline token selection (Yang et al., 2025b). Our framework considers how sampling throughout a DPO step changes both executed computation and the training objective. Controlled profiles separate implementation savings from the effects of reduced supervision and execution (Sec. 4.2).

## Stochastic computation and optimization dynamics.

Dropout randomly removes units (Srivastava et al., 2014) and stochastic depth bypasses sampled layers (Huang et al., 2016), while importance sampling can reduce stochastic-gradient variance using gradient-dependent probabilities (Katharopoulos and Fleuret, 2018). Preference-optimization analyses study gradient entanglement (Yuan et al., 2025), likelihood displacement (Razin et al., 2025), logit-space squeezing (Luo et al., 2026), and gated rejected contributions (Mouiche, 2026). Density-ratio estimation provides a distribution-comparison perspective (Chen et al., 2025) for preference objectives such as DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025), whose update structure is analyzed alongside margin-based losses (Chen et al., 2026). Our analysis separates objective changes from gradient-estimation noise under composed sampling (Propositions 2 and 3.5). Shared-parameter response changes are analyzed in Appendix C.1.

## 3 Stochastic Graph Pruning

## 3.1 Formulation

Let $\mathcal{D}=\{({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{w},{\bm{y}}_{l})\}$ contain prompts ${\bm{x}}$ with chosen and rejected responses ${\bm{y}}_{w},{\bm{y}}_{l}$ . Write $\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}$ for the policy with trainable parameters ${\bm{\theta}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ for the fixed reference (Rafailov et al., 2023). For side $b\in\{w,l\}$ , let $T_{b}\geq 1$ count response tokens, excluding prompt and padding. At position $t$ , define the target-token log-ratio

 $u_{b,t}=\log\frac{\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({y}_{b,t}\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{b,<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}({y}_{b,t}\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{b,<t})}.$ 

(1)

Here ${y}_{b,t}$ is the target token and ${\bm{y}}_{b,<t}$ its preceding response prefix. With mean rewards $R_{b}=T_{b}^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{b}}u_{b,t}$ , margin $\Delta=R_{w}-R_{l}$ , and scale $\beta>0$ , DPO minimizes the loss (Rafailov et al., 2023):

 $F({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\log\bigl(1+e^{-\beta\Delta}\bigr)].$ 

(2)

This length normalization parallels SimPO (Meng et al., 2024), but retains policy–reference log-ratios.

Fig. 1 separates three costs: dense vocabulary projection materializes $T_{b}\times V$ logits for vocabulary size $V$ (Wijmans et al., 2025), sequence execution computes attention and stores or recomputes activations (Dao et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2016), and backpropagation includes both responses (Rafailov et al., 2023).

Write ${\mathbb{I}}_{M}=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ . On side $b$ , sequence pruning selects length $M_{b}\in{\mathbb{I}}_{T_{b}}$ through cutoff fraction $\rho_{b}\in(0,1]$ , retaining $\tilde{\bm{y}}_{b}={\bm{y}}_{b,1:M_{b}}$ . Position pruning selects ${\mathbb{S}}_{b}\subseteq{\mathbb{I}}_{M_{b}}$ with $k_{b}=|{\mathbb{S}}_{b}|$ controlled by retention $\alpha\in(0,1]$ . Branch pruning selects $b^{\star}\in\{w,l\}$ with probabilities $q_{w},q_{l}>0$ , $q_{w}+q_{l}=1$ . All sampling laws are parameter-independent, and rewards average over selected positions. We use $\sigma$ for the sigmoid and $\sg$ for stop-gradient, which preserves values and blocks derivatives. Appendix A summarizes the notation.

## 3.2 Stochastic Position Pruning

Position pruning retains a uniform subset of response positions for scoring while preserving the executed response as context. Draw ${\mathbb{S}}_{b}\sim\positionsample(M_{b},\alpha)$ by

The subset is drawn before the language-model head, without computing policy probabilities. Applying the head only at ${\mathbb{S}}_{b}$ evaluates Eq. 4 exactly, skipping $M_{b}-k_{b}$ vocabulary projections, their logits, and their backward traffic.

Uniform sampling preserves the mean reward, but the nonlinear loss introduces a gap.

title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality--efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.

body_start:
Abstract

Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality–efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.

## 1 Introduction

Foundation models for structured electronic health record (EHR) data have predominantly adopted autoregressive (AR) sequence modelling. By generating possible future patient trajectories, these models have demonstrated strong zero-shot performance across clinical prediction tasks, in some settings approaching or exceeding task-specific supervised baselines [10, 11, 20, 15]. However, AR modelling imposes a strict left-to-right factorisation with each event generated conditionally on all preceding events before subsequent events can be considered. Longitudinal EHRs are only partly sequential in this sense.
Clinical activity often occurs in temporally concentrated bursts, making groups of nearby events a natural target for partially parallel generation (Appendix A.9), and in our MIMIC-IV data, 47.4% of recorded timestamps contain at least eight tokens (Appendix A.4).
This strict factorisation also carries an inference cost, as token-by-token decoding limits parallelism and requires sequential computation for each generated event. This motivates generative objectives that relax strict next-token prediction and instead allow groups of clinical events to be modelled jointly.

Discrete diffusion language models provide one such alternative by learning to reconstruct corrupted tokens through iterative denoising [12].
These models have shown strong generative and representation-learning performance in other structured scientific domains, including protein sequence modelling and molecular graph generation [19, 17].
Block diffusion (BD) introduces an AR factorisation across blocks while denoising tokens jointly within each block, enabling partial parallelism while retaining causal conditioning on previously generated context [1].
Prior work has shown a quality–parallelism trade-off: larger blocks allow more parallel generation but generally degrade likelihood and generation quality, whereas smaller blocks more closely approach AR performance. Discrete diffusion has previously been applied to EHRs for synthetic data generation [16, 3], but its behaviour relative to strong AR foundation models for zero-shot clinical prediction remains less well understood.

In this work, we conduct a controlled empirical comparison between AR and block-diffusion modelling of tokenised MIMIC-IV patient trajectories. We ask three questions: (1) how do block size and denoising budget affect the trade-off between predictive performance and inference efficiency; (2) when diffusion rollout underperforms AR, does the gap arise from poorer learned representations or from the iterative generation process; and (3) can alternative decoding strategies recover performance lost during blockwise generation?

Our contributions are:

1. 

We show that block diffusion is a competitive alternative for longitudinal EHR prediction, achieving rollout performance close to AR while providing up to a $1.43\times$ evaluation speedup in our primary operating regime.

2. 

We show that AR and block-diffusion models encode similarly predictive clinical information, with frozen linear probes achieving near-identical downstream performance across tasks despite a larger gap during generative rollout.

3. 

We provide a systematic study of how block size and denoising budget affect the quality–efficiency trade-off of block diffusion on EHR sequences, and find that alternative decoding strategies are not sufficient to close the remaining performance gap to AR.

## 2 Methods

## 2.1 Models and generative prediction

We represent each longitudinal EHR as a discrete token sequence $x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L})$ , where each token corresponds to a clinical event, quantised measurement, demographic attribute, or discretised time interval from a vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ .
Both AR and BD models operate on this same temporal sequence.

We compare an AR language model with a capacity-matched BD model. The AR baseline is a GPT-2–style decoder with causal self-attention [9], trained using standard next-token cross-entropy:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}\log p_{\theta}(x_{i+1}\mid x_{\leq i})$ 

(1)

For BD, we follow BD3-LM [1]. The trajectory is partitioned into blocks, with causal conditioning across blocks and masked diffusion within each active block. For a clean block $x_{0}$ , we sample $t\sim\mathcal{U}(0.001,0.999)$ and obtain $x_{t}$ by retaining each token independently with probability $\alpha_{t}=\cos(\pi t/2)$ and replacing it with [MASK] otherwise. The model is trained using the continuous-time masked diffusion objective:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MDLM}}=-\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},t,x_{t}}\left[\frac{-\alpha_{t}^{\prime}}{1-\alpha_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathbf{1}\!\left[x_{t}^{i}=\mathrm{[MASK]}\right]\log p_{\theta}\left(x_{0}^{i}\mid x_{t},x^{(<k)}\right)\right]$ 

(2)

where $x^{(<k)}$ denotes the clean preceding blocks. Independent noise levels are sampled across blocks.

At inference time, both models use KV caching [8]. AR generates token by token, whereas block diffusion initialises each new block as fully masked, iteratively denoises it, and then commits the completed block to the cache.
For zero-shot clinical prediction, generation continues until the model predicts one of the preconfigured end tokens, or a maximum number of generation steps is reached.
We perform 20 Monte Carlo rollouts per patient and use the fraction in which the positive endpoint occurs first as the prediction score. We report AUROC, AUPRC, and wall-clock evaluation time.

## 2.2 Data and experiments

We use MIMIC-IV v2.2 [5] and follow the tokenisation framework proposed in Renc et al. [11], with further details in the paper.
We evaluate ICU mortality, ICU readmission, ICU admission, and hospital mortality.
To isolate the effect of the generative formulation, AR and diffusion models use identical tokenisation, data splits, and context length of 1024, with matched capacity: 6 transformer layers, hidden dimension 768, 12 attention heads, rotary positional embeddings, and the same optimizer schedule. We train separate BD models with block sizes $B\in\{2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$ and retain ICU mortality as the primary task for ablations.

We first study how within-block parallelism affects predictive performance and inference efficiency. For the primary block-size comparison, we set the number of reverse steps to $S=B/2$ , fixing the nominal denoising budget at $S/B=0.5$ denoiser evaluations per generated token while varying the degree of joint within-block prediction.
To separate block size from the amount of iterative refinement, we perform fixed-block denoising sweeps for $B=4$ , $B=8$ , and $B=128$ . These experiments test whether additional reverse steps can recover performance lost at larger block sizes.

We next test whether differences in generative performance are already reflected in the learned representations. We freeze the AR and $B=8$ diffusion backbones and fit linear classifiers to their final-token hidden representations for all four clinical outcomes. This removes the generative decoding procedure and directly measures the predictive information encoded by each model. Mean pooling yielded lower performance for both models.

Our default BD decoder uses ancestral random unmasking according
to the reverse masking schedule. Let $t>s$ denote consecutive reverse times,
with $\alpha_{t}$ the token-retention probability at time $t$ . Each currently
masked position is revealed with probability
 $p_{\mathrm{unmask}}=\frac{\alpha_{s}-\alpha_{t}}{1-\alpha_{t}}.$ 
At $B=8$ , $S=4$ , we additionally evaluate two inference-time alternatives.
Confidence-based unmasking preserves the same expected reveal budget:
if $n_{\mathrm{mask}}$ positions remain masked, we reveal
 $k\approx n_{\mathrm{mask}}p_{\mathrm{unmask}}$ positions, selecting those
whose sampled token receives the highest model probability
[22, 2].
ReMDM-style remasking allows previously revealed positions to be masked
and reconsidered during subsequent reverse steps [18].
On non-final steps, revealed positions are remasked independently with probability
 $\sigma=\min\left(\eta,\frac{1-\alpha_{s}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)$ ,
where $\eta$ controls the maximum remasking rate and we evaluate
 $\eta\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}$ .

## 3 Results

BD provides competitive generative performance across the four downstream tasks, although AR remains stronger on three of four outcomes (Figure 1). Hospital mortality is the exception, but an increase in AUROC comes at the cost of AUPRC (Appendix A.6). Importantly, this gap largely disappears when evaluating the learned representations directly with frozen linear probes achieving near-identical AUROC for AR and BD across tasks. This indicates that BD captures similarly predictive clinical information, and suggests that much of the remaining gap emerging during rollout rather than representation learning.

Under a fixed denoising budget, smaller blocks provide the strongest quality–efficiency trade-off.
The BD configuration of $B=8$ , $S=4$ remained
approximately $0.03$ AUROC below AR, while achieving a $1.43\times$ evaluation speedup. Performance generally declines at larger block sizes, and very large blocks eventually lose the latency advantage despite requiring fewer sequential forward passes, reflecting the increased cost of each blockwise denoising step.

Increasing the number of denoising steps initially improves predictive performance, but gains saturate beyond a moderate budget while evaluation cost continues to rise. Alternative decoding strategies do not materially change this picture. ReMDM-style revision produces only small, metric-dependent changes, while confidence-based unmasking degrades AUROC (Appendix A.9).

Figure 1: 
Quality, efficiency, and representation trade-offs of block diffusion. Top-left: BD–AR AUROC difference under rollout and linear probing. Top-right: AUROC across denoising budgets. Bottom: ICU mortality AUROC and evaluation time across block sizes at $S/B=0.5$ . Dashed lines denote AR.

## 4 Discussion

We hypothesised that masked diffusion might be well suited to longitudinal EHR modelling because clinical activity often occurs in temporally concentrated bursts, where the exact ordering of nearby events may be less informative than their joint occurrence. Our results support block diffusion as a practical alternative to strictly autoregressive generation. Small-block BD configurations retain much of the predictive performance of AR while providing faster evaluation, with up to a $1.43\times$ speedup in our primary operating regime. This benefit is not monotonic with block size, however. Large blocks reduce sequential depth but increase per-step compute, producing a U-shaped latency curve and reproducing the quality–parallelism trade-off observed in prior BD work [1].

Increasing the denoising budget improves performance initially, but the gains plateau, suggesting that insufficient iterative refinement alone does not explain the remaining gap to AR. More strikingly, this discrepancy is largely absent under frozen linear probing, where AR and BD representations achieve near-identical predictive performance across downstream tasks. This suggests that BD learns similarly predictive clinical representations, and that much of the remaining difference arises during iterative generation rather than representation learning.

Our decoding ablations further support this interpretation. Confidence-based unmasking [22, 2] degrades performance, consistent with evidence that it can prematurely commit locally easy predictions before resolving dependencies important to the global trajectory [6]. ReMDM-style revision [18] enables iterative refinement but provides no meaningful gain.
These results suggest that the performance gap is unlikely to be resolved through revision of token commitment alone.

One possible source of this mismatch is the use of a fixed block size. Each block must resolve a predetermined number of positions even though clinically meaningful event groups need not align with these boundaries. This may be particularly relevant for EHR trajectories, where the number of events associated with a clinical episode varies substantially. Variable-length diffusion generation therefore represents a natural direction for future work [4, 21, 7].

More generally, EHR structure may motivate diffusion formulations that differ from those developed for natural language. One possibility is to generate events between successive time markers jointly, treating temporally co-occurring events as unordered or partially ordered sets. Alternative corruption processes, including uniform discrete diffusion [14, 13], may also be worth exploring because they require the model to distinguish corrupted clinical events from plausible clean ones rather than relying exclusively on a dedicated mask state.

Finally, generative endpoint prediction captures only one use of diffusion models for EHRs. Their ability to condition on partially observed sequences could support infilling missing events, reconstructing incomplete records, or exploring counterfactual trajectories. Overall, our results suggest that block diffusion is a promising and computationally attractive framework for longitudinal EHR modelling, while also showing that improved decoding remains important for closing the residual gap to AR zero-shot prediction.

\workshoptitle

World Models for High-Stakes Health

## Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?

Ashvin Gupta

Affiliation: Imperial College London

Brendan Delaney

Affiliation: Imperial College London

Alessandra Russo

Affiliation: Imperial College London
headings: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
body_start:
Abstract

Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains.
In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation.
Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM.
We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance.
This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.

## 1 Introduction

Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are longitudinal records of patient-healthcare interactions. Recent work has increasingly focused on EHR foundation models, which aim to learn general-purpose patient representations through self-supervised learning and can be adapted to a range of downstream clinical prediction tasks [19, 17, 18, 15].
Downstream performance therefore hinges on the quality of these representations.

Due to the sequential nature of EHRs, transformer encoders have become a common backbone for EHR representation learning.
A dominant objective for pretraining has been BERT-style masked language modelling (MLM), in which
the model is trained to reconstruct masked medical events from their surrounding context [11, 10, 16, 14]. However, exact token reconstruction may not provide the ideal learning signal for longitudinal clinical data. EHR sequences contain routine, repeated, administrative, and partially unpredictable events, yet MLM treats reconstruction of each masked token as equally important. This may encourage representations that capture the identity of local events rather than the true patient state.

In contrast, clinicians use their medical knowledge to abstract away irrelevant detail and focus on key events, trends, and interactions to form a higher-level representation of the patient state. This motivation is closely aligned with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), which provide an alternative form of self-supervision [9, 2]. Rather than reconstructing observations in the input space, JEPA trains a predictor to estimate latent representations of unobserved targets from an available context. This approach has shown strong representation-learning performance in vision [2, 3], world modelling [12] and language [8].
Latent prediction is intended to produce semantically meaningful features and
avoid unnecessary reconstruction of unpredictable low-level detail. This is particularly appealing for EHRs,
where multiple observed event sequences may correspond to similar underlying clinical states and trajectories.

However, defining a meaningful and predictable JEPA target in longitudinal EHRs is non-trivial. Unlike image patches, EHR events are irregularly sampled, vary substantially in density, and already represent semantically meaningful concepts. Temporal proximity therefore does not necessarily imply semantic similarity, and future clinical events may depend not only on patient state but also on healthcare decisions.

In this work, we ask whether the I-JEPA-style latent prediction framework [2] can be transferred effectively to longitudinal EHR sequences. We evaluate multiple target-construction strategies, including
span masking, future masking and random masking of events.
We investigate (1) whether these JEPA formulations can be trained stably without representational collapse, (2) how the downstream performance compares, and (3) which objective and training characteristics may explain the observed differences.

## 2 Methodology

## 2.1 Medical Event Representation

Figure 1: The context sequence is encoded by the online encoder, while the complete target sequence is processed by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder with gradients stopped through the target branch. A predictor combines the context representations with learnable mask embeddings to estimate target latents, which are matched to the EMA target representations using mean squared error. We evaluate three target constructions: contiguous span masking, prospective prediction of future events, and random masking of individual events.

A patient trajectory is represented as a time-ordered sequence of clinical events, $X=(e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{N})$ , where each event is a triplet $e_{i}=(c_{i},v_{i},t_{i})$ comprising a discrete medical code $c_{i}\in\mathcal{V}$ , an optional continuous value $v_{i}\in\mathbb{R}$ , and timestamp $t_{i}$ . Patient age $a_{i}$ is derived from $t_{i}$ and date of birth. Representing time and continuous values is an important design choice in EHR modelling [4, 13, 7]. Rather than discretising continuous recordings into tokens, we retain them directly in the event representation using triplet embeddings [4]. The input embedding for event $e_{i}$ is

 $\mathrm{h_{i}}={\mathrm{E_{code}}}(c_{i})+\mathrm{Proj_{val}}(v_{i})\cdot\mathbb{I}_{[v_{i}\neq\varnothing]}+\mathrm{Proj_{age}}(a_{i}),$ 

(1)

where $\mathrm{E_{code}}$ is a learned code embedding and $\mathbb{I}$ indicates value presence. Sequence order is encoded using Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE). All models use the same transformer backbone with 6 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden dimension 768, and maximum context length $N=1024$ , ensuring that downstream differences reflect the pretraining objective rather than model capacity.

## 2.2 Objectives

JEPA performance depends strongly on context–target design [8], and as such, we evaluate three EHR target constructions reflecting different assumptions about what should be predictable.

Our first objective, Span JEPA, follows the I-JEPA paradigm as directly as possible [2].
We treat the EHR as a one-dimensional sequence of $N$ clinical events. The complete uncorrupted sequence is passed through the exponential moving average (EMA) target encoder to obtain event-level representations $[\mathbf{z}_{y}={\mathbf{z}_{y_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{y_{N}}}.]$ .
We sample $M$ contiguous target spans from these representations. The (i)-th target span is defined by the set of event positions $B_{i}$ , giving the corresponding target representations ${\mathbf{z}_{y_{j}}},{j\in B_{i}}.$ 
The target events are removed from the input leaving the remaining events as context. The context encoder produces a set of event representations, which are passed to a shallow two-layer transformer predictor together with learnable mask tokens containing positional information for the target locations. As in I-JEPA, the predictor is applied separately for each target span, producing ${\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{y_{j}}},{j\in B_{i}}.$ 
The prediction objective is the mean squared distance between the predicted and target representations across the $M$ target spans:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\frac{1}{|B_{i}|}\sum_{j\in B_{i}}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}_{y_{j}}-\mathbf{z}_{y_{j}}\right\|_{2}^{2}.$ 

(2)

While span masking provides the closest analogue to I-JEPA, EHRs are inherently temporal, and clinically meaningful information may instead lie in how the patient evolves over time. We therefore consider a prospective formulation, Future JEPA, motivated by temporally predictive JEPA and world-model approaches [3]. All events observed up to a time point $T$ form the context, while events satisfying $[T<t_{j}\leq T+24,\mathrm{h}]$ form a single future target region $B_{1}$ . This is equivalent to setting $M=1$ in the JEPA objective above. The architecture and loss are otherwise unchanged.

Finally, we evaluate a random-mask JEPA formulation, Random JEPA, that uses the same random sampling strategy as MLM, but optimises the JEPA objective with $M=1$ . This provides a controlled comparison with MLM under the same corruption scheme, differing only in whether the model predicts discrete medical codes or continuous target representations.

Together, these objectives test three increasingly different assumptions about predictable structure in EHRs: (1) whether latent clinical information can be recovered from neighbouring events, (2) whether it can be predicted prospectively from earlier patient history, and (3) whether latent reconstruction offers an advantage over token reconstruction when the corruption pattern itself is held fixed.

For all JEPA experiments, we use an EMA target encoder with stop-gradient, rather than the shared-encoder SIGReg alternative [5]. In preliminary experiments, SIGReg was unstable and collapsed, with substantially reduced target-embedding variance. The EMA formulation remained stable and non-collapsed, allowing us to assess the JEPA objective without conflating downstream performance with optimisation failure. Standard MLM is retained as the primary baseline.

## 3 Experiments and Results

Each objective is trained for 50 epochs on the full MIMIC-IV training cohort using the same optimisation setup. Our downstream tasks include ICU mortality, ICU readmission, hospital mortality, and hospital readmission using the same 80:10:10 patient-level split as pretraining. Representation quality is assessed using frozen-encoder linear probes with mean pooling, using the checkpoint with the lowest validation pretraining loss, reporting AUROC and AUPRC. The full hyperparameter sweep is provided in Appendix 5.6.

MLM outperformed all JEPA formulations across downstream tasks, with Future JEPA performing closest to MLM, followed by the two others (Table 1). To determine whether this performance gap was caused by representational collapse, we additionally tracked effective rank and feature standard deviation of the target-encoder embeddings throughout pretraining [6]. Both remained stable while training and validation prediction losses decreased (Appendix 5.3, Figure 3), indicating that the JEPA models converged to non-collapsed solutions despite learning representations that were less useful for downstream clinical prediction.

Figure 2: Sensitivity of Span-JEPA downstream performance to target masking ratio across the four downstream clinical prediction tasks.

We further investigated which properties of an EHR target were associated with latent-prediction difficulty.
We performed a post-hoc multivariable regression on per-target prediction error using target size, unique-code fraction, event-type diversity, target–context code overlap, and code rarity as covariates (Appendix 5.4). Target size, a key design parameter in I-JEPA [2],
was the only factor consistently positively associated with prediction error across all three formulations. In contrast, unique-code fraction was negatively associated with prediction error, while event-type diversity had comparatively small effects. To investigate the effect of target size, we varied the masking ratio to alter target size for Span JEPA. Although smaller targets reduced prediction difficulty, this produced no consistent improvement in downstream performance (Figure 2).

## 4 Discussion

Direct JEPA-style latent prediction can be optimised successfully on longitudinal EHRs without representational collapse, yet the resulting representations remain weaker than MLM on the evaluated downstream tasks. The fact that reducing target size also fails to improve downstream performance suggests that the limitation is not simply optimisation difficulty, but may instead lie in how the prediction target is defined.

A likely explanation is a mismatch in the semantic unit of prediction. In I-JEPA, image patches are relatively low-level observations, and predicting larger regions can encourage abstraction toward higher-level structure [2].
However, EHR tokens already have a very specific semantic meaning associated to them.
Predicting masked event-level latents requires reconstructing the semantic meaning of each event, rather than definitely encouraging compression into a coherent patient-state representation. In this setting, increasing the amount of masked information does not necessarily increase semantic abstraction in the same way that predicting larger image regions can. By contrast, MLM retains an explicit token-level objective that directly preserves event identity, which itself is clinically informative. This may also explain why recent JEPA-style EHR work retains explicit token-level supervision alongside latent prediction [1].

The stronger performance of Future JEPA suggests that temporal prediction may provide a more appropriate inductive bias than reconstructing arbitrary internal targets. However, future EHR observations are only partially determined by latent patient state and are also shaped by clinical decisions. The target may therefore contain information about how care is delivered as well as how the patient evolves. Irregular sampling further complicates target construction, since a fixed number of events can span very different clinical intervals, while a fixed temporal window can contain widely varying amounts of information. Consequently, neither token contiguity nor temporal proximity necessarily corresponds to a coherent patient-state target.

These observations suggest that an EHR-specific JEPA may need to operate at a higher semantic level. Rather than predicting one latent representation per recorded event, groups of events could first be aggregated into a smaller number of patient-state representations, with the predictive objective modelling transitions between these states over time. Such targets could better separate persistent clinical state from individual observations, potentially matching the abstraction motivating JEPA more closely.

Overall, our findings suggest that the central challenge in transferring JEPA to longitudinal EHRs is not simply preventing collapse or tuning target difficulty, but defining a prediction unit that corresponds to clinically meaningful patient state. In the formulations studied here, successful latent prediction alone is insufficient to outperform token-level reconstruction.

title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding
abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.

## Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought

with Context-Aware Decoding

Shin’ya Yamaguchi

Affiliation: NTT

Email: shinya.yamaguchi@ntt.com
body_start:
Abstract

While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.

## 1 Introduction

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting Wei et al. (2022); Kojima et al. (2022) has emerged as an effective inference strategy for improving the reasoning performance of Large Language Models (LLMs).
By generating multiple intermediate reasoning steps, or rationales, before producing a final answer, CoT enables LLMs to solve complex problems.
Beyond improving task performance, these rationales are often interpreted as explanations of the model’s predictions.
However, recent studies have revealed that generated rationales do not necessarily reflect the actual decision-making process Turpin et al. (2023); Arcuschin et al. (2025); Lewis-Lim et al. (2025).
In particular, LLMs may rely on shortcut information directly from the input query, even when their rationales suggest a different conclusion.
Such query-shortcut behavior weakens the behavioral dependency between rationales and final answers, raising concerns about the reliability of CoT.

Prior research has investigated this issue by rationale interventions that measure whether changes to reasoning steps affect final predictions Lanham et al. (2023); Turpin et al. (2023) or improving rationale reliability with additional supervision or rationale selection Paul et al. (2024); Sun et al. (2026).
While these studies provide important insights, a complementary question is whether query-shortcut behavior can be mitigated directly during answer decoding, without modifying model parameters or employing external evaluators.
In standard CoT decoding, the query and generated rationale are jointly provided as context for next-token prediction.
However, this formulation does not explicitly distinguish the contributions of the query and the rationale, allowing the model to generate answers primarily from query-conditioned predictions.

In this work, we investigate the application of Context-Aware Decoding (CAD) Shi et al. (2024) to mitigate query-shortcut behavior in CoT.
CAD is an established contrastive decoding approach originally developed to prioritize contextual evidence over a model’s parametric knowledge.
We examine whether the same principle can encourage LLMs to rely more heavily on self-generated rationales during decoding.
Specifically, we study Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), an application of CAD in which the context part is a CoT rationale rather than an external document.
RCD contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on both the query and rationale with those conditioned only on the query.
By subtracting query-only logits, this decoding rule increases the relative preference for tokens supported by the rationale, potentially suppressing query-shortcut behavior without additional training.
We further interpret this established decoding formulation as a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective, in which the reward is the log-density ratio between the rationale-conditioned and query-only distributions.

We empirically investigate RCD through comprehensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
First, intervention analyses with ground-truth and randomly substituted rationales demonstrate that RCD makes final predictions more sensitive to rationale content, providing behavioral evidence of increased rationale–answer dependency.
Second, RCD consistently improves answer accuracy over standard CoT across five reasoning benchmarks and multiple model families.
Third, an analysis of rationale correctness reveals that the performance gains primarily stem from correcting answers that fail to follow valid rationales, rather than repairing incorrect reasoning.
These findings suggest that applying contrastive decoding to CoT can mitigate query-shortcut behavior and improve the utilization of generated rationales.

## 2 Preliminary

## 2.1 Next-token Prediction in LLM

Consider an auto-regressive LLM, parameterized by $\theta$ .
Given a query $q$ , an LLM generates an output token sequence $\bm{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{L})\in\mathcal{V}^{L}$ following:

 $\displaystyle p(\bm{y}|q)=\prod^{L}_{i=1}p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q),$ 

(1)

where $L$ is token length, $\mathcal{V}$ is token vocabulary, and $\bm{y}_{<i}$ are preceding output tokens.
 $p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q)$ over $\mathcal{V}$ is computed by the softmax of the model’s output $\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q)$ as follows.

 $\displaystyle p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q)=\sigma(\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q))$ 

(2)

 $\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q))}{\sum_{{w}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}=w|\bm{y}_{<i},q))}.$ 

(3)

Each token $y_{i}$ is generated from $p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q)$ via a decoding strategy such as greedy decoding and sampling.
We define a function for an arbitrary decoding strategy:

 $\bm{y}=\operatorname{generate}_{\theta}(q).$ 

(4)

## 2.2 Chain-of-Thought (CoT)

CoT aims to enhance LLM reasoning by incorporating multi-step rationale generation during decoding Wei et al. (2022); Kojima et al. (2022).
First, LLMs generate a rationale $r$ from query $q$ with instruction prompt, e.g., Let’s think step-by-step Kojima et al. (2022), as follows.

 $r=\operatorname{generate}_{\theta}(q).$ 

(5)

Adding $r$ to the input context, LLMs generate the final answer by the next-token prediction, similar to Eq. (4):

 $\displaystyle\bm{y}=\operatorname{generate}_{\theta}(q,r).$ 

(6)

For simplicity, we assume that the rationale and answer generation steps are separated, and that the generated rationale can be intervened by alternative rationales, e.g., ground truth.

In Eq. (6), each answer token $y_{i}$ is decoded by the next-token distribution $p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q,r)$ , and thus, it is not guaranteed that the output tokens are based on the rationale $r$ , i.e., LLMs can directly answer from the query $q$ .
In fact, previous works have reported the unfaithful behavior of CoT, such as post-hoc rationalizing by biasing toward the order of multiple-choice options for the answer Turpin et al. (2023), silent error correction, where the model implicitly fixes the computational or logical errors in the rationales due to shortcuts Arcuschin et al. (2025).
These findings indicate that standard CoT can exhibit weak or inconsistent behavioral dependence on its rationale.

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD)

We investigate whether context-aware decoding can mitigate query-shortcut behavior in CoT by increasing the influence of rationales during answer generation.
To this end, we study Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which applies Context-Aware Decoding (CAD; Shi et al. (2024)) to self-generated CoT rationales rather than external contexts (Fig. 1).
Following CAD, RCD instead reweights this distribution using the density ratio:

 $\hat{p}_{\theta}(y_{i})\propto p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q,r)\times\left(\frac{p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q,r)}{p_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q)}\right)^{\alpha},$ 

(7)

where $\alpha$ controls the contrastive strength.
During decoding, this is equivalently implemented by the logit-level computation in a batch-parallel manner:

 $\displaystyle\hat{\operatorname{logits}}_{\theta}(y_{i}):=$ 
 $\displaystyle(1+\alpha)\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q,r)$ 

 $\displaystyle-\alpha\operatorname{logits}_{\theta}(y_{i}|\bm{y}_{<i},q).$ 

(8)

For $\alpha>0$ , the density ratio increases the relative preference for tokens whose probability rises when conditioning on the rationale.
Unlike logit addition, which reinforces tokens favored by both distributions, subtraction emphasizes the information contributed by the rationale beyond the query alone as shown in Section 4.
This aims to mitigate query-shortcut behavior rather than simply increase agreement with query-only predictions.

Rationale Contrastive Decoding

## 3.2 Theoretical Insight

Eq. (7) can be interpreted as the closed-form solution to the following KL-regularized reward maximization problem Schulman et al. (2015); Schulman et al. (2017):
