body_start:
Abstract.

We propose a new generative modeling framework grounded in forward-backward partial differential equations (PDEs).
These equations arise naturally in mean-field game (MFG) theory, and are closely related to nonlinear Schrödinger systems.
Our main contribution is to reinterpret this connection within the setting of generative modeling and to develop an efficient numerical methodology for its practical implementation.
Specifically, we derive and characterize a nonlinear extension of the classical Schrödinger bridge problem through a coupled system of PDEs, yielding a model we call SBNL (Schrödinger Bridge NonLinear).
To compute its solution, we design a simulation algorithm based on branching diffusions and the probabilistic representation of semilinear PDEs.
The resulting method is embarrassingly parallel, scalable to high dimensions, and applicable to a broad class of nonlinear interaction functionals.
We validate the approach through numerical experiments, including recovery of the classical Schrödinger bridge, nonlinear extensions with convex penalties (Gross-Pitaevskii) as well as potential interaction terms, and high-dimensional generative tasks such as image synthesis on the MNIST and FFHQ human face dataset.
Furthermore, the same framework embeds score-based generative modeling, diffusion models, and tractable gaussian Schrödinger bridges.

22footnotetext: Qube Research & Technologies, Paris, France.
mathias.grau@qube-rt.com,
pierre.henrylabordere@qube-rt.com

## 1. Introduction

The Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem [1, 2, 3] has recently attracted significant attention in generative modeling due to its ability to learn an optimally controlled stochastic dynamics that transports between two arbitrary endpoint distributions. By minimizing relative entropy with respect to a reference diffusion (typically Brownian motion), the SB framework reveals deep connections between optimal transport, stochastic control, and score-based generative modeling [4, 5, 6, 7].

When both terminal costs and the evolving marginal law are controlled, the problem extends beyond classical (linear) Schrödinger bridges to mean-field control and mean-field games (MFG) [8, 9, 10, 11]. In this regime, interactions through the marginal distribution induce a semilinear forward–backward structure.

Existing iterative schemes for SB, such as iterative proportional fitting (IPF) / iterative Markovian fitting (IMF) and related diffusion-based approaches [6, 7, 12], are primarily designed for linear entropic transport. These methods rely on alternating optimization procedures, which can be computationally expensive and may suffer from error accumulation. More recent approaches based on Gaussian mixture energy models [13, 14] improve scalability in some settings but remain limited in expressivity in high dimensions. Even recent extensions based on controlled stochastic dynamics [15] are not well suited to law-dependent running costs, which induce intrinsically coupled semilinear dynamics.

Although recent works in MFG and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations clarify the structure of the coupling in terms of forward–backward potentials [16, 17], they often do not yield objectives that are both theoretically grounded and directly amenable to unbiased stochastic optimization in high dimensions.

Our contributions are as follows:

(1) 

We introduce a variational objective for semilinear mean-field Schrödinger bridges with law-dependent running and terminal costs, and characterize optimality through coupled $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ PDEs (equivalently, a Lasry - Lions $(m,v)$ system). We refer to the resulting model as SBNL (Schrödinger Bridge NonLinear).

(2) 

We develop a marked-branching stochastic algorithm for the two-type $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ coupling, prove unbiasedness and $L^{2}$ -integrability of the estimator under explicit conditions, and train the potentials jointly (rather than via alternating refitting), with branching used both during training and sampling.

(3) 

We report experiments ranging from bridge recovery and soft terminal penalties to Gross-Pitaevskii-type couplings and high-dimensional latent image transport.

## 1.1. Related work

Linear Schrödinger bridges.

The Schrödinger bridge problem is classically linked to entropic optimal transport [3, 18, 4], with efficient Sinkhorn-type and iterative fitting procedures in the linear setting. These methods scale well when dynamics are fixed between prescribed marginals. Recent neural approaches approximate bridges through forward-backward SDEs [6] or diffusion-style training [7, 12]; they mainly target linear bridges and often rely on expensive alternating refits (IPF/IMF). A complementary, simulation-free line parameterizes the Schrödinger potentials with Gaussian mixture forms, yielding lightweight solvers [13, 14] at the cost of limited expressivity. Even recent drift-and-volatility extensions (Schrödinger-Bass bridges) [15] still assume (approximately) linear entropic transport and are not tailored to running costs that depend on the evolving marginal law.

Control formulations and mean-field games (MFG).

Once running or terminal terms depend on the marginal law, the problem leaves the linear SB regime and sits in mean-field control / MFG [8, 9], with forward-backward PDE couplings studied in [10, 19, 20, 4]. Extending Sinkhorn-type or alternating schemes to such coupled HJB-Fokker-Planck systems is challenging in high dimension. Recent interaction/unbalanced frameworks [21, 22, 17] encode growth, interaction, or state costs through composite weighted losses and staged training. Trajectory-level optimal-control views, e.g. adjoint matching [23], couple learning to long-horizon simulation and can be costly. We retain entropic regularization while centering law-dependent running costs, starting from the non linear Sinkhorn system with jointly learned coupled Schrödinger potentials, using branching Monte Carlo.

Branching representations for semilinear PDEs.

Branching diffusion methods provide probabilistic representations of semilinear PDEs via weighted particle systems [24, 25, 26]. We extend these ideas to the coupled forward-backward system arising in mean-field Schrödinger bridges, where the interaction between the two potentials introduces a time-reflected dependency. This enables a scalable estimator for both the potentials and their gradients, which we integrate into a neural generative framework.

## 2. Semilinear Schrödinger bridges

We denote by $\mu_{0}$ and $\mu_{T}$ laws on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ .
Let $(X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ be controlled by a drift $\alpha_{\cdot}$ under $\mathbb{P}$ , with $X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ and $\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\alpha_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t}.$ 

## 2.1. Formulation

As a generalization of the classical Schrödinger bridge formulation, we consider the following variational problem:

(1)

 $P:=\inf_{\alpha_{\cdot}}\;\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{2c}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}+f(m(t,\cdot))\right)\mathrm{d}t\;+\;g(m(T,\cdot))\right],$ 

where $c>0$ , $m(t)$ denotes the law of $X_{t}$ , and $f$ and $g$ are functionals. The infimum is taken over the control $\alpha$ , where $m$ is constrained to satisfy the Fokker-Planck PDE.

The three terms appearing in $P$ play different roles:

• 

The quadratic control cost $\tfrac{1}{2c}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}$ penalizes deviations of the dynamics from the reference Brownian motion.
By Girsanov’s theorem, for feedback controls its expectation equals $\tfrac{1}{c}H(\mathbb{P}\mid\mathbb{P}^{0})$ , the relative entropy
between the controlled law $\mathbb{P}$ of the diffusion and the law $\mathbb{P}^{0}$ of the Brownian motion started from $\mu_{0}$ [2].
This quadratic structure is also crucial analytically: it is the only choice of control penalty for which the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation admits a tractable solution through a Cole-Hopf transformation. For this reason, essentially all generative modeling frameworks based on stochastic control can be viewed as particular cases of the Schrödinger bridge.

• 

The functional $f(m(t,\cdot))$ introduces a running cost depending directly on the marginal law of the process at each time $t$ .
Such terms allow for mean-field type interactions, density regularization, or penalization of undesirable behaviors (e.g. concentration, mass spread) during the evolution.
Classical examples include (see the review [9]):

– 

Quadratic interaction:
 $f(m)=\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}m(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x,$ 
which penalizes high concentrations and favors dispersion.

– 

Entropy-type term:
 $f(m)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}m(x)\,\log m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,$ 
encouraging spreading of the distribution.

– 

Potential interaction:
 $f(m)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V(x)\,m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,$ 
where $V$ is an external field acting on the density (as in [21]).

– 

Pairwise interaction kernel:
 $f(m)=\tfrac{1}{2}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}K(x-y)\,m(x)\,m(y)\,\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y,$ 
modeling attractive or repulsive mean-field effects.

• 

The terminal cost $g(m(T,\cdot))$ enforces constraints or preferences on the final law.
In the hard-constraint setting of the classical Schrödinger bridge, $g$ is chosen so that $m(T,\cdot)=\mu_{T}$ , i.e. the terminal distribution matches the prescribed target.
In the relaxed setting, $g$ can encode convex penalties measuring the discrepancy between the final distribution and the target.
For use below, we denote by $g^{*}$ the Legendre transform (convex conjugate) of $g$ :

 $g^{*}(v(T,\cdot)):=\sup_{m(T,\cdot)}\Big\{\mathbb{E}_{X\sim m(T,\cdot)}[v(T,X)]-g(m(T,\cdot))\Big\}.$ 

Note that in practice it does not make sense to perfectly calibrate to the empirical measure, which is only a finite sample approximation of the true law.
Instead, one seeks both proximity to the empirical distribution and sufficient regularity of the solution, precisely what the soft constraint achieves.

Remark 2.1 (State dependence and MFG link).

Running and terminal costs that depend explicitly on the state $x$ can be rewritten in the law-only form (1) by integrating against $m$ ; the resulting forward-backward MFG optimality system and its relation to Theorem 2.1 are recorded in Appendix E.

## 2.2. Main result

Theorem 2.1 (Semilinear Schrödinger bridge).

We assume (A1)-(A4) from Appendix D. The optimal controlled process of (1) is given under a measure $\mathbb{P}$ by

(2)

 $\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\nabla\log\varphi(t,X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t},$ 

with $\mathrm{Law}(X_{t})=\varphi(t,\cdot)\bar{\varphi}(T-t,\cdot)$ and $F:=\tfrac{\delta f}{\delta m(t,x)}$ where the pair $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ satisfies the PDE system

(3)

 $\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\varphi_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=c\,\varphi_{t}\,F(t,x,\varphi_{t}\bar{\varphi}_{T-t}),$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bar{\varphi}_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\bar{\varphi}_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=c\,\bar{\varphi}_{t}\,F(T-t,x,\bar{\varphi}_{t}\varphi_{T-t}),$ 

The terminal conditions $(\varphi(T,\cdot),\bar{\varphi}(T,\cdot))$ are characterized by the coupled nonlinear Sinkhorn system

(5)

 $\left\{\begin{aligned} \varphi(0,x)\,\bar{\varphi}(T,x)&=\mu_{0}(x),\\
\bar{\varphi}(0,x)\,\varphi(T,x)&=G^{-1}\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{c}\log\varphi(T,\cdot),\,x\big),\end{aligned}\right.$ 

where $G:=\tfrac{\delta g}{\delta m(T,x)}$ , $G^{-1}(w,\cdot)$ is the density $m$ solving $G(\cdot,m)=w$ , and $\varphi(0,\cdot),\bar{\varphi}(0,\cdot)$ are obtained by propagating the terminal potentials backward through (3)-(4).

Appendix A proves Theorem 2.1 by a verification argument; see [8] for the well-posedness of the forward-backward system.

Remark 2.2 (Nonlinear Sinkhorn interpretation).

When $f\equiv 0$ with a hard terminal constraint, (5) reduces to the usual Sinkhorn system, with $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ propagated by linear heat kernels and matched to $\mu_{0},\mu_{T}$ . Our formulation adds two nonlinear ingredients: the semilinear propagation (3)-(4) through the running cost $F$ , and the terminal coupling $\varphi(T,\cdot)\mapsto G^{-1}(-\tfrac{1}{c}\log\varphi(T,\cdot),\cdot)$ induced by $g$ . The values $\varphi(0,x),\bar{\varphi}(0,x)$ are obtained from the PDE system via the branching representation of Section 3.

Remark 2.3 (Forward-backward system).

Although Theorem 2.1 is stated in terms of the system (3)-(4) with terminal conditions, it can equivalently be expressed
in the usual forward-backward form familiar from mean field games. Indeed,
defining the density $m(t,x):=\varphi(t,x)\bar{\varphi}(T-t,x)$ , one checks that
 $m$ satisfies the forward Fokker-Planck equation (see proof for details)

 $\partial_{t}m+\nabla\!\cdot\!\big(m\,\nabla\log\varphi\big)-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta m=0,$ 

while $v:=-\tfrac{1}{c}\log\varphi$ satisfies the backward Hamilton-Jacobi
equation

 $\partial_{t}v+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta v-\tfrac{c}{2}\,|\nabla v|^{2}+F(t,x,m)=0$ 

Thus the pair $(m,v)$ solves the standard forward-backward MFG system of
Lasry - Lions type. Our formulation in terms of $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ is
algebraically equivalent but particularly well-suited for the branching Monte-Carlo representation introduced below.

Remark 2.4 (Soft constraint and matching marginal $\mu_{T}$ ).

Consider the terminal cost

 $g(m(T,\cdot))=\lambda\;D_{f}(\mu_{T},m(T,\cdot)),\qquad\lambda>0,$ 

with $f(u):=-\log u-1$ , i.e. $D_{f}(\mu_{T},m)=\int m\log\frac{m}{\mu_{T}}-\int m$ , which is $\mathrm{KL}(m(T,\cdot)\,\|\,\mu_{T})-1$ on probability measures. Over nonnegative measures, the convex conjugate $g^{*}$ is

(6)

 $g^{*}(v(T,\cdot))=\lambda\;\mathbb{E}_{X_{T}\sim\mu_{T}}\!\left[e^{\,v(T,X_{T})/\lambda}\right],$ 

so that the terminal coupling in the nonlinear Sinkhorn system (5) becomes explicit:

(7)

 $G^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{c}\log\varphi(T,\cdot),x\right)=\mu_{T}(x)\,\varphi(T,x)^{-a},\qquad a:=\frac{1}{\lambda c}.$ 

The system (5) then reads

(8)

 $\left\{\begin{aligned} \varphi(0,x)\,\bar{\varphi}(T,x)&=\mu_{0}(x),\\
\bar{\varphi}(0,x)\,\varphi(T,x)&=\mu_{T}(x)\,\varphi(T,x)^{-a}.\end{aligned}\right.$ 

In our numerical experiments, we consider this formulation for various values of $\lambda$ .
In the limit $\lambda\to\infty$ (i.e. $a\to 0$ ), the terminal penalty enforces the hard constraint $m(T,\cdot)=\mu_{T}$ , and the terminal coupling in (8) reduces to the standard marginal constraint

(9)

 $\bar{\varphi}(0,x)\,\varphi(T,x)=\mu_{T}(x),$ 

so that the nonlinear Sinkhorn system recovers the classical Schrödinger bridge.

Appendix F records an analogous soft terminal condition based on a $p$ -Wasserstein discrepancy.

Remark 2.5 (Special cases of semilinear Schrödinger bridges).

Appendix H records several tractable specializations: linear bridges with confining potentials and explicit heat kernels on Coxeter chambers (including Dyson and type- $C$ limits), the Gaussian semilinear bridge for log-linear $F$ [27] and a relative-entropy terminal cost (Proposition H.1), lifted bridges with Gyöngy’s Markov projection (Proposition H.2), and score-based / DDPM models as the exact $F\equiv 0$ solution with $\bar{\varphi}\equiv 1$ and noised-data prior (Appendix H.2), with proofs in Appendices I and J.

## 3. Branching diffusions

The semilinear PDE system (3)-(4) is generally analytically intractable, and thus requires numerical approximation.
A deterministic Sinkhorn-type iterative method based on PDE techniques was introduced by Guéant [11]; however, this approach suffers from the curse of dimensionality and is therefore not suitable in the context of generative modeling.

Figure 1. Branching paths on an 8-Gaussian terminal potential, illustrating Gross-Pitaevskii-type branching (Appendix M).

An alternative and more powerful approach is provided by marked branching diffusion representations,
originating in McKean’s probabilistic solution of the KPP equation [24]
and subsequently extended to broad classes of semilinear and nonlinear PDEs [28, 25, 26].
These representations have been successfully applied to parabolic, elliptic, and even hyperbolic PDEs, including, notably, the complex Gross-Pitaevskii equation developed in Appendix G.

The key idea is to encode the nonlinear terms of the PDE into a branching mechanism: particles follow Brownian dynamics until a random exponential branching time, at which point they reproduce according to rules
determined by the nonlinearity $F$ .
The resulting branching trees provide unbiased MC estimators of the PDE solution.
This stochastic representation is embarrassingly parallelizable, which makes it particularly effective for large-scale simulations and high-dimensional problems.

More generally, when $F$ is local and analytic in $m(t,x)$ , we truncate its power series at order $K$ , yielding a polynomial nonlinearity amenable to branching. Without loss of generality, we write it in the canonical form

(10)

 $F(t,x,m)=1-\sum_{k=0}^{K}a_{k}(t,x)\,m^{k}:=1-F_{p}(t,x,m),$ 

where the coefficients $(a_{k})_{k=0,\cdots,K}$ are functions of $t$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ .
Thus the system (3)-(4) becomes

(11)

 $\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}\varphi_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\varphi_{t}&=c\,\varphi_{t}\Big(1-F_{p}\big(t,x,\varphi_{t}\bar{\varphi}_{T-t}\big)\Big),\\
\partial_{t}\bar{\varphi}_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\bar{\varphi}_{t}&=c\,\bar{\varphi}_{t}\Big(1-F_{p}\big(T\!-\!t,x,\bar{\varphi}_{t}\varphi_{T-t}\big)\Big).\end{aligned}\right.$ 

## 3.1. Branching representation

We use a marked branching Brownian motion with two types of particles:
white vertex $\circ$ represents $\varphi$ ,
black vertex $\bullet$ represents $\bar{\varphi}$ . The branching rate is fixed to be $\beta=c$ , and we choose arbitrarily probabilities $p_{k}>0$ for $k=0,1,\dots,K$ with $\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}=1$ .
Each particle moves as a Brownian motion and lives an exponential time $\tau\sim\mathrm{Exp}(c)$ .
At a branching/death time $s$ , draw $K^{\star}$ with probability $p_{K^{\
conclusion:
We formulate semilinear mean-field Schrödinger bridges with law-dependent $f(m(t,\cdot))$ , $g(m(T,\cdot))$ and characterize optimality through coupled $(\varphi,\bar{\varphi})$ PDEs, equivalently a Lasry - Lions $(m,v)$ system – beyond the linear entropic setting of Sinkhorn and iterative Markovian fitting. We recast the terminal conditions as a nonlinear Sinkhorn system, which we solve by Maximum Mean Discrepancy, using branching diffusions to obtain unbiased stochastic representations of $\varphi$ . Our experiments cover bridge recovery, Gross-Pitaevskii-type couplings, potential interactions, and latent transport.

The numerics are encouraging, but we do not claim systematic superiority over mature diffusion Schrödinger-bridge pipelines in the linear setting. Training in the nonlinear regime still requires careful tuning of the hyperparameters (branching rate $c$ , kernel bandwidths, penalty $\lambda$ ) to remain stable, and both the parallelization of the branching simulation and the variance of the underlying Monte Carlo estimators leave room for improvement. We see this work as a new variational and optimality system whose first mesh-free realization invites variance reduction and hybridization with standard training pipelines.

title: OmniSimulator: Aligning Small Language Models for Authentic Heterogeneous Behavior Modeling
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose user simulators for interactive systems. Prior studies have demonstrated that training on high-quality data can substantially improve model reasoning and downstream task performance. However, the upper bound of user simulation is still constrained by the model's reasoning paradigm: native chain-of-thought often degenerates into shallow pattern matching and fails to adequately model the behavioral factors underlying real user decisions. In this paper, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve the predictive ability of small LLMs for realistic user simulation on short-video platform environments. Specifically, OmniSimulator organizes behavior-oriented reasoning through a structured schema with five dimensions, carefully selects data from real user-behavior scenarios, and introduces a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces under the proposed schema, helping small models learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns rather than relying on superficial behavioral correlations. Based on this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality training instances from three months of historical interaction trajectories of 200 real users, averaging about 50 distilled examples per user. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the average score of Qwen3-8B by 34.33%, achieves performance competitive with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These results suggest that learning structured behavior-oriented reasoning patterns is a promising direction towards scalable and high-fidelity LLM-based user simulation.

body_start:
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose user simulators for interactive systems. Prior studies have demonstrated that training on high-quality data can substantially improve model reasoning and downstream task performance. However, the upper bound of user simulation is still constrained by the model’s reasoning paradigm: native chain-of-thought often degenerates into shallow pattern matching and fails to adequately model the behavioral factors underlying real user decisions. In this paper, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve the predictive ability of small LLMs for realistic user simulation on short-video platform environments. Specifically, OmniSimulator organizes behavior-oriented reasoning through a structured schema with five dimensions, carefully selects data from real user-behavior scenarios, and introduces a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces under the proposed schema, helping small models learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns rather than relying on superficial behavioral correlations. Based on this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality training instances from three months of historical interaction trajectories of 200 real users, averaging about 50 distilled examples per user. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the average score of Qwen3-8B by 34.33%, achieves performance competitive with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment.
These results suggest that learning structured behavior-oriented reasoning patterns is a promising direction towards scalable and high-fidelity LLM-based user simulation11
 1

 Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/icip-cas/OmniSimulator.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong promise in a growing range of downstream applications [30, 13, 22, 12, 8], including recommender systems [5, 10, 7], advertising [20], customer service [27, 14], and interactive agents [29, 26]. Beyond their generative ability, an increasingly appealing direction is to use LLMs as general-purpose user simulators [4, 18, 7], enabling offline evaluation, policy testing, product optimization, and behavior modeling at a scale that would otherwise require expensive online experiments [19, 18]. This trend is especially important for short-video platforms, where user behavior is inherently long-horizon, cross-scenario, and heterogeneous [9]: a user may browse videos, enter live rooms, click ads, shop in e-commerce, search for information, and interact with customer service within one unified behavioral trajectory. Recent studies have shown that training on high-quality data can substantially improve reasoning ability and downstream task performance of LLMs, suggesting that post-training and supervision quality are critical for building stronger simulators. However, real user simulation remains far from solved. On challenging real-world benchmarks such as OmniBehavior [9], even frontier models achieve limited performance, while also exhibiting systematic biases such as overestimating positive actions, generating overly optimistic utterances, and collapsing different users into an average persona [6, 9]. Moreover, although closed-source models such as Claude-Opus-4.5 [2] provide stronger performance, their cost becomes prohibitive when conditioning on long interaction histories, making them difficult to deploy at industrial scale.

A difficulty of user simulation is that real behavior is not generated by direct surface matching between historical interactions and the current scenario. Instead, user actions are mediated by latent mental states, such as stable preference, recent interest drift, transient fatigue, emotional tendency, and momentary decision style. In other words, predicting whether a user will click, purchase, continue watching, or say a particular utterance requires the model to first recover why this user is likely to act in that way at the current scenario. This observation naturally suggests that reasoning capability counts. If the model can explicitly infer the hidden state underlying the next action, it should in principle make more faithful predictions than a model that only performs shallow behavioral imitation. Chain-of-thought (CoT) therefore appears to be a natural candidate for improving user simulation, since it provides an intermediate reasoning process between observed history and predicted behavior. However, our empirical analysis reveals that simply enabling native thinking mode brings almost no benefit for user simulation: across Qwen3 models, the performance of thinking and non-thinking settings is often nearly identical, and in some cases the thinking variant even performs worse. A closer inspection of native CoT outputs explains why: existing models rarely use reasoning to reconstruct the user’s latent mental state; instead, they tend to produce generic justifications, shallow pattern matching, or direct guesses based on superficial correlations. This suggests that the bottleneck is not merely whether the model generates more reasoning tokens, but whether its reasoning follows a behavior-oriented structure.

Figure 1: Overview of OmniSimulator. The framework consists of two stages. (1) Schema Definition: we define a structured chain-of-thought schema that guides the model to simulate human-like internal reasoning from three inputs: user profile, historical interaction logs, and the current scenario. The schema decomposes reasoning into five dimensions: User Profile Grounding, Historical Behavioral State, Content Relevance Alignment, Decision Mode Identification, and Final Decision Declaration. (2) Teacher-driven Distillation: a teacher LLM generates structured reasoning traces under the schema for different task types, and high-quality traces are selected through rejection sampling to construct the distilled training set for small user simulators. The right panel shows a case example of the structured user-state reasoning trace, where the model infers latent user state step by step and then predicts the final correct behavior.

Motivated by this, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve small LLMs for real user simulation on short-video platform environments. The key idea is to teach the model to follow behavior-oriented structured reasoning rather than free-form reasoning. Specifically, OmniSimulator introduces a structured CoT schema that forces the model to infer latent user states through five dimensions: User Profile Grounding, Historical Behavioral State Inference, Content Relevance Alignment, Decision Mode Identification, and Final Decision Declaration. On top of this schema, we build a task-aware causal distillation pipeline: a teacher model (GPT-OSS-120B [1]) generates multiple reasoning traces for each prediction point under task-specific prompting strategies, and only traces consistent with ground truth are retained through rejection sampling. Following this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality distilled training instances from three months of interaction histories of 200 real users.
Experiments show that OmniSimulator substantially improves small models over zero-shot and free-CoT baselines, enables Qwen3-8B to achieve performance competitive with strong proprietary models such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 [3], and alleviates overestimation bias while supporting smaller-scale deployment. These results suggest that the upper bound of LLM-based user simulation is constrained not only by model scale, but also by the reasoning supervision paradigm.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We identify a key weakness of existing LLM-based user simulators: native CoT struggles to predict realistic user behavior, yielding only marginal improvements in behavioral prediction over non-thinking settings.

• 

We propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework that combines a structured five-dimensional CoT schema with a task-aware causal distillation pipeline, enabling small models to learn behavior-oriented reasoning patterns for user simulation.

• 

We construct 9,881 high-quality distilled training instances from real-world long-horizon user trajectories, and OmniSimulator substantially improves small LLMs, achieves performance competitive with strong closed-source baselines and mitigates overestimation bias while supporting efficient small-model deployment.

## 2 Methodology

In this section, we first formulate user behavior simulation on short-video platforms, and then present OmniSimulator, our training framework for improving small LLMs on realistic user simulation. The central idea is that real user behavior is not generated by direct surface matching between historical interactions and the current scenario. Instead, it is mediated by a latent decision process shaped by stable preference, recent interest drift, transient affect, and the decision regime at the current moment. Existing LLMs, even with native thinking mode, often fail to reconstruct this hidden process and instead rely on shallow behavioral priors. To address this issue, OmniSimulator explicitly teaches the model to infer latent user states before predicting behavior. The framework consists of two tightly coupled components: (1) a structured chain-of-thought schema that organizes reasoning into a fixed sequence of human-like internal deliberation steps, and (2) a task-aware rationale distillation pipeline that converts teacher-generated reasoning traces into high-quality supervision for student models.

## 2.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate user simulation as a user-conditioned prediction problem over long-horizon, cross-scenario interaction trajectories. For a user $u$ , let

 $H_{t}^{u}=\{e_{1}^{u},e_{2}^{u},\dots,e_{t}^{u}\}$ 

(1)

denote the historical interaction sequence before time step $t+1$ , where each event $e_{i}^{u}$ may come from different scenarios such as video browsing, live streaming, e-commerce shopping, customer-service dialogue, advertisement recommendation, and search. Let $x_{t+1}^{u}$ denote the current scenario context. The goal is to predict the corresponding user response

 $y_{t+1}^{u}=f_{\theta}(H_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u}),$ 

(2)

where $y_{t+1}^{u}$ may be a binary decision, a continuous value, or a natural-language utterance.

A direct mapping from $(H_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u})$ to $y_{t+1}^{u}$ is often insufficient. In realistic platforms, a user’s next behavior is mediated by hidden mental states that are not explicitly recorded in logs, such as stable preference, short-term tendency, fatigue, emotion, and momentary decision style. We therefore introduce an implicit latent state $z_{t}^{u}$ and decompose user simulation as

 $p(y_{t+1}^{u}\mid H_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u})=\sum_{z_{t}^{u}}p(y_{t+1}^{u}\mid z_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u})\,p(z_{t}^{u}\mid H_{t}^{u}).$ 

(3)

Since $z_{t}^{u}$ is unobserved, OmniSimulator does not supervise it as an explicit label. Instead, we represent it as a structured reasoning trace in natural language, and train the model to infer this trace before answering the final behavior prediction.

## 2.2 Preliminary Analysis: Revealing Native Thinking Effects

Figure 2: Preliminary analysis on native thinking mode. Across Qwen backbones, enabling native thinking yields only marginal or inconsistent gains over standard instruction-following inference.

We first investigate whether native thinking mode alone is sufficient for realistic user simulation. Intuitively, this task appears to benefit from reasoning, since the model must recover the hidden factors that connect long interaction histories to current decisions. However, our preliminary analysis reveals that this intuition does not hold under standard prompting.

Figure 2 compares the average OmniBehavior scores of multiple Qwen3-series [28] backbones under two settings: Instruct and Thinking. We observe that enabling native thinking yields little or no consistent gain over standard instruction-following inference. Across model scales, the two settings are often nearly identical, and in some cases the thinking variant even performs worse. This result suggests that the bottleneck is not the absence of additional reasoning tokens, but the absence of the right reasoning structure. By inspecting native CoT outputs, we find that models often produce generic justifications or shallow guesses, failing to explicitly reconstruct the user’s latent psychological state. This observation motivates our approach: rather than simply allowing the model to think more, we guide it to follow a structured, behavior-oriented reasoning process.

## 2.3 Overview of OmniSimulator

Figure 1 illustrates the overall framework. For each prediction point, we first provide the teacher model with the user’s historical interaction trajectory and the current scenario context. The teacher is required to reason under a structured schema that explicitly reconstructs the user’s latent mental state. To increase diversity, we sample multiple reasoning traces for each example with stochastic decoding. Depending on the task type, we apply different prompting strategies to control the degree of access to ground truth. The resulting traces are filtered by rejection sampling, and only those whose final answers are consistent with the observed outcome are retained as supervised fine-tuning data. Finally, the student model is trained to generate both the structured reasoning trace and the final prediction.

This design follows a simple principle: rather than only teaching the model what to predict, we also provide structured rationale supervision for how the prediction may be derived from behavioral evidence. In this way, latent-state reconstruction becomes explicit, learnable, and distillable.

## Structured Chain-of-Thought Schema.

The first stage of OmniSimulator is a structured CoT schema tailored for user simulation. Our design is motivated not only by the empirical analysis above, but also by cognitive theories of human behavior. Prior work suggests that behavior is mediated by stable person-level characteristics, dynamically activated cognitive-affective states, and their interaction with situational cues [17]. In parallel, dual-process accounts further distinguish between reflective, deliberative decision making and more impulsive behavior pathways [21]. Native thinking mode alone is therefore insufficient, because it leaves this behavioral reasoning path under-specified for human behavior simulation tasks. To address this issue, we require the model to generate reasoning within a <think> block following five fixed dimensions:

1. 

User Profile Grounding: The model first interprets stable user characteristics reflected in long-term history, such as age, gender, educational background. This step provides the global behavioral background of the user.

2. 

Historical Behavioral State: The model then infers the user’s dynamic internal state from recent and long-horizon interactions. This includes long-term interest continuation, short-term preference drift, current fatigue level, and emotional tendency. Compared with the previous step, the focus here is not the user’s general profile, but the user’s state from the history sequences at the current moment.

3. 

Content Relevance Alignment: Next, the model matches the inferred user state with the current scenario and content. This step examines whether the current item is aligned with the user’s active interests, intent, mood, or aversion, and serves as the bridge between historical state and prediction item.

4. 

Decision Mode Identification: The model further determines whether the current behavior is primarily driven by rational decision or random decision. Rational decisions are mainly explained by interpretable factors such as fatigue levels in this session, while random decisions are more influenced by curiosity or stochasticity. This distinction is essential for modeling negative outcomes and low-confidence actions.

5. 

Final Decision Declaration: Before closing the </think> block, the model should explicitly state its final decision, and this declaration is required to be fully consistent with the final output answer. This design reduces reasoning-answer mismatch and improves the controllability of the generated traces.

With this schema, OmniSimulator decomposes user simulation into the following process:

 $(H_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u})\rightarrow r_{t}^{u}\rightarrow y_{t+1}^{u},$ 

(4)

where $r_{t}^{u}$ denotes the structured reasoning trace. In practice, $r_{t}^{u}$ serves as a textual proxy of the unobserved latent state $z_{t}^{u}$ . Compared with unconstrained CoT, this schema forces the model to move from observable behaviors to hidden user states, and then from hidden user states to final actions.

## Task-aware Rationale Distillation.

Structured reasoning alone is not sufficient if teacher-generated traces are noisy. We therefore design a task-aware rationale distillation pipeline to obtain high-quality supervision for student training.

For each prediction item, we use a teacher model (GPT-OSS-120B [1] in our experiment) to rollout $N$ candidate reasoning traces under the structured schema. Formally, given an example $(H_{t}^{u},x_{t+1}^{u},y_{t+1}^{u})$ , we sample

 $\mathcal{R}_{t}^{u}=\{r_{t,1}^{u},r_{t,2}^{u},\dots,r_{t,N}^{u}\}$ 

(5)

with relatively high temperature. This design allows the teacher to generate multiple candidate rationales for each prediction instance. However, different task types have different output spaces and different risks of information leakage, so we use different prompting strategies for different tasks.

• 

Binary tasks: For binary prediction, we use forward-only reasoning. The teacher is not given the ground-truth label, and must predict the outcome solely from historical evidence and the current scenario. This avoids hindsight bias, since
limitations: The current study evaluates held-out users from one short-video platform within a temporally overlapping collection window, and therefore does not establish temporal or cross-platform generalization. Moreover, the structured reasoning traces provide behavior-oriented supervision rather than direct evidence of users’ actual cognitive processes. In particular, the distilled reasoning traces may still inherit part of the teacher model’s own biases, while target-derived guidance for continuous and textual tasks introduces a risk of post-hoc rationalization. Although our ablations support the effectiveness of the full framework, the respective contributions of the schema and filtering have not been fully isolated under strictly matched conditions. Future work will investigate broader-domain generalization, the faithfulness of target-conditioned rationales, and robustness across independent training runs.

title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.

Abstract

Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems,
shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon
interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how
effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating
reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing
approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead
to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations.
To address this, we introduce Harness Scaling, a new scaling
dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to
diverse execution configurations.
Concretely, we construct a factorized
harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial
coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage
with controlled variation for the same task.
Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling
consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations.
Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer
effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models
trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish
harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and
highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for
cross-harness generalization.

## 1 Introduction

Agent harnesses are playing an increasingly central role in modern
agentic systems [31]. By supporting sustained interaction, tool use, state
maintenance, and recovery from failures [4], harnesses have substantially
improved agent performance on complex, long-horizon tasks [38, 32, 16]. Yet the
benefits of a capable harness depend not only on its design, but also on
whether the underlying policy can use it effectively [14]. This naturally motivates optimizing the policy directly through the harness
with reinforcement learning [36, 39], which strengthens its ability to exploit the
available interaction mechanisms during task solving.

However, existing approaches typically optimize the policy through a
single fixed harness [7, 34]. While effective within the training harness, such
optimization may encourage specialization to a particular execution
configuration and weaken transfer across harnesses. We therefore introduce
Harness Scaling, extending policy optimization from a single
harness to diverse execution configurations.
Unlike task or environment
scaling [29, 6, 3, 35], which expands what agents solve or where they operate, Harness
Scaling introduces diversity in how policies execute and interact with the
same underlying task and environment, promoting generalization across
execution configurations.

A key consideration in Harness Scaling is how to model harness variation
and select a compact set of configurations for training.
Given the modular
nature of agent harnesses [7, 23], we factorize harness variation along five
components: system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, and workflow.
Each component contains multiple realizations, whose combinations define a
factorial space of complete harness configurations. As variation along these
components increases, the space expands rapidly, while exhaustive training
can introduce substantial redundancy under a fixed budget. We therefore
preserve low-order factorial structure in a compact training set, balancing
individual component realizations and their pairwise combinations through
an orthogonal design [21, 8]. During reinforcement learning, the same task is paired
with structurally nearby harness configurations, providing controlled local
variation within each task while maintaining broad coverage across the
training space.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of Harness Scaling, we evaluate
cross-harness generalization across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and
RL algorithms. By training across diverse harness configurations, Harness
Scaling reduces specialization to any single harness and encourages more
generalizable agent behavior. Empirically, it consistently outperforms
single-harness RL on unseen white-box configurations.
More importantly, policies trained through structured white-box harness
variation transfer effectively to complex external black-box harnesses [18, 1],
outperforming single-harness black-box training.
These results establish harness diversity as a
meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL, while showing that effective
scaling depends critically on how this diversity is organized during
training. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

• 

We introduce Harness Scaling as a new scaling dimension
for agentic reinforcement learning, distinct from conventional scaling
over tasks and environments, and study how training across diverse
harness configurations affects generalization beyond a single execution
setting.

• 

We develop a structured framework for Harness Scaling that
factorizes harness variation, selects a compact training set with balanced
factorial coverage, and organizes cross-harness training by assigning
structurally nearby configurations to the same task across the training space.

• 

We demonstrate across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms
that Harness Scaling substantially improves generalization to unseen
white-box and external black-box harnesses, establishing both the value
of scaling across harnesses and the importance of organizing this scaling
structurally.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning has emerged as an important paradigm for improving
the capabilities of LLMs [40, 24]. Recent work has extended RL from single-turn
reasoning to increasingly complex agentic settings, including tool use [2, 28], web
navigation [20], software engineering [27], and professional workflows [33]. As agentic RL moves toward broader
capability, recent efforts have increasingly scaled training along the
task and environment dimensions. Task scaling [30, 3, 5] broadens the
distribution of problems used for policy optimization, while environment
scaling [6, 29, 35] expands the range of external settings in which agents interact and
receive feedback. These directions expand what agents learn to
solve and where they learn to operate, while often retaining a fixed
execution harness. In contrast, we study harness diversity as an additional
scaling dimension for agentic RL, focusing on policy learning and
generalization across execution configurations.

## 2.2 Harness Design and Optimization

The design of an agent harness can substantially shape how a language model
uses tools, maintains context, and performs long-horizon tasks [38, 14, 16].
Early agent systems largely relied on manually designed harnesses, while
subsequent work has explored automated harness improvement through search,
editing, and evolution based on task outcomes or execution
trajectories [13, 11, 23]. A complementary line of work directly optimizes
model policies within complex agent harnesses, including reinforcement
learning through black-box harnesses [36, 7, 26, 15, 17, 9]. These directions either
improve the harness itself or adapt a policy to a particular harness.
Harness Scaling instead studies policy optimization over a structured combinatorial space of harness configurations, with the goal of improving generalization to unseen configurations.

## 3 Method

Figure 1: 
Overview of Harness Scaling, from structured harness-space construction
to cross-harness training and generalization to unseen configurations.

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

To study harness scaling systematically, we first formalize the space of
execution configurations and the generalization problem defined over it.
We construct a factorized harness space, define a structural notion of
proximity among its configurations, and formulate the generalization
objectives that motivate the structured harness selection and multi-harness
training procedures shown as in Figure 1.

## 3.1.1 Factorized Harness Space

A harness serves as the execution layer through which a policy interacts
with its environment. Rather than treating it as a monolithic implementation,
we factorize the harness into five components: system prompt,
tool interface, observation, context management,
and workflow, denoted by $S,T,O,C,$ and $W$ , respectively.
These components govern the instructions provided to the policy, tool access,
environment feedback, interaction history, and execution procedure,
collectively shaping how the policy perceives, acts, and maintains state
throughout task execution. This factorization provides an operational
decomposition of the harness, while allowing the effects of different
components to interact.

We instantiate each component through a family of component-specific
transformations. For a component $F\in\{S,T,O,C,W\}$ , let $F^{(0)}$ 
denote its base realization and $\tau_{F}^{(\ell)}$ the $\ell$ -th
transformation applied to it:

 $F^{(\ell)}=\tau_{F}^{(\ell)}\left(F^{(0)}\right).$ 

(1)

A transformation modifies only the target component while preserving the
remaining components, task semantics, and environment. For example, it may
reorganize the system prompt, alter tool schemas or naming conventions,
change observation feedback, modify context retention or compression, or
impose a different execution procedure. Detailed definitions and
implementations are provided in Appendix A.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ , $\mathcal{T}$ , $\mathcal{O}$ , $\mathcal{C}$ ,
and $\mathcal{W}$ denote the resulting realization sets. A complete harness
configuration selects one realization from each set, defining the factorized
harness space

 $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{W}.$ 

(2)

Each configuration $h\in\mathcal{H}$ therefore specifies a complete execution
setting for the same underlying task and environment.

The product structure of $\mathcal{H}$ also induces a natural notion of
structural proximity. For $h_{i},h_{j}\in\mathcal{H}$ , the Hamming distance
 $d_{\mathrm{H}}(h_{i},h_{j})$ counts the number of component dimensions on
which they differ. Equivalently, $\mathcal{H}$ forms a Hamming graph whose
adjacent configurations differ in exactly one component. We use this
distance to organize local cross-harness variation during training.

## 3.1.2 Generalization Objective

The central objective of Harness Scaling is to learn policies that remain
effective beyond the harness configurations observed during training. We
consider two complementary forms of cross-harness generalization: broad
combinatorial generalization within the constructed harness space and transfer
to complex real-world black-box harnesses beyond it.

In-Space Combinatorial Generalization.

Let $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subset\mathcal{H}$ denote the harness
configurations used for training. We evaluate on held-out configurations in
 $\mathcal{H}\setminus\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ , whose complete
combinations are unseen during training. This setting provides broad coverage
of unseen combinations within the controlled factorized space.

Out-of-Space Generalization.

We further evaluate transfer to complex real-world black-box harnesses whose
execution configurations are not represented in $\mathcal{H}$ . This setting
examines whether training over structured white-box harness variation can
transfer to external execution systems beyond the constructed design space.

## 3.2 Harness Scaling with Structured Selection

As the factorized harness space grows combinatorially with its component
dimensions, exhaustive training can introduce substantial redundancy.
We therefore construct a compact training set that preserves broad factorial
coverage under a fixed optimization budget.

## 3.2.1 Factorial Coverage

The harness space in Eq. 2 can be viewed as a
factorial design, where each harness component corresponds to a factor
and its realizations correspond to different levels [21, 8]. To construct a compact
subset without losing basic coverage of this combinatorial space, we preserve
its low-order factorial structure: the representation of individual component
realizations and their pairwise combinations. These correspond to the
first- and second-order projections of the full factorial space, respectively.

Component Balance.

We first require the realizations of each component to be represented
evenly across the selected configurations. This ensures coverage along
every component dimension without overrepresenting particular realizations.

Pairwise Combination Balance.

Component balance alone does not control how realizations from different
components are combined. We therefore additionally balance all pairwise
combinations. Indexing the five component dimensions by
 $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,5\}$ , let $N_{ij}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})$ denote the number
of selected configurations containing the $\ell$ -th realization of
component $i$ together with the $\ell^{\prime}$ -th realization of component
 $j$ . Pairwise balance requires

 $N_{ij}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})=\lambda,$ 

(3)

where $\lambda$ is the common occurrence count for every realization
pair of any $i\neq j$ . In factorial-design terminology, this corresponds
to strength-2 balance, under which every pair of realizations from any two
components appears equally often in the selected set.

## 3.2.2 Harness Set Construction

We construct the training harness set using a strength-2 orthogonal design
over the component realizations in $\mathcal{H}$ . This provides a direct
construction of a compact subset satisfying the component-level and pairwise
balance defined above, without searching over possible subsets of the full
harness space.

The size of such a design is constrained by its pairwise coverage.
Suppose there are $M$ component dimensions, each with $L$ realizations,
and every pairwise realization combination occurs $\lambda$ times.
Since any two components admit $L^{2}$ realization combinations, the number
of selected configurations $N$ satisfies

 $N=\lambda L^{2}.$ 

(4)

Moreover, a strength-2 orthogonal design must satisfy the Rao
bound [21, 8],

 $N\geq 1+M(L-1).$ 

(5)

Pairwise balance determines the replication structure of the design, while
the Rao bound provides a lower bound on the number of configurations.
These conditions restrict the admissible design sizes.

We instantiate a strength-2 orthogonal design satisfying these constraints,
yielding the training harness set
 $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subset\mathcal{H}$ . The resulting set preserves
exact component-level and pairwise balance using only a compact subset of the
full factorial space. While these low-order projections are balanced, many
complete harness combinations remain unseen during training, enabling
evaluation of in-space combinatorial generalization. Further details of the
construction and the resulting training configurations are provided in
Appendix B.

## 3.3 Reinforcement Learning across Harnesses

Training each task under multiple harnesses exposes the policy to different
execution configurations for the same underlying problem, encouraging the
learned behavior to generalize beyond a single harness. We realize this over
the selected harness set $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by pairing each task
with a small group of structurally related configurations. The assignment is
designed to combine controlled variation within each task with broad coverage
across the training harness space, and the resulting task–harness instances
form the basis for rollout collection and policy optimization.

## 3.3.1 Cross-Harness Task Assignment

We use a locality-aware strategy to organize how harness configurations are
assigned to tasks. For each task $x$ , we assign $K$ configurations from
 $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ .
An anchor harness
 $h_{x}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}})$ is first sampled
uniformly from the training set, and the remaining $K-1$ configurations
are chosen from $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}\setminus\{h_{x}\}$ as those
with the smallest Hamming distance $d_{\mathrm{H}}(h_{x},h)$ to the anchor.
This associates each task with a
small set of nearby configurations while allowing different tasks to cover
different regions of the training harness space. The resulting harness set
for task $x$ is

 $\mathcal{H}_{x}=\left\{h_{x},\,h_{x}^{(1)},\ldots,h_{x}^{(K-1)}\right\},$ 

(6)

where $h_{x}^{(1)},\ldots,h_{x}^{(K-1)}$ denote the $K-1$ nearest
configurations to $h_{x}$ under $d_{\mathrm{H}}$ .

This assignment combines local cross-harness variation with broad coverage
over training. For a given task, nearby harnesses provide related but distinct
execution configurations, while random anchor selection distributes different
tasks throughout $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ . Each task therefore yields
 $K$ task–harness instances for rollout collection and policy optimization.
When $K=1$ , only the sampled anchor is assigned to the task, while different
tasks remain distributed across $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}$ .

## 3.3.2 Multi-Harness Policy Optimization

Each task–harness instance $(x,h)$ is executed under its assigned
harness, producing a trajectory $\tau$ and the corresponding reward.
The $K$ harnesses assigned to the same task are used over $K$ 
successive training steps, allowing the policy to receive learning signals
from different execution configurations for the same underlying task.

For a policy-update batch $\mathcal{B}$ induced by the task–harness
training distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{MH}}$ , let
 $N_{\mathcal{B}}$ denote the total number of valid policy-generated
tokens in the batch. We optimize the standard clipped policy objective:

(7)

In this work, we study Harness Scaling as a new scaling dimension for agentic
reinforcement learning, motivated by the limitations of optimizing policies
through a single fixed harness. We formalize harness diversity as a structured configuration space and
develop a framework that integrates structured harness selection with
cross-harness policy training. Across benchmarks,
model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling substantially improves
generalization to unseen white-box configurations and transfers effectively
to complex external black-box harnesses. Our results further show that the
benefits of scaling depend on how harness diversity is selected and incorporated into training, rather than on diversity alone.
More broadly, these findings expand the scope of agentic RL scaling beyond
what agents solve and where they operate to how they interact and execute,
positioning harness variation as a complementary dimension for improving
generalization across diverse execution systems.

Abstract.

Policy-as-Code (PaC) has emerged as a foundational paradigm in cloud-native systems. However, repairing Rego policies remains challenging due to their strict syntax, declarative semantics, and specific verification requirements. Existing automated program repair (APR) methods are mainly designed for mainstream languages and struggle to accommodate the unique policy logic and repair workflows of Rego. Thus, Rego policy repair remains a manual process driven by trial and error. To address this, we introduce RegoBench, the first automated Rego policy benchmark comprising 1,159 real-world defects, and propose RegoMender, a feedback-guided multi-agent framework. Collaborating via a shared blackboard and an atomic toolkit, RegoMender dynamically executes patching, rewriting, or rolling back, to resolve complex repair scenarios. Evaluated on RegoBench, RegoMender achieves syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9% and 77.9%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.4%. Unlike other approaches whose performance drops in complex scenarios, RegoMender maintains effectiveness across single-step and chained repair tasks. Furthermore, it generalizes strongly across HCL and SQL and achieves an 86.4% repair rate on 132 real-world CVE vulnerabilities, proving its robustness and practical utility for security.

Keywords: 
Policy-as-Code, Automated Program Repair, Rego, Multi-agent Systems, Large Language Models, Cloud Native Security

## 1. Introduction

Policy-as-Code has become a core paradigm for enforcing security and compliance requirements in cloud-native systems. It represents policies as executable rules that are continuously evaluated against structured artifacts, such as API requests, configuration objects, and infrastructure-as-code (IaC) plans, across both delivery and runtime environments. A widely adopted implementation of PaC is Open Policy Agent (OPA), which separates policy logic from application code and provides a unified evaluation framework across heterogeneous platforms. In practice, OPA is integrated into CI/CD pipelines for pre-deployment validation and into Kubernetes admission control to prevent non-compliant resource updates. OPA policies are written in Rego, a declarative language designed to express policy rules over inputs and produce authorization decisions (Open Policy Agent (OPA), ).

However, repairing Rego policies is particularly challenging because of their declarative semantics and strict validation requirements. Unlike imperative languages, Rego follows a logic programming paradigm derived from Datalog, where unification combines pattern matching with variable binding.
This context sensitivity means that even a seemingly simple modification may unintentionally alter the logic of the policy. Furthermore, policy evaluation may return undefined when certain data paths are missing. Rather than raising an error, this result may cause conditions to be skipped.

Meanwhile, the current APR benchmarks (Ye et al., 2025; Saavedra et al., 2025; Just et al., 2014; Jimenez et al., 2024) have been developed primarily for mainstream programming languages and rely on test suites as correctness oracles. Classic datasets such as Defects4J (Just et al., 2014) provide standardized collections of real-world Java bugs with regression tests, while repository-level benchmarks like SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) evaluate issue resolution in large-scale Python repositories, collectively advancing research in APR. However, dedicated benchmarks for evaluating the automated repair of Rego policies are absent. Unlike conventional programs, policies written in Rego are validated through a tool-driven workflow that includes linting and compilation, policy-specific testing, and compliance checks derived from domain requirements.

This mismatch presents two fundamental challenges for the automated repair of Rego policies: (i) Lack of benchmarks for Rego repair. To date, there is no publicly available dataset specifically designed for Rego policy repair, making it difficult to systematically evaluate whether existing APR or LLM-based approaches can effectively handle Rego-specific syntax, semantics, and verification workflows. (ii) Heavy reliance on manual or ad hoc LLM-based repair workflows. In practice, Rego policy repair still relies heavily on manual debugging by domain experts or on ad hoc interactions with LLMs
, developers must manually interpret policy failures, construct prompts, invoke opa check and opa test, assess the verification outcomes, and iteratively revise candidate patches. This human-in-the-loop repair process is time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale, especially when repairs must preserve repository-specific policy intent and compliance semantics.

To address the lack of systematic data and reproducible evaluation for Rego policy repair, we mine real-world defect fixes from 2,847 GitHub repositories that actively maintain Rego policies. We then design a strict three-stage filtering pipeline to progressively refine the raw commit-level candidates, including isolated patch extraction, redundancy and noise mitigation, and deterministic verification under a standardized OPA toolchain. This process yields 1,159 high-quality buggy-fix pairs that are fully reproducible. This benchmark covers seven OPA-derived defect types, preserves the natural difficulty distribution of real-world defects and features a high proportion of complex chained repairs, directly measuring how well repair methods handle practical programming tasks.

Furthermore, we design RegoMender, a multi-agent framework for automated Rego policy repair. RegoMender establishes a closed loop between code repair and OPA verification by coordinating three specialized roles, namely the Orchestrator, Analyzer, and Repairer, through a shared Blackboard and an auditable atomic toolkit. Specifically, all repository interactions are carried out through the atomic toolkit, which provides five core operations: Verify, Context Scan, Error Triage, Rewrite, and Patch. This design ensures that each repair step remains precise and reproducible. Guided by real-time verifier feedback, the Orchestrator coordinates the Analyzer and Repairer, records progress on the Blackboard, and rolls back when necessary to avoid stagnation. In this way, RegoMender supports reliable multi-step repair, particularly in cases where resolving one failure exposes additional hidden defects.

To evaluate the effectiveness of RegoMender, we conduct extensive experiments on RegoBench. First, the results show that, compared to existing automated program repair methods (Yin et al., 2024; Bouzenia et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a), RegoMender achieves syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9% and 77.9%, respectively. It
ranks first across all seven defect types, demonstrating the effectiveness of our agent orchestration and task decision-making mechanisms. Second, we analyze the impact of different backbone models on RegoMender and the baselines. We find that RegoMender demonstrates superior robustness across different models
, and DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus (Liu et al., 2024) provides the best balance between performance and cost. Third, we conduct a comparative study on single-step and chained repair tasks. We find that
RegoMender maintains stable performance in both situations. Furthermore, we conduct an ablation study on the designed atomic toolkit. The results reveal that the Context Scan
tool has the most significant impact on the framework’s performance. This indicates that the repair process for the Rego policies relies on context gathering
. To evaluate its cross-language generalizability, we extend our method to two additional domain-specific languages (HCL and SQL). The results show that RegoMender continues to maintain a significant advantage over other baselines. Finally, to verify its practical utility in the real world, we evaluate our method on 132 CVE vulnerabilities.
RegoMender achieves a repair rate of 86.4%, outperforming ThinkRepair and RepairAgent and demonstrating its practical potential for security-related repair.

Figure 1. An Example for Rego Policy Repair.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

• 

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to explore automated repair of Rego policies, laying the groundwork for systematic and reproducible research in this area.

• 

We introduce RegoBench, the first benchmark for automated Rego policy repair. To construct it, we design a three-stage filtering pipeline and apply it to 2,847 GitHub repositories that actively maintain Rego policies, curating a high-quality dataset of 1,159 real-world defects.

• 

We propose RegoMender, a multi-agent framework where Orchestrator, Analyzer, and Repairer agents collaborate via a Blackboard and an auditable toolkit to achieve Rego repairs with rollback-based stagnation control.

• 

Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RegoMender achieves state-of-the-art test-based semantic success rates of 77.9%, outperforming
the strongest baseline by 13.4%. Notably, it exhibits exceptional stability in complex multi-step defects and successfully resolves 86.4% of real-world CVEs.

## 2. Motivation

Figure 1 shows a motivating example of Rego policy repair. In Figure 1(a), the buggy rule uses unification (=) and directly reads input.request.object.metadata.labels after checking that the resource kind is "Pod". Under Rego’s undefined-value semantics, if the labels field is absent or the binding fails, the rule body may become undefined, so the intended deny decision is not produced. In Figure 1(b), the repair uses explicit comparison (==) for the kind check, retrieves labels with object.get(input...metadata, "labels", ), and uses strict assignment (:=) for derived values. These changes handle missing labels explicitly and restore a well-defined admission decision.
This example shows why Rego repair is language-specific. The operators =, :=, and == represent unification, assignment, and comparison rather than simple symbol replacements, and whether an input path is defined depends on the runtime context. Therefore, Rego repairs should be validated with the standard OPA toolchain (opa check and opa test) to avoid deployment failures. Current LLMs also have limited experience with Rego repair because repair data remains scarce, making reliable decisions from prior patterns difficult.

Based on the above analysis, we construct RegoBench, a benchmark of 1,159 Rego repair instances covering a broad range of syntax and semantic errors, and propose RegoMender, a multi-agent framework for automated Rego policy repair. Recent software engineering systems use specialized agents for planning, analysis, coding, and tool use (He et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Tufano et al., 2024). However, such collaboration does not directly address Rego-specific needs in policy semantics, context extraction, and OPA-based verification. To address these needs, our framework coordinates three specialized agents via a shared toolkit and blackboard for automated Rego policy repair.

## 3. Overview

In this section, we first describe the construction of the proposed benchmark, RegoBench (§3.1), followed by a detailed presentation of our multi-agent repair framework, RegoMender (§3.2).

## 3.1. RegoBench Construction

We construct RegoBench, the first benchmark dedicated to real-world Rego defects, follows three main steps. First, we define each repair instance and the evaluation criteria for a successful repair. Next, we execute the data filtering process to collect high-quality instances from open-source repositories. Finally, we classify the benchmark along several characteristic dimensions to provide a comprehensive overview of the dataset.

Figure 2. 
Overview of RegoBench Construction and RegoMender Workflow.

## 3.1.1. Instance Definition.

We define each repair instance through four core components that encapsulate all necessary context, ensuring each defect is self-contained and independently verifiable:

• 

Code Pair. We store two versions of the policy code: $C_{bug}$ and $C_{fix}$ . $C_{bug}$ represents the defective policy, while $C_{fix}$ is the corresponding manual fix. Alongside the raw code, we record metadata, such as the commit hash, repository link, and relative file paths. This information enables the precise historical code state to be retrieved and replayed deterministically.

• 

Controlled Context. This component includes dependency resolution results, the module import graph, and generated code stubs. These elements allow for isolated verification, meaning the policy can be evaluated locally without the need to download or configure the entire repository.

• 

Standardized Toolchain. We enforce a fixed OPA version (v1.10.1) and consistent command line arguments. This ensures consistent diagnostic messages and removes any variability that might arise from using different tool versions.

• 

Two-Tier Oracle Records. We organize verification into two tiers. The first ensures syntactic correctness via opa check, covering syntax errors, linking issues, type mismatches, and safety violations. The second ensures semantic correctness via opa test to prevent logical regressions. To qualify as a valid repair instance, the code must pass both tiers, guaranteeing that every sample is syntactically and behaviorally correct.

## 3.1.2. Data Filtering.

To construct the initial corpus, we query the GitHub Search API for repositories containing .rego files. To ensure data quality and relevance, we apply a strict activity filter, retaining only repositories with at least 40 commits between January 1, 2020, and June 30, 2024. This yields 2,847 qualified repositories. We then analyze their commit histories to extract potential defect repairs, resulting in 54,821 raw candidates.
However, extracting these defects from open source repositories introduces noise. Specifically, we observe four patterns of invalid repairs. First, superficial fixes occur when commits labeled as repairs consist only of formatting changes or code refactoring. Second, invalid repairs occur when developers simply delete code to pass checks without fixing the actual defect. Third, coupling across files scatters the repair logic across multiple formats, such as Rego, YAML, and Go, making it difficult to isolate the core defect. Fourth, environmental instability arises when failures depend on external variables or continuous integration contexts that are difficult to reproduce.
We therefore design a three-stage filtering pipeline to obtain a high-quality dataset.

1) Isolated Patch Extraction. To resolve coupling across files, we enforce a strict single-file pairing rule. Only commits with substantive edits confined to a single .rego file are retained, ensuring a clear mapping between the defective and fixed states at the same file path. Nonfunctional edits
are discarded to ensure each instance represents a meaningful repair. This filtering step reduces the raw corpus from 54,821 to 8,643 candidates.

2) Redundancy & Noise Mitigation. To reduce noise from repetitive patches, we implement a clear deduplication strategy. We first exclude forked and archived repositories and then use file fingerprints, defined by the repository, commit hash, and file path, to prevent redundant processing. Additionally, we apply content hashing to eliminate identical code copies caused by version control operations. Finally, we manually audit the dataset to discard samples where the link between the code change and the verification result is unclear. Through this process, we retain 3,071 candidates.

3) Two-Tier Oracle Verification. Finally, to ensure reproducibility and eliminate environmental inconsistencies, we establish a deterministic two-tier verification process using the standard OPA toolchain. Each retained instance must satisfy strict evaluation criteria. First, the defective policy must trigger a verifiable failure (via either opa check or opa test) to confirm the presence of a bug. Second, the developer fix must successfully pass both verification tiers. This process guarantees that every accepted instance is both syntactically valid and behaviorally correct.

Following this three-stage filtering pipeline, we refine the raw data into a dataset of 1,159 high-quality and reproducible instances.

## 3.1.3. Dataset Characterization.

Following standard practices (Jimenez et al., 2024; Just et al., 2014; Le Goues et al., 2015; Saha et al., 2018) in benchmark construction, we preserve the natural distribution of the filtered dataset. To characterize this dataset, we classify the repair difficulty into three levels: easy, medium, and hard. We then engage three senior developers to manually evaluate and classify the 1,159 repair instances. To measure the consistency of their independent evaluations, we calculate the Fleiss’ Kappa (Fleiss, 1971) statistic. The resulting score is 0.85, which indicates an almost perfect agreement among the three developers.
For the few instances with conflicting classifications, the developers hold discussions to review the instances and reach a final consensus.
The labeling results reveal that 518 instances fall into the easy category, 372 into the medium category, and 269 into the hard category. This proportion is consistent with previous empirical findings (Karampatsis and Sutton, 2020; Purushothaman and Perry, 2005; Zhong and Su, 2015), confirming t

title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.
