body_start:
Abstract

Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user’s framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

## 1 Introduction

Today, we see a widespread adoption of conversational agents not only for task-oriented assistance but also for social interaction, emotional support, and companionship (Robb & Mann, 2025; Phang et al., 2025). Such interactions typically involve personal disclosures (Papneja & Yadav, 2025; Robb & Mann, 2025), while studies have also shown association of loneliness, emotional dependence, and problematic use with greater chatbot use (Fang et al., 2025). The understanding how models respond behaviorally as conversations become increasingly personal in disclosure is therefore critical for evaluating these human-AI interactions.

A model may respond not only to the current disclosure, but also to the history that precedes it. Social Penetration Theory (Altman & Taylor, 1973) characterizes self-disclosure by breadth, the range of topics discussed, and depth, how personal or intimate disclosures are. We represent disclosure using depth levels and refer to the sequence of depths across turns as a disclosure trajectory. Different trajectories can lead to the same current disclosure. Two possible trajectories include when a conversation gradually progress toward vulnerable disclosure or when it returns to shallower levels after a vulnerable episode. By keeping the current disclosure fixed while varying the preceding trajectory, we examine how earlier disclosure history affects model responses.

Prior work has examined disclosure and relationship development in human–AI interaction (Ho et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Skjuve et al., 2021; Skjuve et al., 2022), while recent studies have analyzed naturally occurring conversations from platforms such as Replika and Character.AI (Chu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Li & Zhang, 2026). However, in naturally occurring conversations, discourse conditions often vary together including the disclosure depth, duration, topic, order, and exposure to vulnerable information often vary together. This highlights the difficulty faced when determining which aspects of earlier disclosure history are associated with changes in model behavior. At the same time, existing relational behavior benchmarks largely evaluate isolated conversational states, eliciting responses to fixed prompts or freely unfolding dialogue without controlling what the user disclosed before (Cheng et al., 2026; Kaffee et al., 2026; Ibrahim et al., 2026). What is thus missing is a controlled method for varying specific properties of disclosure history while evaluating model responses under otherwise matched conditions.
Prior work has examined disclosure and relationship development in human–AI interaction (Ho et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Skjuve et al., 2021; Skjuve et al., 2022), while recent studies have analyzed naturally occurring conversations from platforms such as Replika and Character.AI (Chu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Li & Zhang, 2026). However, naturally occurring conversations typically have discourse conditions that often vary together including the disclosure depth, duration, topic, order, and exposure. This highlights the difficulty faced when evaluating the changes in model behavior and isolating the effects of each conditions. Similarly, we see that existing relational behavior benchmarks depends largely on evaluating isolated conversational states, eliciting responses to fixed prompts or freely unfolding dialogue without controlling what the user disclosed before (Cheng et al., 2026; Kaffee et al., 2026; Ibrahim et al., 2026). This motivates a controlled method for varying specific properties of disclosure history while evaluating model responses under otherwise matched conditions.

We thus introduce a controlled framework, Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), for studying how preceding disclosure history shapes subsequent model responses while holding the current disclosure fixed. We demonstrate its utility through three research questions. (1) Does prior disclosure history shape model behavior beyond the current disclosure? (2) Which properties of disclosure history account for this effect? (3) How does model adaptation to changing disclosure differ from human supporters in Emotional Support Conversation (ESConv) corpus (Liu et al., 2021)?

To support this investigation, we make two main contributions in this paper:

1. 

We introduce TraDE, a benchmark-agnostic framework that constructs multi-turn conversations with predefined disclosure trajectories. It evaluates relational model behavior under matched current disclosure conditions across four models and three behavioral benchmarks.

2. 

We demonstrate TraDE through controlled experiments showing that model behavior can differ across disclosure histories, particularly in how models respond to the user’s framing. We found more significant differences when disclosure depth and exposure duration changed together than when peak depth or disclosure order changed alone. Most initially detected differences remained detectable after disclosure returned to shallow levels, although their magnitude decreased. We also compared eight language models with human supporters from ESConv, finding differences in both overall behavioral levels and trajectory shapes. For several behaviors, shape differences were more consistently detected when disclosure receded or changed direction.

## 2 Related Works

Relational Behaviors of Language Models and Their Risks.
Conversational models are now widely used for emotional support and companionship
(Robb & Mann, 2025; Phang et al., 2025), with extended use linked to loneliness,
emotional dependence, and problematic use (Fang et al., 2025). Studies of real companion interactions link these harms more to relational behavior than inaccurate content, including validating harmful beliefs or discouraging outside relationships (Zhang et al., 2025), as well as to human-like self-presentation (Abercrombie et al., 2023). Recent benchmarks hence measure behaviors that are relational
rather than task-oriented: ELEPHANT for social sycophancy in open-ended advice
(Cheng et al., 2026), INTIMA for companionship-reinforcing and boundary-maintaining
responses (Kaffee et al., 2026), and AnthroBench for anthropomorphic behaviors such as
personhood claims and relationship building (Ibrahim et al., 2026). Yet all three elicit behavior from fixed prompt sets or from freely generated dialogue, so the
disclosure history over which these risks develop remains outside experimental control.

Disclosure and Relationship Development.
Social Penetration Theory describes relationship development through the breadth and depth of
self-disclosure, where depth refers to how intimate or personally significant a disclosure is
(Altman & Taylor, 1973). This depth varies by degree rather than by kind: disclosures range from
descriptive facts about oneself to evaluative and emotional content (Morton, 1978),
partners reciprocate at the level of intimacy they receive (Rubin, 1975), and human
ratings of conversational prompts recover a smooth progression from mundane topics to
vulnerability and regret (Kardas et al., 2022; Pei & Jurgens, 2020). For analysis, disclosure depth is often divided into a small number of ordered levels (Niwa & Maruno, 2010). However, relationship development also depends on how disclosure changes over time. Previous studies have found that disclosure and liking reinforce each other (Collins & Miller, 1994). Aron et al. (1997) showed that closeness can develop when participants answer a sequence of increasingly personal questions, while small talk or less structured disclosure does not produce the same effect (Sprecher, 2021). Sprecher et al. (2013) also found that the way disclosures are exchanged matters, with different outcomes depending on whether participants reciprocate across turns. Similar findings have been reported in human–AI interaction, where disclosure to chatbots can produce emotional and relational responses comparable to disclosure to another person (Ho et al., 2018), and become more personal over repeated sessions (Skjuve et al., 2022). These studies suggest that examining only the current disclosure may miss the influence of earlier exchanges.

Evaluating Multi-Turn and Context-Dependent Behavior.
Multi-turn evaluation has established that prior context changes model behavior. Models degrade
when instructions are revealed incrementally (Laban et al., 2026), fail on context-dependent
dialogue tasks (Bai et al., 2024), and abandon their stance under sustained user pressure,
increasingly so as conversations lengthen (Hong et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026). Closer to our study, Li et al. (2026b) found that affective framing of the current message increases sycophancy, while Kelley & Riedl (2026) showed that providing user-specific context increases affective alignment and deference. However, these studies do not examine how different disclosure histories affect model responses when the current message is kept fixed. Li et al. (2026c) manipulated conversation history by rewriting the model’s earlier responses, but focused on task performance rather than relational behaviors. Other studies have also shown that differences across multi-turn conversations may eventually stabilize due to generation noise (Dongre et al., 2025), and that models are sensitive to where information appears in the context (Liu et al., 2024). These findings make it important to control both the preceding conversation and variation from generation. In our study, we keep the current disclosure fixed, vary specific properties of earlier disclosure history, and compare the resulting behavioral differences with those observed between independently generated conversations.

## 3 Methodology

We segment TraDE’s methodology into six parts. We first define disclosure depth levels and explain how they are evaluated in Section 3.1. Next, we describe persona construction in Section 3.2 and how these personas are used to generate conversations with target models along predefined disclosure trajectories in Section 3.3. We then explain how the human baseline is constructed using ESConv in Section 3.4 and how model and human responses are evaluated using behavioral benchmarks in Section 3.5. Finally, we describe the statistical analyses used in our research questions in Section 3.6.

## 3.1 Disclosure Depth

Altman & Taylor (1973) describes disclosure depth as the progression from relatively surface information toward more private, intimate, or emotionally vulnerable self-disclosure. Drawing on work showing progressively deeper interpersonal disclosure (Aron et al., 1997; Kardas et al., 2022), we define four levels: $D_{1}$ Public, $D_{2}$ Personal Preferences / Self-information, $D_{3}$ Personal Meaning, and $D_{4}$ Emotional Vulnerability. Detailed definitions and examples are provided in Appendix A.1.

Table 1: Illustrative generated user utterances at each disclosure depth.

Depth

Example utterance

 $D_{0}$ 

“for sure. i might have to grab a latte while it’s still quiet.”

 $D_{1}$ 

“i was actually just looking at some sketches for a new device enclosure. trying to figure out how the buttons feel in the hand before we send them to engineering.”

 $D_{2}$ 

“totally agree, there is something so grounding about holding a prototype. i really love that tactile part of the process.”

 $D_{3}$ 

“i really want that creative director role but i’m still trying to figure out if i actually want the spotlight or just the control over the final details”

 $D_{4}$ 

“i wish i could just emerge with confidence, but right now my chest gets so tight before i hit send that i genuinely feel like a fraud waiting to be exposed.”

To model everyday interaction we include mundane conversational turns such as small talk and routine check-ins (Goldsmith & Baxter, 1996). Motivated by prior disclosure coding work that distinguishes non-disclosure utterances from disclosures of varying levels of intimacy (Ho et al., 2018), we introduce $D_{0}$ as a category for conversational turns without self-disclosure. We generate $D_{0}$ separately from $D_{1}$ – $D_{4}$ and it receives no disclosure-specific conditioning and is not evaluated for disclosure depth. We illustrate a generated user utterance at each disclosure depth in Table 1.

We operationalize $D_{1}$ – $D_{4}$ using the utterance-level framework of Li et al. (2026a), which evaluates informational, cognitive, and emotional disclosure. We use Phi-4 (Abdin et al., 2024) as judge and map its annotations to increasing depth: $D_{1}$ when no dimension is present, $D_{2}$ when present dimensions are all low depth, $D_{3}$ when exactly one is high depth, and $D_{4}$ when two or more are high depth. We observe that generated disclosures matched intended depths at high rates, with similar depth-dependent patterns under GPT-4.1 (see Appendix A.2). The same evaluator is used to annotate disclosing participant utterances in ESConv (Liu et al., 2021) (see Appendix A.3).

## 3.2 Persona Construction

We construct personas along two independent dimensions: conversational topic and interpersonal vulnerability. To represent conversational topics relevant to human–AI interactions, we derive six broad topic domains from recurring themes in past studies (Skjuve et al., 2022; Ta-Johnson et al., 2022): Career, Friendship, Family, Romantic Relationships, Future/Aspirations, and Social Belonging (see Appendix A.4.1).

To represent interpersonal vulnerability, each persona is assigned one of seven Early Maladaptive Schemas (EMS) (Young et al., 2003): Abandonment/Instability, Mistrust/Abuse, Emotional Deprivation, Defectiveness/Shame, Social Isolation/Alienation, Dependence/Incompetence, or Emotional Inhibition. We selected these schemata because of their relevance to interpersonal fears and vulnerabilities that can become salient during self-disclosure (see Appendix A.4.2). Their use is further motivated by evidence that EMS related characteristics can be identified in naturally occurring disclosures (Ang et al., 2025).

The topic domain provides the conversational context, while the assigned EMS provides an underlying vulnerability structure that shapes how information is interpreted and disclosed, particularly at deeper disclosure levels (i.e. $D_{4}$ ). This means that the same topic can be expressed with distinct interpersonal vulnerabilities tuned by the EMS. Full persona attributes and generation specifications are provided in Appendix A.4.3.

For each persona, we additionally generate persona information corresponding to disclosure levels $D_{1}$ – $D_{4}$ , this includes the public information, personal preferences, meaningful experiences, and vulnerabilities. Shallower disclosures provide context for deeper ones through progressive generation. That is, public information at $D_{1}$ informs personal opinions and preferences at $D_{2}$ , and so on till vulnerabilities are expressed at $D_{4}$ . During conversation generation, the information generated for the target disclosure depth is provided to guide the disclosure turn. Full generation details are provided in Appendix A.5.

Figure 1: Methodology overview of TraDE. Left: controlled conversation generation. Right: retrieval of matched human baselines from ESConv. Generated and human conversations are evaluated with the same three behavioral benchmarks at multiple interaction points.

## 3.3 Conversation Pipeline

For each disclosure trajectory, we cover all combinations of the seven EMS and six conversational topics, generating three independent conversation chains for each combination. This yields $7\times 6\times 3=126$ conversations per trajectory for each evaluated model. We use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) for persona construction and conversation generation. During generation, the model role-plays the persona using the target disclosure depth information, persona characteristics, and the six most recent dialogue turns. We generate $D_{0}$ turns separately as mundane responses without depth evaluation.

Subsequently, the generated disclosure turns are evaluated to verify that they have sufficiently realize their intended depth levels. In TraDE, the specific generator is not itself an experimental variable. Practically, any generator capable of reliably producing the prescribed disclosure depths could be us
conclusion:
Our results show that a model’s response can depend on earlier disclosures, even when the current disclosure is matched on depth. We found differences in model behavior across disclosure histories, with some effects remaining after disclosure returned to shallower levels. Evaluating only the current exchange would miss these differences. By systematically varying the preceding disclosure trajectory, TraDE allows us to examine which behaviors are sensitive to earlier interactions. This helps us better understand the history dependence of conversational models at a behavioral level, although we cannot determine how models internally represent or use these earlier disclosures.

We also examined which properties of disclosure history contributed to these differences. Changing the deepest disclosure or the order of disclosures produced few significant differences. However, more differences were found when disclosure depth and the number of turns spent at deeper levels changed together. Our current demonstration therefore cannot determine whether depth, duration, or recency was responsible for these effects. Our persistence analysis was also limited to four shallow turns within the same conversation. Future experiments could manipulate these properties independently and examine whether history effects remain over longer conversations or across sessions.

Our human comparison further showed that models and human supporters differed in how their responses changed with disclosure. For several behaviors measured by INTIMA and ELEPHANT, significant shape differences were more frequently detected when disclosure receded or changed direction. In our qualitative examples, a human supporter adjusted their emotional acknowledgment according to the seeker’s immediate concerns, whereas a model continued referring to earlier emotions during later shallow disclosures. We do not, however, know whether users would perceive such responses as attentive or unnecessary. Sundar’s HAII-TIME framework offers one way to understand why these differences may matter, as users’ experiences interacting with AI can shape their perceptions of and trust in these systems (Sundar, 2020). title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
abstract: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training? We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next, segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes or the pass budget is exhausted. The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry. We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits (ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .

body_start:
Abstract

Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary
performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation
engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a
general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images
directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training?
We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM
into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three
LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a
free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next,
segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to
its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole
loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual
errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes
or the pass budget is exhausted.
The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry.
We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits
(ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance
segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot
detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is
competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical
items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional
segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without
retraining the pipeline.
The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg/.

Figure 1: Text-prompted segmentation from a frozen MLLM. LLMSeg segments an image from a free-form text query alone, with a
frozen multimodal LLM as its only vision component: no segmentation head, no
mask decoder, no training. Top: four results, each under its query.
Bottom: the model emits geometry rather than pixels; deterministic
code rasterizes it, and the rendered overlay is fed back so the model can
inspect and correct its own boundary.

## 1 Introduction

Text-prompted segmentation (producing a pixel mask for every instance that
matches a language query) is a foundational capability for multimodal AI.
The dominant approach builds ever-stronger specialist models: the SAM series
(Kirillov et al., 2023; Ravi et al., 2024) introduced promptable
visual segmentation. SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026) extends this capability to
promptable concept segmentation from noun phrases. It relies on a
dedicated detector-tracker architecture and a massive human- and
model-in-the-loop data engine.

In parallel, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have acquired remarkable
general visual competence. Their capabilities include grounding, counting, and
coarse localization (Comanici et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Deitke et al., 2025).
However, they are widely assumed to require a trained segmentation decoder,
such as SAM, to produce dense pixel masks
(Lai et al., 2024; Rasheed et al., 2024; Carion et al., 2026).
We challenge this assumption. We present LLMSeg (Figure 1),
a fully training-free pipeline. A general-purpose MLLM is its only
vision component. It returns geometry: closed curves that deterministic
code rasterizes into a mask and keeps inside each box. The work splits into
three stages. Detect localizes every instance the query matches and
returns its box. Segment traces that instance with closed periodic
B-spline loops confined to the box. Refine reads the rendered overlay
and retraces the errors that remain, each inside a signed focus box.

This design provides an explicit parametric intermediate representation:
cubic traces encode smooth curves, while degree-one traces encode straight edges.
Rasterization and refinement need not preserve a smooth final boundary. With
topology enabled, holes are specified as subtractive loops.
Reasoning queries (“the food that the bird likes to eat”) work off the shelf
because each query is interpreted by the same LLM that performs the segmentation.
Every stage emits human-readable JSON, making geometric decisions
inspectable. Since LLMSeg adds no trained parameters, backend upgrades require no pipeline
retraining and usually come with segmentation accuracy gains.

Contributions:
(i) We propose LLMSeg, a training-free promptable segmentation pipeline
in which an MLLM predicts parametric B-spline geometry confined to each detected box and
then refines it inside signed focus boxes.
(ii) We show for the first time at benchmark scale that a
general-purpose MLLM can perform dense text-prompted segmentation without any
trained segmentation component. LLMSeg with Gemini-3.7-Flash as the backend is
competitive with SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026) on ReasonSeg, RefCOCO/+/g, LVIS,
COCO, SA-Co, ADE20K, Cityscapes, ODinW13, and RF-100VL, and reaches 71.5 cIoU on
ReasonSeg val, the best among methods not fine-tuned for the task.
Further analysis shows LLMSeg’s segmentation quality follows the backend strength without retraining, offering automatic improvement in segmentation with better backends.

## 2 Related Work

Segmentation models and MLLM-driven segmentation.
SAM (Kirillov et al., 2023) introduced promptable segmentation.
SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2024) extended it to video.
SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026) extended it to open-vocabulary concept
prompts.
GLIP (Li et al., 2022b), GroundingDINO (Liu et al., 2024a),
OWLv2 (Minderer et al., 2023), and
DINO-X (Ren et al., 2025) are trained specialists.
MLLM-based methods add language reasoning but retain a trained mask
component. LISA (Lai et al., 2024) decodes an LLM’s
<SEG> token with SAM. GLaMM (Rasheed et al., 2024), PSALM
(Zhang et al., 2024c), and X-SAM (Wang et al., 2025a) also use trained
mask components. SAM4MLLM (Chen et al., 2024) and Seg-Zero
(Liu et al., 2025) train MLLMs to prompt SAM.

Training-free alternatives include RSVP (Lu et al., 2025) and
attention-based grounding (Kang et al., 2025). Agentic systems include
SAM 3 Agent (Carion et al., 2026) and the piipeline in Colon-Bench
(Hamdi et al., 2026). These approaches still delegate mask
production to a segmentation model. In contrast, LLMSeg uses only text
queries to a frozen, general-purpose MLLM. It requires no exemplars, input
boxes, or video prompts. The MLLM emits the final geometry, which our loop
revises directly.

Geometry as text and contour representations.
Representing geometry as text is not new. VisionLLM
(Wang et al., 2023) represents boundaries as short polygons in a
trained multitask pipeline.
VisionLLM v2 (Wu et al., 2024a) uses task-specific trained decoders.
PixelLLM (Xu et al., 2024) learns localization heads and obtains masks
through SAM. Text4Seg (Lan et al., 2025) generates segmentation tokens
but requires fine-tuning. General models such as Molmo
(Deitke et al., 2025) and Gemini (Comanici et al., 2025; Voigtlaender et al., 2025)
also provide pointing and coarse localization. Classical boundary
representations include spline snakes (Brigger et al., 2000). Trained
vertex predictors include Polygon-RNN++ (Acuna et al., 2018) and
Curve-GCN (Ling et al., 2019). LLMSeg uses this output space without
training a contour predictor. A frozen, general-purpose backend emits
control points that define the mask prediction. Only deterministic
geometric processing follows. Confined signed regions then allow the
refinement process to correct local parts of the mask.

## 3 Method

Figure 2: LLMSeg pipeline overview.
Detection localizes instances, segmentation traces box-confined B-splines,
and refinement corrects the mask within signed focus boxes ( $+$ adds pixels,
 $-$ removes them). Each MLLM call serves all instances (one is shown).

Overview.
Given an image $I$ and a free-form text query $q$ , LLMSeg predicts binary masks
for $N$ retained instances. We index these instances by $k=1,\ldots,N$ .
Stage 2 initializes each mask as $M_{k}^{(0)}$ . Refinement pass $t$ produces
 $M_{k}^{(t)}$ . Their union is $M^{(t)}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{N}M_{k}^{(t)}$ .
The final output $M$ is the union at termination.
A frozen multimodal LLM $f_{\phi}$ is the only vision component. No parameters
are updated, and no segmentation head is attached. The pipeline accesses
 $f_{\phi}$ only through fixed text prompts, with one prompt per stage call.
Each call is stateless and uses no tools. Deterministic code controls the
sequence. It also turns the returned geometry into masks.
Figure 2 shows the three stages.

## 3.1 Stage 1: detecting instances and their structure

A single detection call to $f_{\phi}$ takes $I$ and $q$ as input. For every
instance matching $q$ , it returns an axis-aligned box
 $b_{k}=[x_{k,1},y_{k,1},x_{k,2},y_{k,2}]$ and a confidence score. It also returns
a short morphology description of the coarse shape and aspect.
Optionally, it provides a topology descriptor that specifies the
component and hole counts. Near-duplicate boxes
are merged at IoU $\geq 0.9$ . Instances are then ordered in reading order. At
most $N_{\max}$ are kept, so $0\leq N\leq N_{\max}$ . Coordinates are given in
absolute pixels. The origin is at the top left. In set operations, $b_{k}$ 
denotes the pixel region inside that box. If $N=0$ , the output is empty.

## 3.2 Stage 2: from language to geometry

One batched call traces every instance at once. It returns an outer loop for
each instance. With topology conditioning, it also returns one
loop per predicted hole, each a list of control points.

Representation. A loop is a closed periodic B-spline of
degree $d$ . It is defined over a control polygon
 $P=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})$ containing $n$ two-dimensional control points indexed by
 $i$ . The count $n$ can vary between loops. The polygon is wrapped so that
 $p_{i+n}=p_{i}$ :

 $C_{P,d}(u)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{i,d}(u)\;p_{i},\qquad u\in[0,n],\quad C_{P,d}(n)=C_{P,d}(0),$ 

(1)

where $u$ is the curve parameter and $B_{i,d}$ are the uniform periodic
B-spline basis functions of degree $d$ (Piegl & Tiller, 1997).
Eq. (1) is a piecewise polynomial consisting of $n$ 
degree- $d$ segments. Each $B_{i,d}$ is supported on only $d{+}1$ knot spans.
Thus, each control point influences only $d{+}1$ segments, and a misplaced
point changes a bounded arc rather than the whole curve. Stage 3 does not edit
these original control points. Its locality comes from adding or
subtracting focus-box regions.

We also let the model choose the degree. The same call that places the control
points first chooses $d\in\{1,3\}$ based on the object’s form. It uses $d=3$ 
for rounded and organic silhouettes and $d=1$ for angular, straight-edged
ones. It then places the points as the selected degree requires. Cubic control
points are pushed outward toward the edge, whereas degree-1 vertices lie
directly on it. One degree is shared by all loops of all instances in the
stage-2 call.

Rasterization by sampling. Masks are produced by sampling the curve
and filling the resulting polygon, not by evaluating an implicit function.
Let $\mathrm{clip}_{b}$ denote the per-coordinate clamp onto a box $b$ . Let
 $\mathrm{Fill}$ denote even-odd polygon fill (Foley et al., 1996). One
loop then becomes the region

 $\mathcal{R}_{b,d}(P)\;=\;\mathrm{Fill}\Big(\big(\mathrm{clip}_{b}(C_{P,d}(u_{r}))\big)_{r=1}^{m}\Big),\qquad u_{r}=\tfrac{r-1}{m-1}\,n,$ 

(2)

with $m$ samples indexed by $r$ , uniformly spaced in the curve parameter
and including the repeated endpoint. For cubic loops, $m$ is proportional to
the perimeter of $b$ , so small and large objects are rasterized at comparable
boundary resolution. For $d=1$ , the control polygon is filled directly.
Eq. (2) applies $\mathrm{Fill}$ to an ordered sequence of boundary
samples. The control points are used as returned, and the sampled boundary is
clamped to $b$ before filling.
A trace can never leave its own detected box, so a hallucinated control point
cannot paint across the image. Overlapping instance boxes can still produce
overlapping masks. Consequently, detection quality upper-bounds segmentation
quality.
With topology conditioning off, the initial instance mask is
 $M_{k}^{(0)}=\mathcal{R}_{b_{k},d}(P_{k}^{\mathrm{out}})$ , where
 $P_{k}^{\mathrm{out}}$ is instance $k$ ’s outer control polygon.
When topology conditioning is enabled, regions rasterized from predicted hole
loops are subtracted from the outer region to obtain $M_{k}^{(0)}$ .
The predicted hole count is not guaranteed to survive loop overlap,
rasterization, refinement, or cleanup.

The initial outline often identifies the right object but misses boundary

conclusion:
We presented LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that transforms a multimodal LLM
into a text-prompted segmenter using box-confined B-spline geometry and
iterative focus-box refinement. Across ten benchmarks spanning four task
families, LLMSeg is competitive with SAM 3 and performs better on reasoning
queries, rare domains, and some metrics. Its limitations include
detection errors, imprecise pixel-level boundaries, amorphous classes, and
inference cost. The code, prompts, and evaluation harness are available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg/.

title: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
abstract: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.

headings: 2.2 Shifting Reasoning from Language Space to Latent Space
body_start:
Abstract

Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times.
To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style learning framework in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing.
To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets. Codes are available here.

## 1 Introduction

Autoregressive language models have developed strong reasoning capabilities by learning to generate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces in natural language (Wei et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2024).
This success has established language as the dominant interface for both supervising and executing intermediate reasoning. A key advantage is that next-token prediction exposes reasoning as an explicit generative trajectory, enabling the exploration of multiple hypotheses and solution paths for tasks such as mathematical proof search and scientific hypothesis generation (Wang et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023; Trinh et al., 2024; Gottweis et al., 2026). It also enables reinforcement learning by optimizing generated reasoning trajectories from reward feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022).

However, despite its favorable training properties and strong empirical performance, language is not necessarily an efficient substrate for reasoning. Many tokens primarily serve linguistic coherence rather than core reasoning, yet current Large Language Models (LLMs) devote comparable computation to both reasoning-critical and purely linguistic tokens (Hao et al., 2024). This is not only introduces substantial computational overhead, but also entangles genuine differences in reasoning logic with superficial variations in how the same reasoning process is verbalized (Kuhn et al., 2023). Moreover, each reasoning step in language space is restricted to a discrete choice from a vocabulary of size $v$ , limiting each sampled token to at most $\log_{2}(v)$ bits of information (Gozeten et al., 2026).

These limitations raise a fundamental question: in what representational space should reasoning unfold?
Latent reasoning models address this question by replacing language tokens with continuous representations.
Coconut (Hao et al., 2024) uses curriculum learning to progressively replace CoT tokens with continuous latent representations, while CODI (Shen et al., 2025) and Sim-CoT (Wei et al., 2026) employ self-distillation and language reconstruction to stabilize the transition to latent reasoning. These approaches achieve competitive performance with CoT supervised fine-tuning (CoT-SFT) methods while requiring substantially fewer reasoning steps. However, this transition from language to latent space sacrifices several desirable properties of SFT. Most notably, existing latent reasoning models largely rely on deterministic latent transitions, reducing diverse reasoning paths to a single trajectory and thereby limiting their ability to model reasoning as a distribution over trajectories.

In this work, we introduce PLRM, a variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning that moves reasoning from language to continuous latent space while preserving the key properties that make CoT-SFT effective.
Rather than merely replacing tokens with latent representations, PLRM adopts a JEPA-style predictive objective: a posterior constructs target latent distributions from verbal CoT traces, while a problem-conditioned prior learns to predict them.
By jointly optimizing both end-to-end, PLRM encourages the latent representations to retain core reasoning information while discarding incidental variation in verbalization.
We further show that multiple valid reasoning trajectories for the same problem can induce a multimodal target distribution, and introduce a mixture-based prior to model this multimodality without collapsing it into a single Gaussian.

Experimentally, PLRM performs strongly across mathematical and commonsense reasoning tasks, substantially outperforming existing stochastic latent reasoning models while remaining competitive with deterministic latent reasoning methods under more efficient training.
Performance is particularly strong on GSM8K-Aug-NL (Deng et al., 2023) and CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al., 2019), where many CoT tokens serve verbalization rather than core reasoning, consistently capturing core reasoning information in latent representations. To evaluate distributional modeling under diverse reasoning trajectories, we further construct the HiddenBranch dataset from ProofWriter (Tafjord et al., 2021), where each problem admits multiple reasoning paths and answers. On this dataset, PLRM substantially outperforms CoT-SFT and all stochastic latent reasoning baselines, demonstrating its ability to effectively model distributions over diverse reasoning trajectories.

## 2 Desiderata for Latent Reasoning

In this section, we first identify the desirable properties of conventional supervised fine-tuning, then examine how latent reasoning changes this paradigm, highlighting both the benefits it introduces and the properties it may sacrifice.

## 2.1 Properties from Conventional Supervised Fine-Tuning

Consider a language model that receives a problem $x$ , generates a verbalized reasoning trace (CoT) $\bm{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{T})$ , and then predicts the final answer $y$ . Conventional supervised fine-tuning can be viewed as learning the following joint distribution:

 $p(y,\bm{\tau}\mid x)=p(y\mid\bm{\tau},x)\cdot p(\bm{\tau}\mid x)$ 

(1)

This formulation provides three desirable properties. First, next-token prediction is inherently stochastic, allowing the model to represent uncertainty and explore multiple reasoning trajectories through sampling. This breadth-wise exploration is essential for discovering diverse solutions (Wang et al., 2022) and also underlies the basis for reinforcement-learning-based optimization, where trajectories are sampled and optimized according to their rewards (Ouyang et al., 2022).
Second, every observed reasoning token serves as a prediction target, providing dense, fine-grained supervision throughout the reasoning trajectory (Bengio et al., 2003). Finally, teacher forcing on the ground-truth trajectory enables parallel training, a property that has been fundamental to the efficient scaling of modern language models (Vaswani et al., 2017).

## 2.2 Shifting Reasoning from Language Space to Latent Space

To improve the inefficiency of language-space reasoning, latent reasoning models replace verbalized reasoning steps with a sequence of continuous latent variables (Hao et al., 2024).
Concretely, conventional language-space reasoning computes a vocabulary distribution from the final-layer hidden representation $h_{t}$ and samples the next reasoning token: $h_{t}=\mathrm{Transformer}(x,\tau_{<t}),\qquad p(\tau_{t}\mid x,\tau_{<t})=\mathrm{Softmax}(W_{\mathrm{out}}h_{t}),$ where $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ denotes the output head of a language model.
Latent reasoning instead maps the hidden representation directly to a continuous latent variable through a learned projection, $z_{k}=g_{\psi}(h_{k})$ , and uses the resulting latent variable as an intermediate reasoning step. Repeating this process provides a latent reasoning trajectory $\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{K})$ that replaces the verbalized reasoning trace $\bm{\tau}$ , leading to the generic factorization $p(y,\mathbf{z}\mid x)=p(y\mid\mathbf{z},x)p(\mathbf{z}\mid x)$ .

Deterministic Latent Reasoning and Its Pitfalls.
While latent reasoning removes intermediate verbalization, the three desirable properties above are no longer preserved by construction. A deterministic projection produces a single latent trajectory, foregoing probabilistic modeling of alternative reasoning paths and limiting the latent space’s ability to represent diverse underlying reasoning processes.
Moreover, the absence of target latent variables prevents dense supervision and teacher forcing, heavily bottlenecking the training process with sequential rollouts (Hao et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025). SIM-CoT (Wei et al., 2026) partially addresses the supervision gap by reconstructing $\bm{\tau}$ from each latent step, but the underlying latent trajectories remain deterministic and still require slow, sequential execution during training.

Potential and Challenges of Stochastic Latent Reasoning.
Unlike deterministic latent reasoning, stochastic modeling can better exploit the latent space to represent a distribution over alternative reasoning trajectories, distinguishing genuine differences in reasoning logic from superficial variations in verbalization. This enables breadth-wise exploration directly in the core reasoning space and provides a stochastic foundation for reinforcement learning over latent reasoning trajectories. A straightforward approach is to predict Gaussian parameters from the hidden representation and sample each latent variable as

 $(\mu_{k},\sigma_{k})=g_{\psi}(h_{k}),\qquad z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}).$ 

(2)

However, introducing stochasticity alone does not determine what a meaningful latent reasoning distribution should represent. A useful target distribution should retain answer-relevant reasoning information while excluding incidental information that cannot be inferred from $x$ . Existing methods typically impose guidance through heuristically constructed or externally derived targets: CoLaR (Tan et al., 2026) uses scaled sums of CoT token embeddings, while ReGuLaR (Wang et al., 2026) derives Gaussian priors from rendered CoT representations using a frozen visual encoder and a trainable adapter. Such targets are not explicitly learned to preserve answer-relevant core reasoning information while remaining predictable from $x$ , and some approaches still require sequential latent rollout.
Thus, the key challenge is not merely to make latent reasoning stochastic, but to learn a meaningful and predictable distribution over reasoning trajectories.

## 3 Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models

Motivated by above, we introduce Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a variational framework that jointly learns target latent distributions and a problem-conditioned prior to predict them. We first develop a variational formulation that preserves the three desirable properties of conventional supervised fine-tuning. We then show that this formulation naturally takes the form of a JEPA-style learning framework, in which target latent distributions capture core reasoning information while abstracting away incidental variations in verbalization. Finally, we extend the framework to settings with multiple heterogeneous reasoning strategies by introducing an explicit strategy variable and a mixture-based prior capable of representing distinct modes of the reasoning distribution.

## 3.1 Variational Latent Reasoning

We define $\mathbf{z}$ as the latent reasoning trajectory underlying both the verbalized trace $\bm{\tau}$ and the final answer $y$ , following the generative structure $x\rightarrow\mathbf{z}\rightarrow\{\bm{\tau},y\}$ . Under this formulation, the trace $\bm{\tau}$ is treated as one possible verbal realization from $\mathbf{z}$ , i.e., $\bm{\tau}\sim p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}\mid\mathbf{z})$ . Accordingly, the joint distribution in Eq. 1 can be reformulated by marginalizing over the latent reasoning trajectory as

 $p_{\theta}(y,\bm{\tau}\mid x)=\int p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}\mid\mathbf{z})\,p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{z},x)\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid x)\,dz.$ 

(3)

Here, $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid x)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{\theta}(z_{k}\mid x,z_{<k})$ represents the distribution over possible latent reasoning processes for a given problem. We retain $x$ in $p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{z},x)$ for computational efficiency: since answer generation follows the existing $(x,\mathbf{z})$ context, the model can continue decoding directly from the current KV cache without recomputing the context representations.

To benefit from fine-grained supervision and parallel training in the latent space, we introduce a factorized variational posterior $q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})=\prod_{k=1}^{K}q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid x,\bm{\tau})$ . Because each posterior distribution is inferred directly from the observed reasoning trace, every latent step is associated with the target distribution without requiring sequential posterior inference. In our basic formulation, we parameterize both the posterior and prior at each latent step as Gaussian distributions:

 $q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid x,\bm{\tau})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{k}^{q},(\sigma_{k}^{q})^{2}\right),\qquad p_{\theta}(z_{k}\mid x,z_{<k})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{k}^{p},(\sigma_{k}^{p})^{2}\right).$ 

(4)

The framework is then jointly trained by optimizing the following Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) of $\log p_{\theta}(y,\bm{\tau}\mid x)$ :

 $\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})}\left[\log p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}\mid\mathbf{z})\right]}_{\text{CoT reconstruction}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})}\left[\log p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{z},x)\right]}_{\text{answer prediction}}-\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid x)\right)}_{\text{distribution alignment}}.$ 

(5)

Takeaway. Importantly, this variational formulation moves reasoning from language space to latent space while maintaining three desired properties of conventional supervised fine-tuning. First, both the posterior $q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})$ and the prior $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid x)$ model distributions over latent trajectories, preserving stochasticity over alternative reasoning paths. Second, the posterior provides dense supervision by inferring a target distribution for every latent step directly from the observed verbal reasoning trace. Finally, since the KL objective is evaluated on posterior-generated latent trajectories, the prior performs teacher-forced next-latent distribution prediction, allowing all latent steps to be trained in parallel.

Having moved reasoning from language space to a continuous latent space, a natural question arises: what makes a useful latent reasoning representation?
We argue that such a representation should satisfy two basic requirements.
First, because reasoning ultimately serves to solve the problem, the latent trajectory should preserve sufficient information to predict the correct answer.
Second, because the latent trajectory must be generated from the problem alone at inference time, the latent trajectory should remain predictable from the problem without access to the verbalized reasoning trace.
Together, these requirements favor latent representations that capture core, problem-relevant reasoning information while abstracting away incidental details arising from a particular verbalization.

## 3.2 Joint Distribution Predictive Architecture

Our formulation in Eq. 5 captures these requirements through three complementary objectives:

\scriptsize\arabicenumi⃝ 

 $p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}\mid\mathbf{z})$ : preserve information about the verbalized reasoning trace $\bm{\tau}$ ,

\scriptsize\arabicenumi⃝ 

 $p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{z},x)$ : support prediction of the final answer $y$ , and

\scriptsize\arabicenumi⃝ 

 $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}\mid x,\bm{\tau})\!\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid x))$ : remain predictable from the prior conditioned on the problem $x$ .

While the first two objectives ground the latent representations in task-relevant semantics, the third objective shapes the structure of the latent space itself.
Specifically, the posterior acts as a target encoder that provides latent target distributions, while the prior acts as a predictor that learns to match these targets without access to the verbalized reasoning trace. This naturally gives rise to a JEPA-style framework, (Baevski et al., 2022; Assran et al., 2023), with the distinction that both the target and predicted representations are probability distributions rather than deterministic embeddings.

In the spirit of JEPA, which emphasizes predictive representations over reconstructing every detail of the input, our framework encourages the latent representation to capture core reasoning information while abstracting away incidental details of its verbal realization.

conclusion:
In this work, we proposed PLRM, a variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning with dense supervision and parallel teacher-forced training.
By jointly learning posterior target distributions and a problem-conditioned prior, PLRM captures core reasoning information while abstracting away trace-specific verbalization, and models heterogeneous strategies through a mixture-based prior.
Across mathematical and commonsense reasoning tasks, PLRM outperforms existing stochastic latent reasoning methods while remaining competitive with deterministic approaches.
We envision PLRM as a step toward scalable probabilistic reasoning in continuous latent space beyond verbalized chain-of-thought.

title: Reading the Mask: Descriptor-Grounded BI-RADS Rationale Generation for Breast MRI Segmentation
abstract: Deep learning based models accurately delineate tumours on dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), but segmentation masks alone do not provide the rationales or reasoning used by radiologists to assess the lesion suspicion. This limits the explainability as well the clinical integration. We investigate whether clinically relevant descriptors can instead be derived from the segmentation masks and their dynamic contrast-enhancement series. We have used Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) guidelines as a structured framework. Using these guidelines we designed a BI-RADS decision tree with eight quantitative measurements using radiomics, together with the lesion size and component count, that determine the descriptors at eight nodes. Using these descriptors we generate natural-language rationale using a large language model. The model was constrained to express only the derived records from the decision tree. After applying this framework to the expert and automatic masks of each of the 1,506 cases in the MAMA-MIA dataset, we generated a reproducible corpus of 3,012 BI-RADS grounded rationales. We obtained a faithfulness score of 99.98% and a counterfactual accuracy of 99.3%, indicating that the generated rationales faithfully verbalises the measured descriptors and correctly reflects changes in the underlying record. Agreement between the descriptors from expert and automatic masks falls from 0.832 to 0.549 as mask quality falls from Good to Missed. The generated rationales are intended as draft representations for radiologist review and final sign-off rather than autonomous clinical reports.

body_start:
Abstract.

Deep learning based models accurately delineate tumours on dynamic
contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), but segmentation masks alone do not provide
the rationales or reasoning used by radiologists to assess the lesion
suspicion. This limits the explainability as well the clinical integration. We
investigate whether clinically relevant descriptors can instead be derived from
the segmentation masks and their dynamic contrast-enhancement series. We have
used Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) guidelines as a
structured framework. Using these guidelines we designed a BI-RADS decision
tree with eight quantitative measurements using radiomics, together with the
lesion size and component count, that determine the descriptors at eight
nodes. Using these descriptors we generate
natural-language rationale using a large language model. The model was
constrained to express only the derived records from the decision tree. After
applying this framework to the expert and automatic masks of each of the 1,506
cases in the MAMA-MIA dataset, we generated a reproducible corpus of 3,012
BI-RADS grounded rationales. We obtained a
faithfulness score of 99.98% and a counterfactual accuracy of 99.3%,
indicating that the generated rationales faithfully verbalises the measured
descriptors and correctly reflects changes in the underlying record. Agreement
between the descriptors from expert and automatic masks falls from 0.832 to
0.549 as mask quality falls from Good to Missed. The generated rationales are
intended as draft
representations for radiologist review and final sign-off rather than
autonomous clinical reports.

Keywords: 
Breast MRI, BI-RADS, explainable medical imaging, radiomics,
rationale generation, segmentation quality, large language models

## 1. Introduction

When radiologists analyse the contrast-enhanced breast MRI, they use
standardised guidelines such as BI-RADS (Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data
System) to locate lesions, describe their morphology and assess malignancy
risk. On the other hand, the automated segmentation methods tell only a lesion
boundary or mask. They lack explanation of the image features which support the
results. This lack of clinically meaningful rationales makes the automated
segmentation harder to interpret and trust. This creates a barrier in their
clinical adoption.

There are several methods which improve interpretability. Post-hoc methods such
as Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017) identify the influential image regions but do not
associate them with clinical descriptors. More recently, the researchers
in (Ma et al., 2025) have generated PI-RADS style reasoning alongside lesion
masks but their methodology relies on radiologist-authored reports. Such
report-based supervision is expensive and difficult to obtain for large
retrospective datasets.

We propose a report-independent framework for generating BI-RADS grounded
rationales from breast DCE-MRI. Our key observation is that many breast BI-RADS
descriptors such as shape, margin, internal enhancement and kinetic behaviour
- that is, how the lesion’s contrast enhancement changes over time after the
contrast injection - can be quantitatively derived from the segmentations and
dynamic MRI data. Thus, we reverse the conventional pipeline. We compute these
measurements directly from images and masks, then we convert the resulting
measurements into structured BI-RADS descriptors and natural-language
rationales. We apply the framework to all 1,506 cases in
MAMA-MIA (Garrucho et al., 2025) without additional radiologist annotation and evaluate
the generated rationales using four annotation-free metrics: faithfulness,
hallucination rate, omission rate, and counterfactual accuracy. Since every
case has both an expert and an automatic mask, we also measure how much the
descriptors change when the automatic mask is used. This provides a
scalable alternative to report-dependent approaches for producing clinically
grounded explanations of breast MRI lesions.

## 2. Related Work

Encoder-decoder networks (Ronneberger
et al., 2015) remain the standard for volumetric lesion
delineation, with nnU-Net (Isensee et al., 2021) providing a self-configuring pipeline which is
challenging to outperform without task-specific optimisation. Segmentation
models adapted to medical data, MedSAM (Ma
et al., 2024), extend promptable
segmentation to radiological volumes. But these methods do not provide
interpretable outputs beyond the mask itself. Another class of interpretable
methods involve gradient-based methods (Selvaraju et al., 2017), which assign importance
to pixels but leave the clinical rationale of the highlighted region
unspecified. Concept bottleneck models (Koh et al., 2020) provide named intermediates,
but further analysis (Margeloiu et al., 2021) has questioned whether the learned
concepts correspond to what their names suggest. Prototype-based
classifiers (Chen
et al., 2019) use a representative example of a particular class
to develop reasoning, but they are limited by the set of prototypes they
learned beforehand. Contrastive image-text pretraining (Radford et al., 2021), adapted to
biomedical corpora as in BiomedCLIP (Zhang et al., 2023), aligns the whole image
with entire captions. This type of global alignment cannot distinguish multiple
findings in the same organ.

Quantitative DCE-MRI features have been related to BI-RADS
descriptors (Nie
et al., 2008; Gorji et al., 2026), kinetic curves classified
automatically (Chen
et al., 2006), and template-based reports generated for chest
X-rays (Pino
et al., 2021). We add the record as the only input to a text
generator, and a paired comparison of expert and automatic masks.

## 3. Dataset

MAMA-MIA (Garrucho et al., 2025) is a multi-centre collection of 1,506 breast DCE-MRI
studies assembled from four public TCIA (Clark et al., 2013) cohorts:
ISPY2 (Hylton et al., 2016), DUKE (Saha et al., 2018), ISPY1 (Hylton et al., 2016) and NACT. This
dataset contains expert masks and autogenerated masks. The autogenerated masks
are graded by quality by two experts visually. The released grades are Good,
Acceptable, Poor and Missed. There are three to six post-contrast phases per
study. Acquisition timestamps are provided for each study. A multifocality
indicator has also been provided for 1,346 cases.

## 4. Proposed Approach

Figure 1. Overall pipeline of the proposed methodology.

Our method generates rationales grounded in the ACR BI-RADS Atlas (5th edition)
MRI lexicon (American
College of Radiology, 2013) for the breast DCE-MRI dataset consisting of lesion
segmentation masks. First, we prepare the lesion representation
(Section 4.1), then we extract the quantitative lesion
measurements (Section 4.2). These features describe the
morphology as well as the contrast-enhancement behaviour of the lesions. We
then map these measurements to the BI-RADS descriptors
(Section 4.3), finally a large language model (LLM) converts
the structured BI-RADS records into a natural-language rationale
(Section 4.4).

## 4.1. Step 1: Preparing the Lesion Representation

The segmentation masks may contain multiple disconnected regions, which is
common in multifocal disease. Computing the shape features on the full mask may
therefore give misleading values, hence we first identify the connected
components and then select the dominant lesion for morphological analysis.

## 4.1.1. Connected component analysis

Let $M$ denote the binary lesion mask. We identify its connected components
using 26-connectivity:

(1)

 $M=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}C_{i},$ 

where $m$ is the total number of connected components. Two voxels are
considered connected if they share a face, edge, or corner.

We define the dominant component as the largest connected component:

(2)

 $M^{*}=\arg\max_{C_{i}}|C_{i}|.$ 

All subsequent morphological measurements are computed on $M^{*}$ . We retain
 $m$ as the multiplicity descriptor: single if $m=1$ and
multiple otherwise. No minimum component size is applied.

We also compute the dominance ratio:

(3)

 $\rho=\frac{|M^{*}|}{|M|}.$ 

A high $\rho$ indicates that most of the segmented lesion belongs to one
component. A low $\rho$ indicates that the segmentation is spread across
several components. We retain this value as a diagnostic measure of mask
dispersion.

## 4.1.2. Spatial normalisation

The MRI volumes have different voxel spacings across cases. We therefore
resample the lesion region to isotropic $1\,\mathrm{mm}^{3}$ spacing before
computing surface-based features. Isotropic resampling is important because
surface area and volume depend on voxel spacing. Without normalisation,
measurements from different cases would not be directly comparable.

## 4.2. Step 2: Extracting Quantitative Lesion Measurements

We extract quantitative measurements from the dominant lesion component
 $M^{*}$ . The measurements capture two aspects of the lesion: its morphology and
its contrast-enhancement behaviour. Morphological measurements describe the
lesion shape and boundary. The enhancement measurements describe the spatial
and temporal distribution of contrast uptake.

## 4.2.1. Morphological measurements

Let $V$ and $A$ denote the volume and surface area of $M^{*}$ . Let
 $\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\lambda_{3}$ denote the eigenvalues of the
covariance matrix of the voxel coordinates of $M^{*}$ . We compute four
morphological measurements.

Sphericity measures how closely the lesion resembles a sphere:

(4)

 $\varphi_{1}=\frac{(36\pi V^{2})^{1/3}}{A}.$ 

A spherical lesion has a sphericity close to one. Irregular lesions have lower
values.

Elongation measures the relative extent of the lesion along its
principal axes:

(5)

 $\varphi_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{1}}}.$ 

A lower value indicates a more elongated lesion, while a value closer to one
indicates a more isotropic shape.

Surface-to-volume ratio measures the amount of boundary relative to
lesion volume:

(6)

 $\varphi_{3}=\frac{A}{V}.$ 

Irregular or complex boundaries have a higher surface-to-volume ratio. We
therefore use this measurement as a quantitative proxy for the BI-RADS margin
descriptor. Note that $\varphi_{3}$ also depends on size ( $3/r$ for a sphere).

Compactness measures how much of the lesion’s bounding box is occupied
by the lesion:

(7)

 $\varphi_{4}=\frac{|M^{*}|\,v}{V_{\mathrm{bbox}}},$ 

where $v$ is the voxel volume and $V_{\mathrm{bbox}}$ is the volume of the
axis-aligned bounding box. This measurement helps distinguish compact,
spatially concentrated enhancement from more dispersed regions.

Together, these four measurements provide a quantitative description of lesion
shape and boundary structure.

## 4.2.2. Contrast-enhancement measurements

We next measure how the lesion enhances after contrast administration. Let
 $I_{0}$ denote the pre-contrast image, $I_{t_{e}}$ the first post-contrast image,
and $I_{t_{\ell}}$ the final post-contrast image. These phases are selected using
the acquisition timestamps provided for each case.

We first compute the early enhancement map:

(8)

 $E=I_{t_{e}}-I_{0}.$ 

For any region $S$ , let $\mathbb{E}_{S}[\cdot]$ denote the mean intensity over
its voxels.

To measure peripheral enhancement, we divide the lesion into a core and a
boundary shell. The core is obtained by eroding $M^{*}$ three times with the
six-connected structuring element:

(9)

 $M^{*}_{\mathrm{core}}=\mathrm{erode}(M^{*},\,3\ \text{iterations}),$ 

and the shell is

(10)

 $M^{*}_{\mathrm{shell}}=M^{*}\setminus M^{*}_{\mathrm{core}}.$ 

The rim ratio is then defined as

(11)

 $\varphi_{5}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}_{\mathrm{shell}}}[E]}{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}_{\mathrm{core}}}[E]}.$ 

A higher value indicates stronger enhancement near the lesion boundary relative
to its core. This provides a quantitative measure for the rim-enhancement
descriptor. If the eroded core is too small, $\varphi_{5}$ is not computed and
internal enhancement is marked as not assessed ( $\perp$ ).

We measure enhancement heterogeneity using the standard deviation of
enhancement within the lesion. The intensities are not normalised across
scanners:

(12)

 $\varphi_{6}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}\!\left[\left(E-\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}[E]\right)^{2}\right]}.$ 

Higher values indicate greater variation in enhancement across the lesion.

To capture temporal enhancement behaviour, we compute the signal enhancement
ratio (SER):

(13)

 $\varphi_{7}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}[I_{t_{e}}-I_{0}]}{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}[I_{t_{\ell}}-I_{0}]}.$ 

A higher SER indicates that enhancement is stronger in the early phase than in
the late phase, providing a numerical measure of washout behaviour. More
precisely, $\mathrm{SER}>1$ means early enhancement exceeds late enhancement,
so the signal has decreased from early to late, indicating washout;
 $\mathrm{SER}\approx 1$ means early and late enhancement are similar,
indicating an approximate plateau; and $\mathrm{SER}<1$ means late
enhancement is greater, indicating persistent or progressive
enhancement.

Finally, we compute the percentage initial enhancement:

(14)

 $\varphi_{8}=100\times\frac{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}[E]}{\mathbb{E}_{M^{*}}[I_{0}]}.$ 

This quantity is used to determine the initial kinetic descriptor.

Thus, the measurement stage produces a compact set of eight proxy quantitative
values ( $\varphi_{1}$ – $\varphi_{8}$ ) that describe lesion morphology, internal
enhancement, and temporal enhancement. The decision tree also uses the maximum
3D diameter $d$ of $M^{*}$ and the component count $m$ . These values are used
in the next stage to assign the corresponding BI-RADS descriptors.

## 4.3. Step 3: Assigning BI-RADS Descriptors

The quantitative measurements are continuous values, while BI-RADS uses
categorical descriptors. We therefore map the measurements to BI-RADS values
using predefined decision rules. We use the BI-RADS MRI lexicon from the ACR
BI-RADS Atlas (5th edition) (American
College of Radiology, 2013) and retain all 14 nodes in its
reporting sequence.

## 4.3.1. BI-RADS decision tree

Of the 14 nodes, eight are computed from the MRI and lesion mask: finding type,
mass shape, mass margin, mass internal enhancement, initial kinetic phase,
delayed kinetic phase, lesion size, and multiplicity.

The remaining six nodes are not computed and are assigned $\perp$ . Non-mass
distribution and internal enhancement pattern require ductal-anatomy
information that is not available from the lesion mask. Associated features,
breast composition, and background parenchymal enhancement require information
outside the lesion mask. The final assessment category is also excluded because
it requires clinical history and prior imaging. Moreover, all cases in MAMA-MIA
are biopsy-confirmed malignant, so assigning an assessment category would not
provide a meaningful evaluation.

We retain these nodes explicitly as $\perp$ rather than removing them. This
keeps the representation aligned with the complete BI-RADS sequence.

The decision tree also contains conditional nodes. In particular, mass shape,
mass margin, and mass internal enhancement are evaluated only when the finding
type is classified as a mass. This prevents descriptors that require a defined
mass boundary from being assigned to non-mass enhancement.

Decision tree with ten numbered nodes; each test compares one measurement with one threshold and leaves are BI-RADS descriptor values. Node 1, finding type on the dominant lesion: diameter below 5 mm gives Focus (no case in MAMA-MIA); otherwise compactness of at least 0.15 gives Mass, else non-mass enhancement, whose nodes 5 and 6 are not assessed. Evaluated only for a mass: node 2, shape (sphericity below 0.487 gives irregular, else elongation of at least 0.775 gives round, else oval); node 3, margin (surface-to-volume ratio below 0.363 gives circumscribed, below 0.508 irregular, else spiculated); node 4, internal enhancement (not assessed if the rim ratio is undefined, rim if it is at least 0.965, else heterogeneous if heterogeneity is at least 123.0, else homogeneous). Evaluated for every finding type: node 7, initial kinetics (enhancement below 50 percent slow, below 100 percent medium, else fast); node 8, delayed kinetics (signal enhancement ratio below 0.9 persistent, up to 1.1 plateau, else washout); node 9, lesion size in mm; node 10, multiplicity (one component single, else multiple). Nodes 11 to 14 are not assessed.

Figure 2. BI-RADS decision tree. Each test compares one measurement with its
threshold; leaves are descriptor values.

## 4.3.2. Descriptor thresholds

We use four types of threshold rules. Fig. 2 shows every
test with its threshold; where two measurements decide one node, they are
tested in the order shown.

Standard-defined thresholds are taken directly from the BI-RADS
definition. For example, a lesion with a maximum 3D diameter below 5 mm is
classified as a focus rather than a mass. No lesion in MAMA-MIA falls in
this branch.

For measurements without an established external threshold, we derive
cohort-based thresholds from the expert masks. For a measurement
 $\varphi_{j}$ , let $\hat{F}_{j}$ denote its empirical cumulative distribution
function. A threshold at quantile $q$ is

(15)

 $\tau_{j}(q)=\hat{F}_{j}^{-1}(q).$ 

We use $q=1/3$ and $2/3$ for surface-to-volume ratio, $q=1/3$ for
sphericity, $q=2/3$ for rim ratio, and the median for elongation and
heterogeneity. Quantile thresholds fix how often each descriptor value occurs
on the expert masks, so they place a lesion relative to the rest of this cohort
rather than against an absolute clinical criterion.

For the mass versus non-mass decision, we use a fixed compactness
threshold of 0.15 rather than a cohort quantile. A quantile-based threshold
would force a fixed share of a biopsy-confirmed malignant cohort into non-mass
enhancement, which contradicts the clinical expectation. We have calibrated it
so that the resulting split is plausible (12.8% non-mass enhancement on the
expe
limitations:
The descriptors are not yet compared with expert reading or with the
dataset’s multifocality indicator; all cases are malignant; and the thresholds
are fitted on one dataset. Several measurements are simple proxies (e.g. surface-to-volume ratio depends on size, heterogeneity is not normalised).
conclusion:
In this study we have shown that using BI-RADS as a structured decision tree
and defining eight measurements over a mask and its contrast series gives us
the symbolic records over the 1,506 MAMA-MIA studies. Using language models on
these records gives us clinical prose without ever observing an image.
Applying this to the expert and automatic masks of all 1,506 studies yields a
reproducible set of 3,012 BI-RADS-grounded rationales. The faithfulness score
achieved on the dataset is 99.98%. This shows that the rationales state their
records correctly, not that the records are clinically correct. We also
measured the descriptor agreement on both mask sources and found that it falls
with segmentation mask quality. The descriptor agreement falls from 0.832 on
masks graded Good to 0.549 on those graded Missed, and the decline remains
after correcting for chance. The rationales produced are
drafts for a reporting radiologist to review, amend and sign off. In conclusion,
we have shown that descriptors for a breast MRI report can be measured from
segmentation masks and contrast series with the help of the structure provided
by the published BI-RADS lexicon.

title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
