body_start:
Abstract

Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.

Non-parametric memory

Parametric memory

Figure 1: Memory scaling across two substrates. Theoretical illustrations:
left, joint allocation of storage and reading resources sustains improvement
beyond fixed-capacity limits; center, greater experience requires more
parametric memory capacity; right, load-induced interference emerges at
substrate-dependent thresholds. Curves are synthetic illustrations;
see Section 4.3 and Figures 7 and 11.

## 1 The Landscape: Why Agents Need Continual Learning via Memory

Autonomous agents powered by foundation models have demonstrated strong
capabilities in multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use across digital and physical
domains Agashe et al. [2024], Wang et al. [2024b], Yao et al. [2023].
However, current agents cannot reliably improve from experience over long deployments.
Although modern agent harnesses can systematically track execution logs, timestamps,
and environment states, they often treat accumulated history as raw text to be retrieved
and inserted back into the prompt.
Simply retrieving raw text does not guarantee behavioral improvement. As interaction
trajectories grow, unmanaged context dilutes relevant signals, increases inference latency,
and degrades model attention Wang et al. [2026d].

Conventional adaptation methods face clear trade-offs. Expanding context windows is bounded
by session limits and suffers from attention degradation over long contexts. Meanwhile, continual
fine-tuning requires substantial computation, risks catastrophic forgetting of general abilities,
and lacks reliable mechanisms to roll back errors Gu et al. [2024], Luo et al. [2025].
Without mechanisms to distill, update, and transfer accumulated experience, deployed agents cannot
retain what they learn. Consequently, they repeatedly commit the same errors, struggle with
conflicting or outdated information, and fail to improve across sequential tasks Cattan et al. [2025], Hu et al. [2026a], Yu et al. [2026a].

Agent memory has emerged as a primary approach to support persistence across sessions and
personalization Chhikara et al. [2025], Packer et al. [2023], Park et al. [2023].
However, despite rapid progress, most existing methods focus on specific engineering implementations
rather than systematic continual learning. Many approaches adopt an information retrieval view,
treating memory simply as an external database or a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) cache
designed to feed past tokens back into the prompt Lewis et al. [2020], Luo et al. [2026].
Furthermore, existing classifications often blur distinct system choices, including where memory is
physically stored, what form knowledge takes, and how memory operations are managed.
Evaluation also remains limited. Many benchmarks primarily test whether an agent can recall or answer
questions over a static past history, rather than whether experience accumulated during deployment
improves subsequent actions under interference and drift Du et al. [2024], Maharana et al. [2024], Wu et al. [2025a].
Moreover, as memory stores grow, unmanaged external memory suffers from retrieval noise, memory
pollution, and negative transfer when task distributions shift Chen et al. [2026a], Zhang et al. [2026a].

To bridge this gap, we propose the framework of Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL).
We argue that addressing the stability–plasticity dilemma does not strictly require continuous
gradient updates to foundation model weights.
Instead, memory itself can serve as an evolving learning infrastructure through which an agent
incorporates feedback, refines strategies, and resolves knowledge conflicts during deployment,
while keeping the base model intact.
In this framework, continual learning operates as a coupled dynamical system. An inner
memory-state loop updates stored knowledge from sequential deployment experience, while an
outer policy-adaptation loop refines memory management policies based on task performance.
By connecting task outcomes back to memory management, MCCL provides a principled route toward
Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), where agents not only accumulate experience but also
improve how that experience is organized and used. We summarize our core contributions as follows.

1. 

A unified taxonomy of memory architecture.
We clarify existing classifications through a three-axis taxonomy:
where experience persists (substrates: contextual, activation, external addressable, and adaptive parametric),
what form it takes (assets: episodic, semantic, and procedural), and
how operations are managed (policies: prescribed, deliberative, and learned).
This separates physical storage from cognitive representation and operational control
(Section 2).

2. 

The memory lifecycle as an engine for continual learning.
We formalize memory dynamics across five core stages: selective formation, structural consolidation,
reactivation and utilization, knowledge revision and selective forgetting, and feedback-driven policy evolution.
This formulation explains how raw interactions turn into generalizable knowledge while mitigating memory pollution and drift
(Section 3).

3. 

A behavioral evaluation framework.
We distinguish retrieval-level checks from genuine continual learning outcomes.
We introduce a four-gate retention cascade (preservation, access, utilization, and effect) to diagnose failure points,
use matched stateful-versus-reset comparisons ( $\Delta P_{t}$ ) to isolate the effect of accumulated memory,
and establish evaluation protocols to measure retention under interference, adaptation under drift, and cross-task transfer
(Section 4).

4. 

A memory scaling law.
We model how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across both non-parametric and parametric memory.
Both share a resource-limited scaling frontier, but differ in how new writes interact with existing content.
This shifts the focus from whether larger memory helps to how experience, capacity, and compute should scale together
(Section 4.3).

In summary, this paper reframes agent memory from a passive storage component into an active learning
infrastructure, focusing on whether an agent can continually learn over time rather than simply retrieve
past records. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 presents the taxonomy across substrates, assets, and policies.
Section 3 details the memory lifecycle as a continual learning engine.
Section 4 formalizes the evaluation framework and memory scaling laws.
Section 5 analyzes applications across digital and physical domains.
Section 6 discusses open challenges in credit assignment, parametric synergy, and trustworthy memory governance.
Section 7 concludes the paper.

Figure 2: Memory-centric continual learning as a coupled dynamical system.
A task stream is executed by the agent and produces outcome feedback.
Experience is organized as episodic, semantic, and procedural assets that
persist across contextual, activation, external, and parametric
substrates. An inner memory-state loop forms, consolidates, reactivates,
and revises these assets, while prescribed, deliberative, or learned
policies govern the corresponding operations. An outer
policy-adaptation loop uses task feedback to update memory management.

## 2 A Unified Framework: Architecting Memory for Continual Learning

Classical continual learning theory has primarily focused on the
stability–plasticity dilemma within model weights, seeking
to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during sequential gradient
updates McCloskey and Cohen [1989], Wang et al. [2024c].
In contrast, foundation-model-based agents decouple computation from
persistent storage, distributing experiential adaptation across physical
media, semantic abstractions, and control mechanisms.
However, existing taxonomies often mix these levels, confusing where an experience
is stored with what form it takes and how it is managed Huang et al. [2026], Zhoubian et al. [2026].
To establish a principled foundation for memory-centric continual learning,
we organize the design space around three core axes, covering
where experience persists, what reusable form it takes,
and how memory operations are managed
(Figure 2).

• 

Memory Substrates (WHERE): Physical Storage Media.
Substrates define the physical medium where experience persists. They govern trade-offs
between write latency, volatility, capacity, and durability, determining whether
experience is held in active context, model activations, external stores, or model parameters.

• 

Memory Assets (WHAT): Cognitive Representations.
Assets describe the form knowledge takes. Independent of physical substrates,
assets balance specific detail against general abstraction, grouping experience into
episodic traces, semantic facts, or procedural skills.

• 

Memory Policies (HOW): Mechanisms for Memory Management.
Policies define the rules for writing, consolidating, retrieving, updating, and
forgetting memories. They span fixed heuristics (prescribed), runtime language model
reasoning (deliberative), and feedback-driven control (learned), determining whether
memory management remains static or adapts over time.

These three axes are complementary dimensions rather than isolated categories.
A concrete agent memory system combines specific choices across all three axes,
such as compiling episodic traces into an external addressable store governed by
deliberative policies powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).
Decoupling these dimensions clarifies that possessing an external substrate
does not by itself yield transferable capability, nor does storing an
episodic asset indicate that an agent has an effective policy to retrieve
and use it.
By formalizing this three-axis architecture, we establish a principled framework
to diagnose where existing architectures succeed or fail under non-stationary streams,
and to compose hybrid systems that support RSI.

## 2.1 Memory Substrates: Physical Foundations for Stability and Plasticity

Memory substrates define where experience persists and how it can be accessed
and modified. Existing taxonomies commonly separate internal from external memory,
or computation-coupled from addressable memory Huang et al. [2026], Zhoubian et al. [2026].
We distinguish substrates by where state physically persists, rather than how it appears
during inference. For example, text retrieved from a database remains external memory even when
placed in a prompt; conversely, offloading the KV cache to disk changes its storage location
but keeps it an activation-level representation. Following this principle, we identify
four basic substrates: contextual memory, activation memory, external addressable memory,
and adaptive parametric memory.

This distinction is independent of memory assets and policies. A substrate
specifies how long experience can persist, how it can be addressed, and at
what granularity it can be updated. It does not, by itself, tell us whether
those updates yield transferable improvement; that depends on the assets
built from experience and on the policies that govern their formation and
use.

Contextual memory.

The most direct memory substrate is the sequence of tokens currently visible
to the model. Thoughts, actions, and observations can be recorded in a shared
prompt so that the trajectory influences subsequent decisions through
self-attention Yao et al. [2023]. Ever-growing traces are replaced with
subgoal-level summaries or compressed reasoning
states Hu et al. [2024], Wu et al. [2025b], and deletion, compression, and
rewriting are exposed as agent actions Zhang et al. [2025b]. These
methods require little architectural modification and offer nearly immediate
plasticity, with relatively high fidelity over short horizons. Their
stability, however, is bounded by the session limit. As trajectories grow,
older observations consume context tokens and degrade model attention.
Even within the supported context window, performance can drop sharply with
sequence length, evidence position, and task complexity Liu et al. [2024], Hsieh et al. [2024].
Summarization and compaction extend the effective horizon but introduce an irreversible,
often lossy selection step Cim et al. [2026].

Activation memory.

A second family compresses history into machine-native states, including
hidden activations, KV caches, recurrent states, and dedicated memory slots.
Hidden states are reused across segments, and KV entries are selectively
retained under a fixed budget Dai et al. [2019], Zhang et al. [2023], Liu et al. [2025c]. Previously computed
internal representations are placed in a retrievable memory
bank Wang et al. [2023], Wu et al. [2022], and latent pools or designated
slots are introduced that can be repeatedly read and
updated Wang et al. [2024e], Kang et al. [2025b]. Compared with textual context,
these states participate in the forward pass at higher bandwidth and need not
be translated back into natural language. Gating, state transitions, and
isolated slots can also confine rapid adaptation to a restricted state
channel, leaving the pretrained backbone unchanged. This efficiency shifts
the capacity cost to runtime memory and limits controllability: activation
memories are tied to a particular model, layer structure, and representation
space, and their contents are difficult to inspect, edit at the level of
individual facts, or transfer across models Kwon et al. [2023].
Fixed-dimensional latent states also face capacity limits as experience
accumulates. Offloading activation states or the KV cache to disk does not turn them
into external text memory, because they can still only be processed as internal
representations by the original model.

External addressable memory.

External memory separates storage from model computation. Experience persists
as independently maintained entries that can be explicitly retrieved and
modified. Implementations range from natural-language logs and summaries to
vector indices, relational tables, knowledge graphs, hierarchical trees, code
repositories, and collections of specialized stores. Observation streams are
combined with higher-order reflections, language-level diagnoses are retained
from failed trials, and information is moved between a bounded active context
and larger archival
stores Park et al. [2023], Shinn et al. [2023], Packer et al. [2023]. Memory
extraction, dynamic organization, and structured retrieval are further
developed in recent
systems Chhikara et al. [2025], Xu et al. [2025], Gutiérrez et al. [2025], Rezazadeh et al. [2024].
This substrate offers a direct route to non-parametric
continual learning: new experience can survive across sessions without
altering the foundation model, individual records can be revised or
versioned, and capacity can grow independently of model size.

Structural separation changes rather than resolves the
stability–plasticity dilemma. External stores avoid catastrophic forgetting
caused by parameter updates, but an old memory can become inaccessible when
its retrieval rank declines, producing a form of functional
forgetting. Summarization, deduplication, and conflict resolution may also
overwrite earlier records or change whether they still count as valid
evidence. As the store grows, redundant, stale, and conflicting entries
raise retrieval noise. Indexing, provenance tracking, and deletion become
more expensive as well. Irrelevant or
conflicting retrieval can be actively
harmful Wang et al. [2024a], Cattan et al. [2025], and current memory
agents do not reliably combine retrieval, online updating, long-range use,
and selective forgetting Hu et al. [2026b], Uddin et al. [2026].

Adaptive parametric memory.

Parametric substrates encode deployment experience in model weights,
detachable adapters, or designated fast parameters. Static pretrained weights
are not sufficient for this category; the defining property is that
parameters can still be updated from experience after deployment. Consecutive
edits are isolated in a side parameter space, and behavior obtained with
visible context is distilled into a model that no longer receives that
context Wang et al. [2024d], Wang et al. [2024f]. Test-time neural memory and
rapidly updated LoRA parameters are used to preserve behavioral effects after
the corresponding evidence has left the active
prompt Behrouz et al. [2025], Ren et al. [2026]. Once internalized, it can be used
during a standard forward pass without external retrieval
and may generalize beyond the
conclusion:
Existing suites occupy different cells of this design rather than a common
scale. Access-oriented histories, incremental ingestion, and sequential
interactive tasks are not interchangeable measurements of the same
construct, and they rarely match context budgets, retrieval depth, or
inference compute. Numerical comparison across papers is therefore
unreliable unless the protocol specifies the behavioral outcome in
Section 4.1, the experience regime above, and the
matched and sequential controls that isolate memory. Scores should be
read within that evidentiary scope, not as a generic ranking of memory
systems.

headings: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
5.2 Temporal Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs
body_start:
Abstract

Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.

Keywords:
temporal knowledge graphs, question generation, synthetic data generation

## 1 Introduction

Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence, often conditioned on a local subgraph and a target answer Chen et al. (2020). Recent database and graph-data research has advanced knowledge-graph querying and temporal graph processing Arenas et al. (2021); Tang et al. (2025). KGQG supports the construction of question-answer pairs and evaluation benchmarks for graph-based question answering Xiong et al. (2022); Guo et al. (2022); Zhao et al. (2024b), and it also helps expand the coverage and diversity of questions over the same graph semantics Ren et al. (2025).

Temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG) extends KGQG from static triples to time-scoped facts. In a temporal knowledge graph (TKG), a fact may be valid at a timestamp, over an interval, or in relation to another event. This temporal structure changes what a generated question needs to express. Two questions involving the same entities and relation may have different answers because one asks “before 2014”, another asks “after 2014”, or one asks for the “last” event before a reference event. Changing the answer field, reference point, or temporal order can change the answer set even when the wording remains fluent, as illustrated in Figure 1. Temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) benchmarks such as CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ make this dependence explicit through questions over timestamps, intervals, and event ordering Saxena et al. (2021); Chen et al. (2023). TKGQG must preserve the temporal condition that determines the answer. We refer to this requirement as temporal faithfulness.

Figure 1: Motivating examples of temporal semantic drift. The prompting baselines are fluent but change the time condition, reference event, answer field, or order cue.

Despite the importance of TKGQG, generating questions that preserve temporal constraints remains challenging. Closely related KGQG methods generate questions through graph encoding, pattern transfer, or reasoning and refinement with large language models (LLMs) Chen et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2024a); Guo et al. (2022); Xiong et al. (2022); Liang et al. (2023); Guo et al. (2024); Zhao et al. (2024b); Ren et al. (2025). However, preserving entities and relations does not ensure that a question retains the temporal conditions governing its answer. As shown in Figure 1, prompting baselines can reverse a time condition or omit a reference event or order cue despite producing fluent questions. We call this temporal semantic drift: the generated question departs from the intended temporal query and may change its answer set.

TKGQG requires addressing three challenges. First, the same temporal facts can support different questions, requiring the intended answer field and temporal rule to be identified from the input graph, constraints, and target answers. Second, similar relation patterns can express different temporal requirements, so pattern reuse must account for temporal compatibility. Third, generation can alter these requirements or disclose the answer, making output validation necessary even when the question is fluent.

This paper studies TKGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question generation problem. Given a local temporal subgraph and an answer set, the goal is to generate one answerable question that preserves the temporal intent of the input instance. Our central idea is to make this intent explicit before question realization and use it to retrieve compatible typed question patterns. Under this view, temporal rules are semantic constraints rather than optional surface cues.

To address these challenges, we propose ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware framework for TKGQG. It constructs a Temporal Intent State to specify the intended question, builds an indexed pattern memory from training questions, and retrieves patterns by temporal compatibility. Typed adaptation binds the patterns to the input graph, while validation and feedback refinement check the generated question. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ show improved generation quality across both datasets and generator backends.

We make the following contributions.

• 

We formulate TKGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and introduce a Temporal Intent State that makes the answer field, temporal rule, reference point, and graph context explicit.

• 

We propose ChronoSynth, which uses temporal intent to retrieve and adapt reusable question patterns, followed by constraint validation and feedback refinement.

• 

We evaluate ChronoSynth on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ, demonstrating stronger generation scores than the compared baselines and examining component contributions, temporal faithfulness, and synthesis efficiency.

## 2 Preliminaries

Temporal Knowledge Graph. 
A temporal knowledge graph is defined as

 $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F}),\quad\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{T},$ 

(1)

where $\mathcal{E}$ , $\mathcal{R}$ , and $\mathcal{T}$ are the entity, relation, and time domains. Each fact $(s,r,o,\tau)\in\mathcal{F}$ states that relation $r$ holds between subject $s$ and object $o$ at timestamp or interval $\tau$ .

Temporal KG Question Generation. 
Given an instance $x=(G_{x},A_{x})$ , where $G_{x}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$ is a local temporal subgraph and $A_{x}$ is the target answer set, TKGQG generates a natural-language question $q_{x}$ . The question should satisfy three requirements: fluency, as a well-formed question; answerability, with $A_{x}$ derivable from $G_{x}$ ; and temporal consistency, preserving the input’s time condition, reference point, temporal order, and answer field. Explicit constraints are supplied as part of the input graph representation. Temporal rules such as before, after, first, and last govern answer selection. They are semantic constraints: reversing a direction or dropping an extremum condition can change the answer set. The full rule inventory is given in the appendix.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Overview

Figure 2: Overview of ChronoSynth. ChronoSynth constructs a Temporal Intent State, retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates and refines the generated question.

ChronoSynth addresses temporal semantic drift by making temporal intent explicit before question realization and using it to guide pattern reuse (Figure 2). It first constructs a Temporal Intent State from the input graph and answers. An indexed pattern memory supplies training questions and typed patterns with compatible temporal requirements. The generator then realizes a question from these patterns and the input evidence, followed by validation and feedback refinement. Memory construction is performed offline; the same index is reused across generation instances and backends. Algorithm 1 summarizes generation using this memory.

## 3.2 Temporal Intent State Construction

To select a compatible question pattern, ChronoSynth must distinguish the intended answer field, temporal rule, and reference point. We represent these choices and their graph context as

 $S_{x}=\langle a_{x},y_{x},\omega_{x},g_{x},e_{x},h_{x},c_{x},\phi_{x}\rangle.$ 

(2)

Here $a_{x}$ is the answer field, $y_{x}$ the answer type, $\omega_{x}$ the temporal rule, and $g_{x}$ the time granularity. The remaining fields specify the focus edge $e_{x}$ , reference entity or event $h_{x}$ , comparison value $c_{x}$ , and graph context $\phi_{x}$ . Together, they distinguish questions that share a relation but ask for different entities, times, or event orders.

The state is inferred from normalized graph records and supplied answers. Explicit constraint records take precedence in determining $\omega_{x}$ . Answer strings and timestamp formats determine $y_{x}$ and $g_{x}$ . Matching the answers against edge sources, targets, and time fields identifies $a_{x}$ and the focus edge. The matched temporal pattern then provides the reference point and graph context. Applying this construction to both training instances and new inputs makes their temporal requirements comparable. Field definitions and rule details are provided in the appendix.

## 3.3 Indexed Pattern Memory Construction

Typed pattern normalization. 
For each training instance $z$ , ChronoSynth replaces instance-specific mentions in its reference question with typed placeholders. The resulting record is

 $m_{z}=(q_{z},\pi_{z},k_{z},\eta_{z}),$ 

(3)

where $q_{z}$ is the reference question, $\pi_{z}$ the typed pattern, $k_{z}$ its primary index key, and $\eta_{z}$ its relation, topology, and surface metadata. Normalization retains the question structure while separating it from particular entities and dates. Anchor, comparison-time, source, and target placeholders preserve distinct semantic roles when the pattern is transferred to a new input.

Memory organization. 
Each record is indexed by fields derived from its Temporal Intent State. The primary key combines the dataset dialect, temporal rule, answer field and type, time granularity, and edge-count bucket. Complementary relation-pattern and graph-shape indexes broaden the candidate pool beyond exact temporal matches; a bounded global pool supplies fallbacks when the combined pool is too small. This organization supports reuse across different entities while retaining the temporal distinctions needed for ranking. The complete index definitions are given in the appendix.

## 3.4 Memory-guided Question Generation

Rule-aware memory retrieval. 
Given $S_{x}$ , ChronoSynth collects candidates from the temporal bucket, relation-pattern, and graph-shape indexes, supplementing them from the fallback pool when necessary. It ranks each candidate $m_{z}$ by a fixed compatibility score:

 $\operatorname{score}(m_{z},S_{x})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\lambda_{j}\kappa_{j}(m_{z},S_{x}).$ 

(4)

Here $\mathcal{J}$ indexes compatibility features, $\kappa_{j}$ their values, and $\lambda_{j}$ their fixed weights. The features measure agreement in temporal rule, answer field and type, granularity, relation, dataset dialect, and graph shape, together with edge-count similarity, reference-token overlap, and reusable placeholders. The temporal rule receives the largest weight because relation-similar instances can require opposite temporal conditions. Relation and graph features provide additional ranking evidence. The weights are fixed before test evaluation. The expanded score and index settings are provided in the appendix.

Typed pattern adaptation. 
For each top-ranked pattern $\pi_{z}$ , ChronoSynth constructs a substitution map $\mu_{x}$ from the current state and graph:

 $\tilde{q}_{x,z}=\operatorname{Adapt}(\pi_{z},\mu_{x}).$ 

(5)

The map binds anchors, comparison values, and focus entities or times to their respective roles. Keeping these roles distinct prevents relation similarity from making a reference entity interchangeable with an answer entity. ChronoSynth discards drafts with unresolved placeholders, literal answer disclosure, or duplicate wording. It retains at most four valid drafts and uses rule-specific default patterns when too few retrieved drafts remain.

Constraint-aware realization. 
The generation context $P_{x}$ combines the Temporal Intent State, input graph and answers, retrieved memory records, adapted drafts, and generation constraints. A fixed language model produces the initial question:

 $\hat{q}_{x}=\arg\max_{q}p_{\theta}(q\mid P_{x}).$ 

(6)

Here $\theta$ denotes the fixed generator parameters. The state specifies the intended temporal choices, while the retrieved questions and adapted patterns provide examples of how to express them. The constraints require a single question without unresolved placeholders or answer disclosure and with the intended order cues, temporal rule, and answer field. Generation does not update model parameters or pattern memory.

## 3.5 Validation and Refinement

After realization, ChronoSynth cleans the output and checks question format, placeholders, answer leakage, order cues, temporal-rule compatibility, and the answer field. Failed checks trigger the original repair or draft fallback, producing the base question $q_{0}$ .

The final stage checks the meaning of $q_{0}$ against the input graph, target answers, and explicit temporal constraints. An interpreter maps the question to a temporal query program, which is executed on the graph. When a supported inconsistency is detected, the resulting feedback guides a targeted revision. A second interpretation must confirm that the revised wording expresses the selected correction and preserves the target answers and explicit constraints. If verification fails or no supported correction is available, the base question is retained. This stage refines individual questions without changing the state construction, retrieval procedure, or memory. Detailed indexing, validation checks, and complexity analysis are provided in the appendix.

## 4 Experimental Evaluation

We compare ChronoSynth with existing generation methods, examine its components through ablation, and assess question quality and utility through human evaluation and downstream QA. Additional analyses and detailed experimental settings are provided in the appendix.

## 4.1 Experimental Setting

Datasets. 
We evaluate ChronoSynth on the graph-converted test splits of CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ Saxena et al. (2021); Chen et al. (2023). CRONQUESTIONS mainly contains timestamp-centered temporal questions. MultiTQ contains more diverse temporal rules and larger local subgraphs. Dataset statistics and additional settings are provided in the appendix.

Baselines. 
We compare
limitations: ChronoSynth relies on a predefined temporal-rule inventory and heuristic state construction, which may require adaptation to new graph schemas or temporal expressions. Pattern reuse depends on the coverage of the training memory, while verification depends on the question interpreter and does not guarantee semantic correctness. Our evaluation focuses on temporal question-generation benchmarks; performance in other domains and languages remains untested.
conclusion: We have presented ChronoSynth, a constraint-aware question generation framework for temporal knowledge graphs. By making temporal intent explicit through Temporal Intent State construction, indexed pattern-memory retrieval, typed pattern adaptation, and validation with feedback refinement, ChronoSynth has reduced temporal semantic drift during question realization. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ have shown consistent gains over parametric trained methods and training-free baselines across multiple backends. Ablation and grouped analyses have shown that pattern memory is the main source of improvement. The local efficiency study further demonstrates its quality–cost advantage over KQG-CoT. Future work will extend the temporal-rule inventory and strengthen temporal-consistency checking for broader query styles.

title: OpenMAP-HIE: Pathology Informed Score-based Diffusion Model for Unsupervised Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Accurate localization of neonatal hypoxic--ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) lesions on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images is clinically important but is limited by scarce expert annotations and substantial variation in lesion appearance. We propose OpenMAP-HIE, a pathology-informed score-based diffusion model for unsupervised HIE lesion localization without voxel-wise lesion supervision. A denoising diffusion model learns the healthy neonatal ADC distribution, while a ControlNet-based conditional branch preserves patient-specific anatomy. Optional population-derived ADC $Z$-map refinement further increased Dice to $0.602\pm0.269$. These findings support pathology-informed score discrepancies as a useful signal for neonatal HIE lesion localization, while highlighting remaining challenges in detecting small and low-contrast lesions.

Abstract

Accurate localization of neonatal hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) lesions on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images is clinically important but is limited by scarce expert annotations and substantial variation in lesion appearance. Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a clinical syndrome of neurological disorder caused by impaired cerebral oxygen delivery and blood flow around the time of birth. It affects approximately 1–5 per 1,000 term-born neonates (Long and Brandon, 2007). Therapeutic hypothermia reduces the risk of death and disability in infants with moderate-to-severe HIE (Silveira and Procianoy, 2015). However, mortality and adverse long-term outcomes, including neurodevelopmental delay and cognitive or motor impairment, still affect approximately $30\%$ – $50\%$ of affected infants (Bao et al., 2025). Accurate identification and localization of HIE-related brain injury are therefore important for quantitatively characterizing lesion severity and for understanding disease progression (Vermeulen et al., 2008; Martinez-Biarge et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2020; Bobba et al., 2023).

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) has been applied for detecting acute HIE-related injury, because abnormalities may appear earlier and more observable than signal changes on conventional T1- or T2-weighted MRI (Triulzi et al., 2006; Bano et al., 2017). Cytotoxic edema restricts water diffusion, typically producing increased signal intensity on DWI and decreased apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values (Onda et al., 2024). ADC maps thus provide quantitative information for identifying HIE-related injury and assessing its severity and prognosis (Bobba et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2025).

Automated localization remains challenging because HIE lesions are often small, multifocal, diffuse, and heterogeneous in appearance. In the BONBID-HIE cohort, more than half of affected neonates had lesions occupying less than $1\%$ of the brain volume (Bao et al., 2025), resulting in severe foreground–background imbalance and poorly defined lesion boundaries. Scanner field strength, acquisition protocol, developmental anatomy, and postnatal imaging time further complicate the distinction between pathology and normal neonatal variability. These characteristics also make manual delineation difficult. Quantitative lesion analysis typically requires experienced pediatric neuroradiologists, often using multi-reader consensus (Bao et al., 2025), but lesion boundaries may remain ambiguous and dependent on reader judgment. Consequently, expert voxel-level annotation is labor intensive and difficult to scale.

Supervised deep-learning approaches have achieved encouraging performance for neonatal HIE lesion segmentation (Bao et al., 2025; Rao et al., 2025; Almansour et al., 2025). However, the scarcity of publicly available neonatal HIE data (Bao et al., 2025), along with the substantial expertise and effort required for annotation, restricts the scalability and external generalizability of these methods. Unsupervised anomaly detection provides an alternative by learning a normative representation from healthy images and identifying deviations in a potentially pathological subject without directly optimizing on lesion labels (Schlegl et al., 2019; Fernando et al., 2021). A common strategy is to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy counterpart of the observed image and interpret the reconstruction residual as abnormality (Schlegl et al., 2019; Wolleb et al., 2022; Wyatt et al., 2022).

However, reconstruction-based anomaly detection must balance pathology removal against preservation of healthy subject-specific anatomy. Excessive corruption or insufficient conditioning may alter normal structures and generate false-positive residuals, whereas strong subject conditioning may reproduce pathological signals and reduce lesion contrast. This trade-off is particularly problematic for HIE because diffusion abnormalities may be subtle, spatially diffuse, and poorly separated from normal neonatal variability (Forbes et al., 2000).

Diffusion models have recently emerged as expressive generative priors for unsupervised medical anomaly detection (Wolleb et al., 2022; Wyatt et al., 2022; Frotscher et al., 2026). Their multi noise level denoising process provides an opportunity to identify deviations from learned normal anatomy other than the residual of a single final reconstruction. However, reliably distinguishing subtle pathological signals from subject-specific anatomy, acquisition-related variability, and stochastic denoising errors remains challenging.

In this work, we propose OpenMAP-HIE, an anatomy-conditioned, pathology-informed score-based diffusion framework for unsupervised neonatal HIE lesion localization (Fig. 1). A diffusion model learns a healthy neonatal ADC prior, and a ControlNet branch incorporates the observed image as a spatial condition to capture patient-specific anatomy. We derive anomaly evidence from discrepancies between the healthy-prior and subject-conditioned score estimates, implemented through their noise-prediction differences (Fig. 2). These discrepancies characterize how subject-specific conditioning modifies the local denoising response of the
learned healthy prior. Both branches evaluate the same noisy input at each noise level, with inputs generated directly from the observed image rather than propagated through a sequential reverse-diffusion chain. This formulation avoids dependence on a final pseudo-healthy reconstruction and the
propagation of errors between reverse-diffusion steps.

To improve pathological specificity, we incorporate a directional prior based on the characteristic ADC reduction associated with
acute HIE (Forbes et al., 2000; Bobba et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2025). Specifically, we retain discrepancies whose corresponding
denoising estimates indicate a higher ADC under the healthy prior than under subject conditioning, and suppress discrepancies
in the opposite direction. The retained responses are aggregated across independently evaluated noise levels using a geometric mean to emphasize directionally consistent evidence. Population-derived ADC $Z$ -maps
(Bao et al., 2025; Rao et al., 2025) are additionally investigated as an optional refinement, while the core framework requires only the subject’s ADC image at inference.

The principal contributions of this work are:

• 

We introduce an anatomy-conditioned diffusion framework that contrasts healthy-prior and subject-conditioned
responses without using lesion masks as optimization targets.

• 

We formulate anomaly evidence through
conditional–unconditional score discrepancies, implemented
as noise-prediction differences and aggregated across independently evaluated noise levels, without requiring a sequential reverse-diffusion chain or a final pseudo-healthy reconstruction.

• 

We incorporate an HIE-specific directional prior that retains score discrepancies consistent with the expected ADC reduction of acute injury, adding pathology informed directionality to the
score-based anomaly representation.

• 

We evaluate the framework on the public BONBID-HIE benchmark using voxel-ranking, lesion-overlap, and surface-distance metrics, and further assess population-derived ADC $Z$ -map refinement as an optional extension.

The proposed ADC-only method achieved improved lesion overlap and surface localization relative to the evaluated unsupervised baselines, while the pathology-informed directional constraint provided substantial gains in lesion localization. Population-derived $Z$ -map refinement further improved overlap and boundary accuracy when population-level normative information was available. The code of this work is available at github.com/OishiLab/OpenMAP-HIE.

## 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Supervised Anomaly Detection

Supervised medical image segmentation has advanced through encoder–decoder architectures such as U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) and UNet++
(Zhou et al., 2019; Rao et al., 2025). Recent HIE segmentation systems have extended to three-dimensional U-Net variants, SegResNet, Swin-UNETR (Hatamizadeh et al., 2021; Almansour et al., 2025), ensembles, and loss functions designed for highly imbalanced lesions (Bao et al., 2025). These approaches learn lesion appearance directly from voxel-wise annotations. In contrast, our framework learns a healthy-image prior and derives lesion evidence without using lesion masks as optimization targets.

## 2.2 Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

Reconstruction-based anomaly detection learns normal image appearance and identifies abnormalities through discrepancies
between an input and its reconstructed counterpart. Autoencoders and variational autoencoders learn constrained representations of healthy images (Baur et al., 2021), while f-AnoGAN combines a GAN-based normal-image model with an encoder for efficient latent inference (Schlegl et al., 2019). Denoising autoencoders instead learn to recover healthy images
from artificially corrupted inputs, where appropriately designed coarse noise can improve anomaly detection while preserving
normal anatomical detail (Kascenas et al., 2022).
IterMask2 combines iterative spatial mask refinement with high-frequency image information to improve reconstruction
of normal tissue and reduce false-positive responses (Liang et al., 2024).

These methods depend on reconstruction errors being larger in pathological regions than in healthy regions. However, normal anatomy may be reconstructed imperfectly, while sufficiently
expressive models may partially reproduce pathological structures. Consequently, reconstruction fidelity alone does not guarantee pathological specificity.

## 2.3 Diffusion Model and Score Method

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) learn a data distribution by progressively perturbing images with noise and training a neural network to predict the noise of removal for the reverse process (Ho et al., 2020). Under the standard Gaussian perturbation formulation, noise prediction provides a parameterization of the score, the gradient of the perturbed data log density with respect to the noisy input
(Song et al., 2021). This connection enables anomaly assessment through both reconstructed images and noise-level dependent noise predictions. Further, compared with GANs, diffusion models generally offer stable training and high-fidelity outputs (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021), making them suitable for learning healthy anatomical priors.

Early diffusion-based methods primarily used pseudo-healthy reconstruction. AnoDDPM uses structured Simplex noise to obscure abnormalities at lower diffusion noise levels while retaining more image context (Wyatt et al., 2022). Wolleb et al. (2022) combined deterministic Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) inversion (Song et al., 2020) with classifier guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021) to generate counterfactual healthy images. Patched diffusion models restrict corruption to local image regions and use surrounding anatomy as contextual information for denoising process, with pseudo-healthy reconstruction based on ensembles of predictions through sliding-window procedure (Behrendt et al., 2024).

Subsequent methods have attempted to restrict restoration to suspected pathological regions to avoid unnecessary modification of healthy anatomy. AutoDDPM first generates an anomaly-likelihood map and then uses masking, stitching, and joint-noise resampling to inpaint candidate abnormalities while harmonizing the reconstructed content with the original image (Bercea et al., 2023). Temporal Harmonization for Optimal Restoration (THOR) instead constructs intermediate anomaly maps during reverse diffusion and uses them as implicit guidance to repeatedly restore presumed healthy regions from the original input (Bercea et al., 2024). These methods are conceptually related to diffusion-based inpainting approaches such as RePaint (Lugmayr et al., 2022), in which known image regions are repeatedly reintroduced during sampling to constrain the generated result.

Masking and local restoration have also been explored in latent diffusion frameworks, with introducing localized latent-space corruptions during
training as proxies for anomalous regions. MAD-AD applies forward diffusion only to randomly selected patches of healthy latent representations during training and jointly learns to reconstruct the clean latent representation and predict the region of corruption. At inference, its mask-prediction head identifies candidate anomalous patches, which are exclusively corrected during reverse diffusion while the remaining regions are preserved (Beizaee et al., 2025b). DeCo-Diff reformulates latent diffusion to learn a direction of deviation from normality. It progressively corrects anomalous latent patches while leaving normal patches unchanged and combines reconstruction discrepancies measured in the latent and image spaces to produce the final anomaly map (Beizaee et al., 2025a).

Rather than producing a final pseudo-healthy reconstruction or iteratively refining a candidate inpainting mask, Aggregated Normative Diffusion (ANDi) derives anomaly evidence directly from deviations within the diffusion process (Frotscher et al., 2026). At each noise level, ANDi compares the analytical reverse-posterior mean conditioned on the observed image with the reverse mean
predicted by the diffusion model, both evaluated at the same noisy input. The resulting voxel-wise squared differences are aggregated across noise levels using a geometric mean. The voxel-wise squared deviations are aggregated across multiple sampled noise levels using a geometric mean. Consequently, ANDi does not require an additional inpainting stage or calculate its anomaly map only from a final reconstruction residual. The population $Z$ -map analysis demonstrates that voxel-wise normative information can substantially improve lesion localization when an appropriate reference population and accurate spatial correspondence are available. However, this improvement introduces requirements that may limit generalizability in routine clinical settings. Constructing a meaningful ADC $Z$ -map requires spatially resolved estimates of the healthy population mean and standard deviation. These reference statistics may vary with postmenstrual age, scanner vendor, magnetic field strength, diffusion acquisition protocol, reconstruction procedure, and preprocessing pipeline. This issue is particularly relevant in neonatal imaging because brain structure and diffusion properties change rapidly during early development.

Voxel-wise $Z$ -maps also depend on accurate alignment between the observed scan and the normative template. Errors in nonlinear registration may generate artificial deviations near tissue boundaries, ventricles, and rapidly developing anatomical structures. Consequently, a $Z$ -map derived from one cohort may not transfer reliably to a population with different demographics, acquisition characteristics, or spatial normalization quality. Site-specific recalibration or construction of a new normative reference may therefore be required before deployment.

For these reasons, we consider the $Z$ -map refinement an optional population-reference assisted extension rather than the principal contribution of the proposed framework. The primary ADC-only model does not require population-level voxel-wise means and standard deviations or the precise nonlinear normalization required to construct a normative $Z$ -map. Although its localization performance is lower than that of the $Z$ -map assisted configuration, it reduces dependence on cohort-specific reference data and may therefore offer greater portability across clinical populations and acquisition settings. Future work should evaluate whether normative harmonization, age-conditioned reference models, or registration-robust population representations can retain the localization benefit of $Z$ -scores while improving cross-cohort generalizability.
